New dyspnoea, reduced exercise tolerance or arrhythmia may reflect rejection or graft failure. [2–4]
- **Remember silent ischaemia.** Cardiac denervation blunts angina; CAV can cause silent myocardial ischaemia/infarction, arrhythmia or graft dysfunction. Risk assessment should use clinical status and transplant follow-up, not absence of chest pain. [2–4]
- **Review immunosuppressants and organs.** Maintain tacrolimus/ciclosporin, mycophenolate and corticosteroids unless the transplant team directs otherwise; plan alternatives if nil-by-mouth. Check blood count, creatinine, electrolytes, glucose, drug interactions/levels and infection or wound-healing risk. Coordinate major surgery with the transplant service. [3,4]

### Intraoperative

- **Denervated physiology.** Resting HR is often approximately 90–110/min. No rapid vagal or sympathetic reflex change in HR with hypovolaemia, pain, laryngoscopy or hypotension; some late reinnervation is possible. Output relies more heavily on venous return and circulating catecholamines. Do not use HR alone as a gauge of volume status or anaesthetic depth. [2,3]
- **Maintain haemodynamics.** Avoid abrupt reductions in preload/SVR (rapid induction, high neuraxial block, haemorrhage), but do not reflexively volume-load a failing graft. Choose GA or regional according to procedure and anticoagulation; add invasive monitoring for major surgery or impaired graft function. [2–4]
- **Choose effective rescue drugs.** Use direct-acting agents (noradrenaline, phenylephrine or adrenaline as appropriate) for hypotension; ephedrine may be less reliable. Atropine/glycopyrrolate may not raise HR; for significant bradycardia, prepare isoprenaline/adrenaline and pacing. ISHLT notes that sugammadex is a reasonable neuromuscular reversal option when appropriate. [3]
- **Asepsis and drug interactions.** Strict infection prevention; ensure appropriate antibiotics. Avoid unnecessary nephrotoxins and check interactions with calcineurin inhibitors (notably macrolides/azoles); immunosuppression can complicate healing and infection detection. [2–4]

### Postoperative

- **Protect graft and organs.** Restart scheduled immunosuppression promptly, verify drug dosing/troughs as indicated, and monitor renal function, electrolytes, glucose, fluid balance and infection/wound healing. Steroid supplementation, if required, depends on chronic exposure and adrenal suppression—not transplant status alone. [3,4]
- **Investigate deterioration early.** Hypotension, arrhythmia, reduced output or pulmonary oedema requires assessment for bleeding/sepsis, rejection, CAV-related ischaemia and graft dysfunction, with ECG, troponin/echo and transplant-team input as indicated. [2–4]

> **Key point:** a transplanted heart can have a normal EF yet no normal autonomic reflexes; think direct-acting vasoactives, careful loading, silent CAV, infection and uninterrupted immunosuppression.

## Selected linked references

- [1. Edwards S, Allen S, Sidebotham D. Anaesthesia for heart transplantation. BJA Education 2021;21:284–291.](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.02.006)
- [2. Choudhury M. Post-cardiac transplant recipient: implications for anaesthesia. Indian J Anaesth 2017;61:768–774.](https://doi.org/10.4103/ija.IJA_390_17)
- [3. ISHLT. Guidelines for the care of heart transplant recipients. J Heart Lung Transplant 2023;42: e1–e141 (intercurrent surgery / Table 14).](https://www.ishlt.org/docs/default-source/standards-guidelines/2022_guideline_ishlt_careofhtxrecipients.pdf)
- [4. AHA/ACC et al. Guideline for perioperative cardiovascular management for noncardiac surgery. Circulation 2024 (Section 6.3.5).](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001285)

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
These are not merely names to memorise. For each, know **who was studied, what intervention was compared, what the primary outcome showed, and what you must not over-extrapolate**. Trials from a non-cardiac surgery population or from acute MI shock do not automatically determine postcardiotomy practice.

| Trial | Topic | Key message |
|---|---|---|
| [CORONARY](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1601564) (Lamy et al., NEJM 2016, five-year follow-up) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | 4,752 patients randomised to off- versus on-pump CABG. The five-year composite of death, stroke, MI, renal failure or repeat revascularisation was **23.1% versus 23.6%** (no significant difference). Use: operator experience, completeness of grafting and patient anatomy are important; off-pump is not uniformly safer. |
| [ROOBY five-year follow-up](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1614341) (Shroyer et al., NEJM 2017) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | In a largely male veteran population, five-year death was **15.2% off pump versus 11.9% on pump**. Use: apparently less invasive strategies can produce inferior long-term outcomes in certain contexts; do not generalise one trial to every centre. |
| [GOPCABE](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1211666) (Diegeler et al., NEJM 2013) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Elderly patients (≥75 years) having CABG: no major difference in primary composite outcomes at 30 days, although repeat revascularisation differed. Use: the operative method is not chosen on age alone. |
| [ATACAS tranexamic acid](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27774838/) (Myles et al., NEJM 2017) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | TXA in coronary surgery reduced blood product use (4,331 vs 7,994 units total) and reoperation for major haemorrhage/tamponade (1.4% vs 2.8%) **but increased seizures** (0.7% vs 0.1%). No statistically significant improvement in its primary composite thrombotic/death outcome. Use: give TXA for blood conservation with a sensible, renal-adjusted dose; seizures are dose/context related. |
| [TRICS III](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1711818) (Mazer et al., NEJM 2017) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | 4,860 moderate/high-risk cardiac surgical patients; restrictive RBC transfusion trigger **Hb 7.5 g/dL** was non-inferior to liberal transfusion for death, MI, stroke and new dialysis (11.4% vs 12.5%). Use: restrictive transfusion is reasonable in stable patients; reassess active haemorrhage and ischaemia individually. |
| [TRICS III six-month follow-up](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30146969/) (Mazer et al., NEJM 2018) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Noninferiority of restrictive strategy persisted for the composite clinical outcome at six months. Use: reinforces that using less blood did not worsen the trial’s specified outcomes. |
| [TITRe2](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1403612) (Murphy et al., NEJM 2015) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Postoperative cardiac surgical patients allocated to different restrictive/liberal transfusion thresholds: no significant difference in the primary serious infection/ischaemic composite, but a mortality signal favoured the liberal group, creating earlier uncertainty. Use: contextualise subsequent TRICS III rather than pretending all cardiac transfusion evidence is identical. |
| [BART](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0802395) (Fergusson et al., NEJM 2008) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Compared antifibrinolytic agents in high-risk cardiac surgery; aprotinin associated with concerning mortality compared with lysine analogues. Use: the choice of antifibrinolytic is a safety decision; policy/regulatory status varies by jurisdiction. |
| [SIRS trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26460660/) (Whitlock et al., Lancet 2015) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | 7,507 patients on CPB randomised to methylprednisolone versus placebo: no reduction in 30-day mortality or major morbidity. Use: routine prophylactic high-dose corticosteroid is not an evidence-based default for CPB-related inflammatory response. |
| [DECS](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2012.14144) (Dieleman et al., JAMA 2012) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | High-dose dexamethasone in cardiac surgery did not significantly improve its composite major-adverse-event primary outcome, despite some secondary differences. Use: avoid translating anti-inflammatory biomarker changes into assured clinical benefit. |
| [TRACS](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2010.1446) (Hajjar et al., JAMA 2010) | Cardiac surgery, CPB and blood conservation | Compared restrictive versus liberal transfusion based on haematocrit after cardiac surgery, finding no significant composite outcome difference in its sample. Use: original transfusion evidence is limited by selected patients, thresholds and statistical power. |
| [IABP-SHOCK II](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24011548/) (Thiele et al., NEJM 2012; follow-up) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Around 600 patients with MI-related cardiogenic shock and planned early revascularisation: routine IABP did **not** lower 30-day or one-year mortality. Use: indications for IABP now focus on selected bridging physiology rather than a universal survival benefit. |
| [DanGer Shock](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2312572) (Møller et al., NEJM 2024) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Selected STEMI-related shock patients: Impella CP decreased 180-day mortality **45.8% vs 58.5%**, but increased severe bleeding, limb ischaemia, haemolysis and renal replacement. Use: selected phenotype and procedure expertise are central; do not apply indiscriminately to postcardiotomy patients. |
| [ECLS-SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307227) (Thiele et al., NEJM 2023) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Early VA-ECMO for infarct-related shock did not improve 30-day mortality (**47.8% vs 49.0%**); more bleeding and vascular complications. Use: ‘more flow’ does not guarantee improved survival and imposes a complication burden. |
| [ECMO-CS](https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.122.062949) (Ošťádal et al., Circulation 2023) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Immediate VA-ECMO versus early conservative management with rescue ECMO in rapidly deteriorating severe cardiogenic shock; no clear improvement in the primary composite clinical outcome from immediate routine ECMO. Use: timely selected rescue rather than automatic cannulation. |
| [SHOCK](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199908263410901) (Hochman et al., NEJM 1999) | Cardiogenic shock, mechanical support and extracorporeal life support | Early coronary revascularisation in MI-associated cardiogenic shock improved longer-term outcomes even though the 30-day primary mortality difference was not statistically significant. Use: definitive correction of ischaemia remains fundamental; support devices are bridges. |
| [CESAR](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19762075/) (Peek et al., Lancet 2009) | VV-ECMO for respiratory failure | Randomised **referral to an ECMO-capable centre**, not ECMO itself in every patient: 63% versus 47% survived without severe disability at six months. Use: supports specialist service organisation/referral but does not isolate the benefit of the pump alone. |
| [EOLIA](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1800385) (Combes et al., NEJM 2018) | VV-ECMO for respiratory failure | Severe ARDS: 60-day mortality **35% ECMO versus 46% control**, P=0.09 for prespecified primary comparison; 28% crossed over from control to rescue ECMO. Use: important signal underpowered/interpreted with crossover, not a definitive positive primary mortality trial. |
| [ERAS Cardiac Society consensus](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamasurg.2019.1153) (Engelman et al., JAMA Surgery 2019) | Recovery and postoperative haemodynamics | Evidence-based expert recommendations for bundled cardiac enhanced recovery, including prehabilitation, opioid-sparing analgesia, glycaemic control and early mobilisation. Use: fast tracking is a pathway, not just extubation speed; this is consensus and mixed-level evidence rather than one mortality RCT. |
| [Temporary epicardial pacing](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.003) (BJA Education 2023 clinical review) | Recovery and postoperative haemodynamics | Not a landmark trial, but a high-yield illustrated teaching publication on pacing modes, threshold checks, capture/sensing and postoperative safety. Use: directly supports practical weaning and the 2026.1 examiner-style pacing question. |
| [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae354) | Recovery and postoperative haemodynamics | High-impact evidence synthesis rather than a clinical trial: perfusion, temperature, neurological protection, circuit safety, anticoagulation and myocardial protection. Use: this is the best contemporary synthesis for the technical CPB sections. |

items.title: References by subtopic
items.body:
## BJA Education reading guide: what to read and why

- **1.** [Principles of cardiopulmonary bypass](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/6/5/176/337119) (BJA Education, 2006). **Start here for the circuit.** Older but exceptionally useful for how venous drainage, pump, oxygenator, heat exchange and cannulation actually work; update practice thresholds from the 2024 CPB guideline.
- **2.** [Anticoagulation for cardiopulmonary bypass: part one — Cartwright & Mundell](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2022.12.003) (BJA Education, 2023). **Highest-yield for heparin, ACT, resistance, rebound and protamine.** Read with the anticoagulation chapter and repeat the protamine-reaction differential aloud.
- **3.** [Anticoagulation for cardiopulmonary bypass: part two — Cartwright & Mundell](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.03.008) (BJA Education, 2023). **Highest-yield for HIT and alternatives to heparin.** Particularly useful for distinguishing expected post-CPB thrombocytopenia from HIT and managing bivalirudin on bypass.
- **4.** [Temporary epicardial pacing after cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.05.003) (BJA Education, 2023). **Essential for pacing, weaning and ICU capture troubleshooting**; directly relevant to recent ANZCA questions.
- **5.** [Anaesthesia for adult cardiac surgery requiring repeat sternotomy](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.10.001) (BJA Education, 2024). **Best set-specific reading for SS_CS 1.15**: CT, previous grafts, emergency access, pre-sternotomy CPB and haemorrhage.
- **6.** [Perioperative care in cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2021.05.008) (BJA Education, 2021). **Best for fast-track/ERAS concepts**, sedation, analgesia, mobilisation and recovery care.
- **7.** [Veno-venous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in severe acute respiratory failure](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.01.001) (BJA Education, 2024). **Practical VV-ECMO overview**: referral, indications, oxygenation/sweep, ventilation and weaning.
- **8.** [Physiology of VV-ECMO, Part 1: terminology, circuits and gas exchange](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2026.03.003) (BJA Education, 2026). **Best newer physiology-focused follow-up**; useful for explaining recirculation, blood-flow versus sweep effects and oxygen delivery.
- **9.** [Management of cardiogenic shock after acute coronary syndromes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2023.01.006) (BJA Education, 2023). **Use for MCS physiology** and the distinction between revascularisation, pressors/inotropy and device-supported circulatory rescue; update device trial interpretation using DanGer Shock/ECLS-SHOCK.
- **10.** [Anaesthesia for minimally invasive cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2018.06.004) (BJA Education, 2018). **Useful for procedure variations, cannulation, positioning and TOE**; supplement with contemporary techniques and local practice.
- **11.** [Pulmonary artery catheterisation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.08.003) (BJA Education, 2024). **Useful for haemodynamic phenotyping** of LV versus RV failure and the limits of filling pressures; read selectively alongside the difficult-weaning chapter.
## ANZCA Blue Book, guidelines, examiner reports and reference texts

### ANZCA and Australasian sources

- [ANZCA — Anaesthesia training program curriculum, Appendix Five](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/all-handbooks-and-curriculums/anzca-anaesthesia-training-program-curriculum.pdf). Source of exact Final Examination learning outcomes; the workbook determines which components belong to Set 13.
- [ANZCA — PG27(A), Guideline for major extracorporeal perfusion](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/professional-documents). Australasian professional framework for safe major extracorporeal perfusion. Local team protocols should operationalise the details.
- [ANZCA — PG46, perioperative echocardiography (2025)](https://libguides.anzca.edu.au/anaestrain/ssu/cardiac). Practice and competency standards for echocardiography use; relevant to diagnosis during difficult separation and ICU instability.
- [Hegde S, Pearse B, Santifort K et al. Goal-directed bleeding management: understanding and implementing viscoelastic haemostatic assays across patient blood management](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1387). Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) 2025, pages 59 onwards. Core source for applying ROTEM/TEG to actively bleeding patients and avoiding indiscriminate product administration.
- [Johnstone L. The perioperative management of lung transplantation](https://airr.anzca.edu.au/anzcacrisjspui/bitstream/11055/1305/5/00_2025_Blue_Book.pdf). Australasian Anaesthesia (Blue Book) 2025. Relevant application of VA-ECMO/CPB versus off-pump support in non-cardiac/thoracic surgery; use as a clinical example, not as a universal transplant protocol.
- [CALS-ANZ: Australasian ANZSCTS/ANZICS cardiothoracic advanced life support](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10692601/). Source for cardiac surgical postoperative arrest management, pacing/shocks and the importance of trained early resternotomy.
- **ANZCA Final Examination chair reports:** 2019.2 Question 1 on DHCA (rationale and physiology); 2016.2 and 2012.2 questions on separation from CPB; 2026.1 Question 7 on epicardial pacing and loss of capture. The reports complement current guidelines but are **exam-expectation sources**, not practice guidelines.
### Current specialty guidelines

- [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP Guidelines on cardiopulmonary bypass in adult cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae354) (published 2025). Primary modern reference for circuit, perfusion flow, temperature, cerebral/myocardial protection and CPB safety.
- [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP Guidelines on patient blood management](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae352) (published 2025). Primary reference for transfusion, antifibrinolytics, haemostasis, protamine, VHA and postoperative bleeding.
- [2024 EACTS Guidelines on perioperative medication in adult cardiac surgery](https://doi.org/10.1093/ejcts/ezae355). Relevant to preoperative antithrombotic decisions and postoperative resumption of therapy.
- [ELSO guidelines and resources](https://www.elso.org/ecmo-resources/elso-ecmo-guidelines.aspx), including the 2021 adult VV respiratory failure guidance. Relevant to ECMO referral, patient selection, circuit and weaning; centres should use their latest approved protocols.
- [2025 ERC Guidelines — special circumstances in resuscitation](https://www.resus.org.uk/professional-library/2025-resuscitation-guidelines/special-circumstances-guidelines). Relevant to arrest in patients early after cardiac surgery, rapid shocks/pacing and expert resternotomy.
- [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/). For current valve-treatment decisions and prosthesis context; the actual cardiac-surgery anaesthetic sequence is explained in Chapters 2–3.
- [Australasian VV-ECMO clinical practice guideline (2026)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12955552/). Australia/New Zealand GRADE guidance on selecting adults with severe hypoxaemic respiratory failure; conditional recommendation and explicit assessment of longer-term neurological and functional outcomes.
- [2025 ESC/EACTS Guidelines for valvular heart disease](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/46/44/4635/8234488). Prosthetic valve selection and postoperative anticoagulation; useful with the surgical-procedure chapters.
### Authoritative textbooks for deeper reading

The guidance and articles above were directly searchable; the following are **recommended authoritative textbooks**, not claims that their entire chapters were available for direct line-by-line verification here:
- Kaplan’s Cardiac Anesthesia — cardiopulmonary bypass, myocardial protection, difficult separation, cardiac surgical haemodynamics and TOE.
- Miller’s Anesthesia — cardiac anaesthesia and extracorporeal circulation sections, ventilation and postoperative critical care.
- Cardiopulmonary Bypass: Principles and Practice (Gravlee et al.) — fundamental perfusion science, pump/oxygenator physiology and myocardial protection.
- Clinical Perfusion for Cardiac Surgery: A Step-by-Step Guide to the Fundamentals (Awad, DiNardo, Huang, Hancock; 2026) — particularly useful for the perfusionist’s perspective and circuit troubleshooting.

**Set 13 curriculum coverage check:** SS_CS 1.1 (Chapter 6); 1.3 (Chapter 2); 1.5 and 1.7 (Chapters 2–3); 1.9 (Chapter 7); 1.15 (Chapter 2); 1.16 (Chapter 9); 1.17 (Chapters 1, 4–7); 1.18 (Chapter 5); 1.19 (Chapter 7); 1.20, 1.21, 1.22 and 1.23 (Chapters 10–11); 1.27 (Chapter 12); 1.28 (Chapter 8); SS_IC 1.39 (Chapter 8); SS_IC 1.62 (Chapter 9). All 18 workbook outcome rows are represented without importing unrelated Set 14 vascular surgery material.

## Evidence and source key (Speak, Retrieve and SAQ content)

- **cpb**: [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/)
- **bb21**: [Blue Book 2021: RV dysfunction pp115–124; VAD noncardiac surgery pp125–134; AF ablation chapter](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/381330f0-81cf-464d-a220-60a7da9dd1a0/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book_2021-Version8.pdf?language=en)
- **bb25**: [Blue Book 2025: Goal-directed bleeding management, pp59–79](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/d8402efb-afbb-4300-8c72-c86edd93edad/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/2025_Blue_Book_PDF.pdf?language=en)

items.title: List the prerequisites for separation from cardiopulmonary bypass.
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: List the prerequisites for separation from cardiopulmonary bypass.
items.a:
- Native circulation: suitable sinus/AV-paced rate, reliable mechanical capture, assessed filling, biventricular function and coronary perfusion; individualise MAP rather than one number.
- Repair/grafts complete, cross-clamp off, reperfusion and de-airing satisfactory; lungs ventilated with appropriate oxygenation.
- Temperature, pH, K/Mg/calcium, Hb/oxygen delivery and glucose appropriate.
- Anaesthesia, monitoring, drugs and rescue CPB ready. Keep heparin adequate until separated; protamine follows team agreement.

items.title: What are the causes of hypotension immediately after separation from bypass?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: What are the causes of hypotension immediately after separation from bypass?
items.a:
- Pump failure: LV stunning or ischaemia, RV failure, valve problem.
- Rate and rhythm disturbance, heart block.
- Preload: hypovolaemia, bleeding, tamponade, tension pneumothorax.
- Afterload: vasoplegia, protamine reaction, anaphylaxis.

> **Closing point:** Use TOE to tell them apart.

items.title: What are the first steps when a patient fails to wean from bypass?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: What are the first steps when a patient fails to wean from bypass?
items.a:
- Stay on bypass and decompress the heart appropriately while maintaining myocardial/systemic perfusion.
- Check rate, rhythm, electrolytes, temperature, ventilation and anaesthesia.
- TOE for LV, RV, valve, air and tamponade; surgeon checks grafts.
- Optimise preload, contractility and afterload; escalate to IABP or ECMO.

> **Closing point:** Diagnose before escalating inotropes.

items.title: How do you recognise and treat right ventricular failure after bypass?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: How do you recognise and treat right ventricular failure after bypass?
items.a:
- Rising CVP, low forward output and systemic hypotension with a dilated poorly contracting RV, TR and septal shift on TOE; PA pressure may rise or fall.
- Exclude coronary air/graft injury, poor protection, protamine reaction, pulmonary hypertension, residual valve lesions and tamponade; TAPSE alone is unreliable after pericardiotomy.
- Assess preload and avoid overdistension; restore rhythm/AV synchrony and systemic coronary pressure.
- Choose inotrope/vasopressor by phenotype, correct hypoxia/hypercarbia/acidosis/airway pressure and add inhaled pulmonary vasodilator. Resume CPB and consider RVAD/VA ECMO if refractory.

items.title: What is vasoplegia after bypass and how is it treated?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: What is vasoplegia after bypass and how is it treated?
items.a:
- Vasodilatory shock after CPB: low SVR and hypotension with preserved/high output, but low-output/mixed shock can coexist.
- Inflammatory NO signalling, receptor hyporesponsiveness, vasopressin depletion and capillary leak; ACEi/ARB, poor function and long CPB increase risk.
- Assess filling and true pressure; noradrenaline and/or low-dose vasopressin with repeated CO/perfusion review.
- Methylene blue is selected rescue after G6PD/serotonergic/PVR checks; angiotensin II/hydroxocobalamin have limited outcome evidence. Steroids are contextual, not automatic.

items.title: How do you set up epicardial pacing for complete heart block?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: How do you set up epicardial pacing for complete heart block?
items.a:
- Complete block requires ventricular pacing; DDD with reliable A/V wires and sinus atrial activity can preserve AV synchrony; VVI for AF/ventricular-only wires.
- Select and justify rate against output, filling and ischaemia; AV interval is individualised, often initially 160–200 ms.
- Confirm electrical and arterial mechanical capture; assess thresholds safely with backup and adequate output margin, commonly ≥2× threshold.
- Lower mV means more sensitive. Asynchronous pacing is reserved for a specific supervised indication such as EMI inhibition; consider R-on-T risk.

items.title: How do you troubleshoot intermittent failure to capture in a pacing-dependent patient?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: How do you troubleshoot intermittent failure to capture in a pacing-dependent patient?
items.a:
- Stabilise perfusion, call help, increase output if spikes fail to capture and have transcutaneous/transvenous rescue ready; do not deliberately stop effective pacing in a dependent patient.
- Patient: temperature, electrolytes/pH, ischaemia, drugs, effusion/tamponade.
- Leads: skin position, fracture/migration, every connection and cable. Generator: power, battery, mode, output and sensing.
- No spikes suggests inhibition/output failure; spikes without QRS are capture failure. Lower mV increases sensing; asynchronous rescue requires monitoring. Confirm mechanical output and arrange definitive specialist pacing.

items.title: What are the effects of protamine on the right ventricle?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: What are the effects of protamine on the right ventricle?
items.a:
- Protamine may trigger pulmonary vasoconstriction, sometimes abrupt within minutes, producing high RV afterload, dilation and systemic collapse.
- Stop protamine; assess TOE/PA pressures and exclude bleeding, ischaemia and anaphylaxis.
- Restore systemic/RV coronary perfusion, correct respiratory/metabolic triggers and use inhaled NO/prostacyclin and inotropy as indicated.
- For refractory collapse, re-heparinise and return to CPB with the team. Slow infusion reduces rate-related hypotension but does not prevent every severe reaction.

items.title: What TOE findings would you look for when weaning from bypass?
items.sub: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.eyebrow: Weaning from bypass and post-bypass failure
items.q: What TOE findings would you look for when weaning from bypass?
items.a:
- LV: filling, global and regional function, ischaemia, air and LVOT/SAM obstruction.
- RV: size, global/regional function, septal position, TR and loading; TAPSE alone is unreliable after open cardiac surgery.
- Valve repair/prosthesis: movement, regurgitation/paravalvular leak and gradients interpreted against flow and rate.
- Aorta/cannulation and pericardial or localised collections; combine TOE with pressures, surgical view and graft-flow assessment rather than relying on one echo number.

items.title: How does an intra-aortic balloon pump work?
items.q: How does an intra-aortic balloon pump work?
items.a:
- The descending-aortic balloon inflates after aortic closure at the dicrotic notch and rapidly deflates before systole.
- Diastolic augmentation increases aortic-root coronary driving pressure; deflation reduces LV afterload, wall stress and oxygen demand.
- Support is modest and depends on native ejection, balloon/anatomy and timing; it is not a guaranteed fixed additional flow.
- Use ECG/pressure or appropriate pacing trigger and compare assisted/unassisted pressures safely. Irregular rhythm complicates timing but is not always prohibitive.

items.title: List the indications for an IABP.
items.q: List the indications for an IABP.
items.a:
- Selected cardiogenic shock or severe cardiac failure awaiting definitive treatment/recovery; routine IABP in revascularised AMI shock has no proven survival benefit.
- Failure to wean from bypass; post-infarction.
- Mechanical complications: acute MR, VSD.
- High-risk revascularisation; LV decompression on VA-ECMO.

> **Closing point:** A bridge to recovery or definitive treatment.

items.title: List the contraindications to an IABP.
items.q: List the contraindications to an IABP.
items.a:
- Moderate/severe AR: diastolic augmentation increases regurgitant flow; mild AR requires individual assessment.
- Aortic dissection, major aneurysmal/anatomical disease or unsuitable severe aorto-iliac disease/access may preclude safe placement.
- Active major bleeding/coagulopathy and infection at access require benefit–risk assessment; uncontrolled tachyarrhythmia can impair performance.
- Review goals and reversibility: a device with no useful destination or no meaningful native ejection may not achieve the intended support.

items.title: How is IABP timing set and what are the errors?
items.q: How is IABP timing set and what are the errors?
items.a:
- Inflate at aortic valve closure/dicrotic notch; deflate rapidly just before LV systole.
- Early inflation opposes ejection; late inflation loses useful coronary augmentation. Early deflation loses diastolic support; late deflation increases systolic impedance.
- Check correct balloon position and size, ECG/pacer/pressure trigger and native rhythm.
- Compare assisted and unassisted end-diastolic and systolic pressures in a brief safe 1:2 assessment, alongside perfusion; a high diastolic peak alone does not establish correct timing.

items.title: What are the complications of an IABP?
items.q: What are the complications of an IABP?
items.a:
- Limb ischaemia (commonest), bleeding and retroperitoneal haematoma.
- Thrombocytopenia and haemolysis.
- Aortic dissection, stroke or embolism, visceral or left arm malperfusion.
- Infection and balloon rupture.

> **Closing point:** Check limb perfusion every hour.

items.title: What types of durable LVAD exist and how do they work?
items.q: What types of durable LVAD exist and how do they work?
items.a:
- Durable continuous-flow devices include older axial HeartMate II and centrifugal HeartMate 3; HVAD persists in existing recipients but is no longer newly implanted.
- Inflow is from the LV apex and an internal outflow graft returns to the aorta; the external driveline supplies power/control, not blood return.
- Flow depends on preload/RV delivery and afterload; little pulsatility makes standard pulse/cuff/oximeter assessment less reliable.
- Uses include bridge to transplant/candidacy, selected recovery or destination therapy, with specialist device and anticoagulation follow-up.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic principles for a patient with an LVAD?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic principles for a patient with an LVAD?
items.a:
- Plan with VAD centre, confirm baseline controller settings, RV/valve function, power/spare batteries and protected driveline.
- Choose arterial monitoring/echo by procedure; Doppler opening pressure approximates MAP only with low pulsatility. Maintain appropriate preload, systemic pressure and low PVR.
- Individualise warfarin interruption/bridging/reversal, rather than automatic bridging for every operation. HM3 aspirin is not universally required after ARIES-HM3.
- Protect CIED function, plan low-flow/suction rescue and laparoscopy effects, assess perfusion rather than pulse alone, and restart antithrombotic therapy when safe.

items.title: What are the complications of an LVAD?
items.q: What are the complications of an LVAD?
items.a:
- Bleeding (gastrointestinal, intracranial) and infection of the driveline.
- Stroke, pump thrombosis.
- Right heart failure and arrhythmia.
- Aortic regurgitation and device malfunction.

> **Closing point:** Bleeding and infection dominate.

items.title: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.q: Compare IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO.
items.a:
- IABP gives modest counterpulsation support, improving diastolic coronary pressure and reducing systolic impedance; depends on native ejection.
- Impella pumps LV-to-aorta and unloads LV; flow is device-dependent, with haemolysis, bleeding, vascular and valve/anatomical limitations.
- VA ECMO supports circulation/oxygenation but increases LV afterload; watch LV distension, differential hypoxaemia and limb injury.
- Select by ventricle/oxygenation and destination. DanGer-Shock supports selected STEMI LV-shock use, while routine IABP and early VA ECMO in AMI shock have not shown survival benefit.

items.title: What are the indications for VV ECMO?
items.q: What are the indications for VV ECMO?
items.a:
- Potentially reversible severe respiratory failure refractory to optimal protective ventilation, appropriate PEEP and prone positioning, or a defined bridge-to-transplant plan.
- Typical referral considerations include PaO2/FiO2 <80 mmHg after optimal care, or severe hypercapnic acidaemia despite safe ventilation. Referral is not automatic acceptance.
- Discuss trajectory early with an ECMO centre; assess frailty, ventilation duration, neurological and extrapulmonary organ failure and reversibility.
- VV supports gas exchange and permits lung protection; VA directly supports circulation. CESAR/EOLIA support selected use with important trial/crossover limitations.

items.title: Compare VV and VA ECMO.
items.q: Compare VV and VA ECMO.
items.a:
- VV drains and returns to the venous circulation, providing gas exchange; any haemodynamic benefit is indirect through improved gases/lower RV load.
- VA drains venous blood and returns arterially, directly supporting circulation and oxygenation.
- VA risks include LV distension/afterload, peripheral differential hypoxaemia and limb ischaemia; both risk bleeding, clot, haemolysis, infection and cannulation injury.
- Anticoagulation is usual but intensity/temporary interruption is individualised by the ECMO team when major bleeding occurs; monitoring and an exit plan are essential.

items.title: What are the complications of ECMO?
items.q: What are the complications of ECMO?
items.a:
- Bleeding and intracranial haemorrhage.
- Circuit clotting, haemolysis, air embolism.
- Limb ischaemia (VA), infection, renal injury.
- Harlequin syndrome in peripheral VA ECMO.

> **Closing point:** Intracranial haemorrhage is the most devastating.

items.title: Which non-cardiac surgeries may need bypass or ECMO support?
items.q: Which non-cardiac surgeries may need bypass or ECMO support?
items.a:
- Tumour with caval or atrial extension.
- Critical airway or tracheal surgery; lung transplant.
- Massive pulmonary embolism; rewarming after severe hypothermia.
- Cardiac arrest (E-CPR).

> **Closing point:** A plan for cannulation and anticoagulation is needed.

items.title: What are the common causes of low cardiac output after cardiac surgery?
items.q: What are the common causes of low cardiac output after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Low output: LV/RV stunning or ischaemia, graft/valve dysfunction and arrhythmia/heart block.
- Impaired filling/obstruction: bleeding/hypovolaemia, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, excessive intrathoracic pressure and LVOT obstruction.
- Vasoplegia is a frequent hypotension cause and can coexist with low output, but is not itself synonymous with pump failure.
- Use ECG, reliable pressure/CO and TOE with surgical review to distinguish mechanisms; do not give fluid or inotropes for every postoperative low BP.

items.title: How do you recognise and treat tamponade after cardiac surgery?
items.q: How do you recognise and treat tamponade after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Tamponade may cause rising CVP, impaired output, hypotension and narrow pulse pressure; a localised postoperative clot may lack classic signs.
- Check drain patency: sudden low output is not reassuring when the patient deteriorates.
- Urgent echo/TOE if needed, without delaying treatment in collapse. Call surgeon and arrange definitive evacuation; loculated clot often needs surgical reopening.
- Resuscitate perfusion and avoid unplanned induction/positive-pressure ventilation; in a suitable recent-cardiac-surgery arrest pathway prepare resternotomy within five minutes while providing circulation.

items.title: How is bleeding managed after cardiac surgery?
items.q: How is bleeding managed after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Call surgeon promptly for ongoing significant drainage or shock; surgical and coagulopathic bleeding can coexist.
- Correct temperature, ionised calcium/pH and resuscitate perfusion; assess drains, Hb, platelets, fibrinogen, residual heparin and viscoelastic/heparinase channels.
- Give targeted fibrinogen, platelets, factor replacement and antifibrinolytic according to defect/protocol; excess protamine and excess TXA can harm.
- Do not postpone necessary re-exploration while repeating products or waiting for a numeric drain threshold; reassess after every intervention.

items.title: What is the incidence and treatment of AF after cardiac surgery?
items.q: What is the incidence and treatment of AF after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Postoperative AF is common, varying with CABG/valve/combined surgery and often peaking around days 2–3.
- Correct hypoxia, pain, electrolyte and volume/perfusion triggers; continue indicated beta-blockade where tolerated.
- Cardiovert synchronously if AF causes instability. For stable patients choose rate/rhythm treatment by ventricular function, symptoms and drug risks.
- Anticoagulation depends on duration, stroke risk, valve indication and postoperative bleeding; arrange follow-up rather than automatically giving OAC from an isolated score or assuming AF is harmless/transient.

items.title: What is the risk of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery?
items.q: What is the risk of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- AKI is common after cardiac surgery, with risk varying markedly by definition and operation; severe/dialysis-requiring disease has high morbidity.
- Mechanisms combine renal medullary oxygen imbalance, inflammation, haemolysis/emboli, low output and venous congestion.
- Identify CKD, diabetes, poor cardiac reserve and long/complex CPB; monitor KDIGO creatinine/urine criteria.
- Use a perfusion/oxygen-delivery/nephrotoxin/glucose bundle. PROTECTION showed reduced AKI with IV amino acids in selected CPB patients; it did not establish universal dialysis or survival benefit.

items.title: Which neurological complications follow cardiac surgery?
items.q: Which neurological complications follow cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Stroke (1 to 3%) and TIA; delirium and cognitive decline.
- Embolic, hypoperfusion and inflammatory mechanisms.
- Strategies: no-touch aorta, MAP targets, avoid hyperthermia, NIRS.
- Delirium screening and avoidance of benzodiazepines.

> **Closing point:** Aortic manipulation is a key embolic source.

items.title: Which factors influence the duration of ventilation after cardiac surgery?
items.q: Which factors influence the duration of ventilation after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Patient factors: age/frailty, pulmonary disease, obesity/OSA, cardiac dysfunction and kidney disease.
- Surgical factors: urgency/complexity, redo, long CPB/cross-clamp, bleeding and complications.
- Anaesthetic factors: drug accumulation, temperature, residual neuromuscular block, analgesia and airway issues.
- Postoperative factors: perfusion/rhythm, gas exchange, neurological state, pain/delirium and staffing. ERAS elements can help higher-risk patients even if early extubation is inappropriate; physiological readiness overrides a clock target.

items.title: What is fast-track cardiac anaesthesia?
items.q: What is fast-track cardiac anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Early extubation within about 6 hours.
- Short-acting drugs and multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia.
- Normothermia, minimal bleeding, haemodynamic stability.
- Now part of enhanced recovery (ERAS Cardiac) with early mobilisation.

> **Closing point:** Do not extubate an unstable or bleeding patient to meet a target.

items.title: What are the issues with redo cardiac surgery?
items.q: What are the issues with redo cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Re-entry may injure adherent RV, aorta or patent grafts and cause catastrophic haemorrhage; dissection adds bypass and bleeding risk.
- Review CT, prior operation and graft routes/function; agree access, myocardial-protection and rescue plans with surgeon/perfusionist.
- Prepare pads, large-bore access, rapid infusion, blood/cell salvage and a primed circuit. Select pre-entry peripheral CPB for high risk, weighing anticoagulation/time/vascular harms.
- During injury control bleeding, resuscitate and rapidly establish safe CPB; anticipate postoperative tamponade, graft/renal/neuro injury and infection.

items.title: Outline the surgical steps of coronary artery bypass grafting.
items.q: Outline the surgical steps of coronary artery bypass grafting.
items.a:
- Sternotomy/access and conduit harvest: LITA, radial and/or vein as planned; protect a radial harvest arm from cannulation.
- On-pump: heparin, validated anticoagulation, cannulation, CPB, cross-clamp and cardioplegia, then distal/proximal anastomoses.
- Reperfuse, de-air, rewarm, check graft flow and ventricular function, separate and only then titrate reversal/haemostasis.
- Place/check wires and drains and reassess with closure. Off-pump uses displacement/stabilisation instead of planned CPB; it may still involve proximal aortic clamping unless an anaortic strategy is used.

items.title: What are the haemodynamic goals for coronary artery bypass anaesthesia?
items.q: What are the haemodynamic goals for coronary artery bypass anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Maintain coronary oxygen balance and diastolic driving pressure, considering LVEDP; avoid tachycardia, hypotension, hypertension and excessive wall stress.
- Preserve appropriate preload/contractility, oxygenation and Hb delivery, and monitor ischaemia with ECG/TOE and graft assessment.
- Continue established beta-blocker unless contraindicated; individualise RAAS medications and antiplatelet interruption with the cardiac team.
- Titrate induction/maintenance to cardiac reserve, prepare support and reassess during sternotomy, CPB transitions, reperfusion and closure rather than targeting one HR for all patients.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic considerations for TAVI?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic considerations for TAVI?
items.a:
- Hybrid theatre with surgical and perfusion back-up.
- Local with sedation or GA; TOE with GA.
- Rapid pacing may be required depending on valve/technique; anticipate transient loss of output and prompt perfusion recovery. Local/minimal sedation is common for transfemoral access; GA/TOE is selected, not universal.
- Complications: vascular injury, annular rupture, conduction block, stroke, leak.

> **Closing point:** Plan for conversion to open surgery.

items.title: Compare surgical aortic valve replacement and TAVI.
items.q: Compare surgical aortic valve replacement and TAVI.
items.a:
- Heart Team selection considers age/life expectancy, valve/access anatomy, frailty, coronary/aortic/other valve disease, durability, reintervention and preference.
- ESC/EACTS 2025 favours suitable transfemoral TAVI in tricuspid AS at age ≥70 and SAVR in younger low-risk patients; age alone is not the whole decision.
- TAVI avoids sternotomy/CPB but has conduction, vascular, coronary-obstruction and paravalvular-leak risks.
- SAVR enables concomitant CABG/aortic/valve surgery and choice of prosthesis, with surgical/bleeding/recovery risks.

items.title: What monitoring is used for a standard cardiac surgical case?
items.q: What monitoring is used for a standard cardiac surgical case?
items.a:
- ECG with ST analysis, arterial line before induction, CVC (± PAC).
- TOE, temperature at appropriate sites and urine output; NIRS/processed EEG and PAC according to risk, technique and the question to be answered.
- ACT, blood gases, glucose and haemoglobin.
- Pacing wires and defibrillator pads.

> **Closing point:** Invasive monitoring before induction.

items.title: How would you reduce anxiety in a patient presenting for cardiac surgery?
items.q: How would you reduce anxiety in a patient presenting for cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Identify the patient’s specific fears, prior experiences, language/hearing needs and understanding; distinguish anxiety from angina, dyspnoea or withdrawal.
- Use clear visual/verbal information, teach-back, a support person, surgery-school/prehabilitation and relaxation, and address thirst, pain and sleep.
- Explain ICU/tubes, analgesia and recovery honestly; agree personal goals.
- Avoid routine heavy sedative premedication. If needed, titrate short-acting anxiolysis with monitoring, considering frailty, OSA, haemodynamics and concurrent opioids; reassess and hand over preferences.

items.title: What are the components of a cardiopulmonary bypass circuit?
items.q: What are the components of a cardiopulmonary bypass circuit?
items.a:
- Venous cannula and reservoir.
- Pump (roller or centrifugal).
- Membrane oxygenator with heat exchanger.
- Arterial filter and return cannula.

> **Closing point:** Blood leaves the right atrium and returns to the aorta.

items.title: How much heparin is given for bypass and how is it monitored?
items.q: How much heparin is given for bypass and how is it monitored?
items.a:
- UFH often starts at 300–400 units/kg, with demonstrated adequate anticoagulation before CPB; the dose alone is insufficient.
- A common conventional ACT target is >480 seconds, instrument/protocol-dependent; repeat at the local frequency, commonly every 20–30 minutes and after changes.
- ACT is affected by dilution, temperature, platelets/factors and drug effects; heparin concentration/AT/validated anti-Xa testing can clarify selected problems.
- Investigate resistance at an inadequate response rather than waiting for one universal >500-unit/kg definition; give additional UFH or AT according to mechanism.

items.title: How do you manage heparin-induced thrombocytopenia for cardiac surgery?
items.q: How do you manage heparin-induced thrombocytopenia for cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Use clinical probability (4Ts: 0–3 low, 4–5 intermediate, 6–8 high), PF4 immunoassay and functional testing in context; antibody positivity alone is not active HIT.
- Acute/subacute A: stop all heparin, use non-heparin anticoagulation and defer elective CPB until functional activity resolves if feasible.
- Urgent surgery: experienced-service bivalirudin protocol; selected plasma-exchange/heparin or heparin-plus-antiplatelet alternatives require specialists.
- Subacute B/remote HIT may permit heparin limited to intraoperative exposure with postoperative platelet surveillance. Bivalirudin accumulates in renal dysfunction; argatroban is a difficult specialist alternative in severe renal failure.

items.title: How does protamine reverse heparin and what is the dose?
items.q: How does protamine reverse heparin and what is the dose?
items.a:
- Cationic protamine binds anionic heparin and removes its AT-potentiating effect; reversal begins rapidly.
- Give only after safe separation/team agreement, slowly and with haemodynamic monitoring.
- Dose to residual heparin/validated titration, often less than a fixed total-administered-heparin calculation; approximately 1 mg per 100 units remaining heparin is the reference relationship.
- Excess protamine itself impairs coagulation/platelets; ACT alone is imperfect for residual heparin. Watch rebound and severe vasodilatory, pulmonary and immune reactions.

items.title: What are the adverse effects of protamine?
items.q: What are the adverse effects of protamine?
items.a:
- Rate-related vasodilation/hypotension, pulmonary vasoconstriction with RV failure, and immune/non-immune anaphylaxis can cause collapse.
- Stop administration, assess phenotype/other causes and support oxygenation/perfusion; use adrenaline for anaphylaxis and pulmonary/RV therapy when indicated.
- Refractory collapse may require re-heparinised CPB. Excess protamine also worsens platelet/coagulation function.
- Prior reaction and protamine-containing insulin matter; fish allergy or vasectomy alone does not prove contraindication. Slow administration/test dosing cannot guarantee avoidance of a severe reaction.

items.title: How does aortic atheroma influence aortic cannulation?
items.q: How does aortic atheroma influence aortic cannulation?
items.a:
- Risk of embolic stroke and dissection.
- Epiaortic ultrasound and TOE grade the atheroma.
- Alternative cannulation: axillary, femoral or innominate.
- No-touch or off-pump techniques.

> **Closing point:** Assess the aorta before clamping.

items.title: What is cardioplegia and how is it delivered?
items.q: What is cardioplegia and how is it delivered?
items.a:
- Cardioplegia reduces myocardial work during cross-clamping, commonly with hyperkalaemic depolarised arrest and temperature control.
- Blood/crystalloid and warm/cold strategies, route and redosing follow the operation/formulation rather than a universal interval.
- Antegrade root/ostial delivery can fail with severe coronary obstruction or AR; vent LV distension.
- Retrograde sinus delivery can help maldistribution/AR but may underprotect the RV and risks sinus injury. Check pressure/distribution, return of activity, K load and function after reperfusion.

items.title: What is the rationale for deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.q: What is the rationale for deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.a:
- DHCA permits a bloodless field during systemic circulatory arrest, particularly arch surgery, while cooling reduces cerebral oxygen demand.
- At approximately 18–20 °C metabolism is markedly reduced but not eliminated. No duration such as 30 minutes is guaranteed safe; risk rises with time and patient/procedure factors.
- Controlled cooling/rewarming and neuromonitoring are essential.
- Antegrade cerebral perfusion can reduce cerebral ischaemia during systemic arrest, often with moderate hypothermia; it is a different strategy from DHCA alone and does not make all organs continuously perfused.

items.title: What are the consequences of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.q: What are the consequences of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest?
items.a:
- Neurological injury: stroke, delirium, seizures, cognitive decline.
- Coagulopathy: platelet dysfunction, fibrinolysis.
- Arrhythmias on cooling and rewarming; renal and visceral injury.
- Hyperglycaemia and inflammatory response.

> **Closing point:** Not the same as cardioplegia or ECMO.

items.title: What are the problems with rewarming after bypass?
items.q: What are the problems with rewarming after bypass?
items.a:
- Rewarm slowly; outflow temperature at most 37 °C.
- Cerebral hyperthermia and gas emboli.
- After-drop, shivering, vasodilation and bleeding.
- Target nasopharyngeal 36 to 37 °C before separation.

> **Closing point:** Avoid overshooting.

items.title: What are the cardiac effects of hypothermia?
items.q: What are the cardiac effects of hypothermia?
items.a:
- Bradycardia and conduction slowing (J waves).
- Ventricular irritability/VF risk rises with deep cooling; there is no deterministic threshold at which every heart fibrillates.
- Reduced oxygen demand and better protection.
- Arrhythmias on rewarming.

> **Closing point:** Cooling protects but makes the heart unstable.

items.title: Which factors determine the success of cardioversion in AF?
items.q: Which factors determine the success of cardioversion in AF?
items.a:
- Duration of AF and left atrial size.
- Underlying structural disease and reversible causes.
- Electrolytes, amiodarone pre-treatment.
- Biphasic device-appropriate energy, good pad contact and either effective anterior-posterior or anterolateral positioning; R-wave synchronisation prevents an unsafe shock.

> **Closing point:** Answer both success and safety.

items.title: What makes cardioversion safe?
items.q: What makes cardioversion safe?
items.a:
- For elective AF >24 hours/uncertain onset, ESC 2024 requires ≥3 weeks effective anticoagulation or TOE exclusion of thrombus with periprocedural anticoagulation; most require ≥4 weeks afterwards.
- Long-term therapy follows stroke/valve risk despite successful conversion; verify adherence and device/valve-specific eligibility.
- Assess airway/aspiration, cardiac disease, electrolytes and digoxin toxicity; consent and provide short monitored anaesthesia with capnography and rescue equipment.
- Confirm R-wave synchronisation and oxygen/fire safety; anticipate hypotension, brady/asystole and VF. Unstable AF needs urgent cardioversion without delaying for elective anticoagulation.

items.title: What is the role of cardioversion for intraoperative arrhythmias?
items.q: What is the role of cardioversion for intraoperative arrhythmias?
items.a:
- For haemodynamically significant organised tachyarrhythmia, synchronised cardioversion is appropriate; VF/pulseless VT requires unsynchronised defibrillation and resuscitation.
- Treat oxygenation, perfusion, electrolyte/ischaemic and surgical triggers in parallel, because recurrence is likely if the cause persists.
- An already anaesthetised patient still needs adequate depth, monitoring and a safe shock/pacing plan.
- Do not shock sinus tachycardia as a compensatory automatic rhythm; stable arrhythmias require diagnosis and considered drug/rhythm treatment rather than a universal electrical-first rule.

items.title: What is internal defibrillation?
items.q: What is internal defibrillation?
items.a:
- Sterile paddles applied directly to the heart with an open chest.
- 10 to 20 J biphasic.
- Lower energy than external shocks is used because transthoracic impedance is bypassed; use the internal-paddle device specification, not an assumed universally safe energy.
- Used in theatre or after resternotomy.

> **Closing point:** Open chest, low energy.

items.title: What changes in the arrest algorithm after cardiac surgery?
items.q: What changes in the arrest algorithm after cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Use the trained recent-cardiac-surgery pathway in an appropriate monitored setting, calling surgeon/perfusionist immediately.
- Witnessed VF/pVT: up to three sequential shocks within the first minute; start CPR if unsuccessful or shocks not immediately available. Brady/asystole: immediate wire pacing, but CPR within one minute if ineffective.
- Prepare trained resternotomy, generally within five minutes when indicated, while maintaining circulation.
- Full-dose adrenaline is not routine in the specialised pathway; follow its drug protocol. If the specialised pathway/team is absent, give standard ALS without delay.

items.title: What are the major complications of percutaneous coronary intervention?
items.q: What are the major complications of percutaneous coronary intervention?
items.a:
- Coronary perforation and tamponade.
- Vessel closure, no-reflow and infarction.
- Arrhythmia, access-site bleeding and retroperitoneal haematoma.
- Contrast reaction, AKI and stroke.

> **Closing point:** Know them before the call comes.

items.title: How do you manage coronary perforation?
items.q: How do you manage coronary perforation?
items.a:
- Immediately alert operator, resuscitate perfusion and assess echo/haemodynamics for tamponade while preparing blood and surgical help.
- The operator may use balloon tamponade, covered stent or embolisation according to perforation anatomy; urgent pericardial drainage treats tamponade.
- Coordinate heparin reversal with the interventional team, balancing haemorrhage against wire/device/stent thrombosis; it is not an automatic isolated first action in every perforation.
- Persistent haemorrhage or instability requires surgical rescue. Reassess drainage, perfusion and reaccumulation after apparent control.

items.title: What are the complications of TAVI?
items.q: What are the complications of TAVI?
items.a:
- Vascular injury, annular rupture, coronary obstruction.
- Aortic dissection, valve embolisation, paravalvular leak.
- Conduction block needing a pacemaker.
- Stroke and tamponade.

> **Closing point:** Pre-agree emergency vascular, pacing, surgical/perfusion and airway rescue pathways; the exact backup arrangements depend on local service and case risk.

items.title: What are the complications of AF ablation?
items.q: What are the complications of AF ablation?
items.a:
- Tamponade (about 1%).
- Stroke or air embolism.
- Atrio-oesophageal fistula (delayed).
- Phrenic nerve injury and pulmonary vein stenosis.

> **Closing point:** Rates vary by technology and centre. Delayed fever/chest pain/neurological signs may signal atrio-oesophageal fistula: urgent specialist CT assessment, avoiding routine oesophageal instrumentation.

items.title: Why is the catheter laboratory a high-risk location for anaesthesia?
items.q: Why is the catheter laboratory a high-risk location for anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Remote site with limited access and radiation.
- Anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy.
- Unfamiliar team and equipment.
- Need for surgical and perfusion back-up.

> **Closing point:** Plan for crisis before the case starts.

items.title: How does off-pump CABG differ, and what is your first response to hypotension during cardiac displacement?
items.q: How does off-pump CABG differ, and what is your first response to hypotension during cardiac displacement?
items.a:
- Beating-heart displacement and local stabilisation replace planned CPB/cardioplegia; proximal aortic clamping may still be used unless specifically anaortic.
- Displacement may compress RV/venous return, distort filling and induce ischaemia; alert the surgeon and release/reduce the manoeuvre immediately.
- Use TOE/ECG/pressure to assess loading, rhythm and ischaemia; support coronary pressure and give assessed volume only when helpful.
- Prepare controlled CPB conversion if instability persists, before profound collapse.

items.title: Outline the operative steps of mitral valve replacement.
items.q: Outline the operative steps of mitral valve replacement.
items.a:
- Access, heparinisation, cannulation/CPB, cross-clamp and cardioplegia, then atrial exposure of the valve.
- Excise diseased tissue as required, preserve chordal continuity where feasible, size/seat the prosthesis and check unrestricted movement.
- Close the atrium, de-air, reperfuse, rewarm and separate.
- TOE checks prosthesis, gradients/leak, biventricular function, new regional ischaemia and LVOT; anticipate pacing and prosthesis-specific anticoagulation.

items.title: Contrast anaesthetic haemodynamic goals for mitral stenosis and regurgitation.
items.q: Contrast anaesthetic haemodynamic goals for mitral stenosis and regurgitation.
items.a:
- MS: avoid tachycardia, preserve sinus/AV contribution, maintain appropriate preload without pulmonary oedema and support systemic perfusion.
- MR: preserve forward flow/contractility, avoid marked bradycardia and excessive SVR; rate/preload are individualised.
- For both, protect RV function by avoiding hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis and excessive airway pressures.
- Severity, acute versus chronic lesion, ventricular reserve and pulmonary hypertension determine actual targets.

items.title: Why can LV failure or LVOT obstruction appear after mitral surgery?
items.q: Why can LV failure or LVOT obstruction appear after mitral surgery?
items.a:
- After MR correction the LV loses a low-impedance outlet and faces greater effective afterload; afterload mismatch can reveal impaired contractility.
- Exclude circumflex injury, coronary air, inadequate protection, prosthetic/residual lesions and RV failure on TOE.
- After repair, SAM may produce dynamic LVOT obstruction: support filling/afterload, reduce excessive inotropy/tachycardia and seek surgical review if persistent.
- Choose treatment from the mechanism; more inotrope can worsen dynamic obstruction.

items.title: Outline the main steps of type A dissection repair.
items.q: Outline the main steps of type A dissection repair.
items.a:
- Urgent assessment identifies rupture/tamponade, AR, coronary and branch malperfusion; prepare blood and expert team.
- Heparinise/cannulate with confirmed true-lumen perfusion, commence CPB, cool, vent/protect myocardium.
- Resect the tear/diseased ascending segment and graft; root/valve and hemiarch/arch extension depend on pathology, often with systemic arrest and cerebral perfusion.
- Reperfuse, de-air, rewarm and check repair, ventricular function and cerebral/renal/visceral/limb perfusion before and after separation.

items.title: How do aortic dissection or atheroma alter your cannulation plan?
items.q: How do aortic dissection or atheroma alter your cannulation plan?
items.a:
- Review imaging and use epiaortic ultrasound/TOE appropriately; TOE does not visualise every ascending-aortic segment.
- Avoid plaque disruption and false-lumen perfusion. Consider axillary/innominate or imaging-guided central inflow; femoral may be needed urgently but risks retrograde malperfusion.
- Compare pressures and bilateral cerebral trends and inspect the true lumen during initiation.
- High line pressure or unilateral cerebral change demands immediate circuit/cannula/anatomical assessment, not simply more pump pressure.

items.title: What do you do for a sudden unilateral NIRS fall during arch or minimally invasive cardiac surgery?
items.q: What do you do for a sudden unilateral NIRS fall during arch or minimally invasive cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Tell surgeon/perfusionist and assess actual patient perfusion while checking sensor/contact and comparing baseline.
- Review cannula/endoballoon position, arch-vessel obstruction and selective cerebral perfusion; compare arm pressures.
- Check flow, MAP, oxygenation, Hb and CO2, particularly for a bilateral fall.
- Correct the demonstrated cause promptly; NIRS is a contextual trend, not a direct guarantee of cerebral flow or an isolated transfusion trigger.

items.title: Give your structured response to a major CPB circuit emergency.
items.q: Give your structured response to a major CPB circuit emergency.
items.a:
- Announce/call team, verify event and protect systemic/cerebral perfusion and continuing anaesthesia.
- Low reservoir/drainage: inspect loss, kinks/cannula/air lock and excessive vacuum; avoid pumping air from an empty reservoir.
- High arterial pressure/asymmetry: consider obstruction, wall impingement, dissection/false-lumen perfusion; do not force unsafe flow.
- Check gas supply versus oxygenator failure; isolate air delivery and coordinate trained de-airing/exchange/native or alternative support under the rehearsed device protocol.

items.title: How do you prevent awareness during CPB?
items.q: How do you prevent awareness during CPB?
items.a:
- Make anaesthetic delivery an explicit team check before, during and after bypass.
- Use a reliable IV route reaching the patient/circuit or compatible volatile delivery via the oxygenator with appropriate monitoring/scavenging.
- The machine vaporiser being on does not prove drug delivery on full CPB; verify line/circuit transitions and pump interruptions.
- Account for dilution, temperature, binding and altered clearance; interpret processed EEG in context and continue analgesia/appropriate block.

items.title: Why can ACT mislead you about heparin effect on bypass?
items.q: Why can ACT mislead you about heparin effect on bypass?
items.a:
- ACT reflects whole-blood clotting, not solely heparin concentration; instrument/activator matters.
- Temperature, dilution, platelet/factor deficiency and drugs alter ACT; high factor VIII/fibrinogen may create apparent resistance.
- Validate dose/delivery/sample and consider heparin concentration, AT activity and appropriately validated anti-Xa; laboratory turnaround/CPB-range assay limits matter.
- After reversal a normal ACT does not exclude residual heparin; heparinase comparison can clarify bleeding, while excess protamine can itself prolong clotting.

items.title: Explain the haematological and inflammatory effects of CPB.
items.q: Explain the haematological and inflammatory effects of CPB.
items.a:
- Artificial surfaces, blood–air contact and tissue injury activate complement, platelets, coagulation, leukocytes and fibrinolysis.
- Dilution, consumption, hypothermia, residual heparin and platelet dysfunction promote bleeding; thrombosis/microembolism may coexist.
- Shear/haemolysis releases free Hb/iron, injuring kidney and scavenging NO.
- Cytokines/endothelial-glycocalyx injury cause leak, oedema, microcirculatory dysfunction and vasoplegia; use adequate perfusion and targeted haemostasis rather than empirical products for all abnormalities.

items.title: Evaluate TXA in cardiac surgery.
items.q: Evaluate TXA in cardiac surgery.
items.a:
- Lysine analogue inhibits plasminogen–fibrin interaction and fibrinolysis.
- Reduces bleeding, transfusion and re-exploration risk as part of patient blood management.
- Use a validated cardiac/renal-adjusted regimen; high exposure increases seizures, especially with renal dysfunction, and wrong-route administration is catastrophic.
- It does not correct surgical bleeding or replace targeted fibrinogen/platelet/factor treatment; do not import obstetric/hip dosing as a universal cardiac regimen.

items.title: What is ischaemia–reperfusion injury in cardiac surgery?
items.q: What is ischaemia–reperfusion injury in cardiac surgery?
items.a:
- Reoxygenation after ischaemia generates oxidants, calcium/mitochondrial dysfunction, endothelial/microvascular injury and inflammation.
- Consequences include myocardial stunning, arrhythmias, oedema/no-reflow and renal/pulmonary/neurological injury.
- Limit ischaemic time, provide effective distributed myocardial protection, avoid distension and correct oxygen-delivery/metabolic disturbances during reperfusion.
- Allow recovery on CPB when needed but actively exclude graft/valve obstruction or persistent ischaemia; stunning is not a diagnosis of convenience.

items.title: What is ischaemic preconditioning, and how strong is its clinical role?
items.q: What is ischaemic preconditioning, and how strong is its clinical role?
items.a:
- Brief sublethal ischaemic episodes activate endogenous protective signalling before a larger insult.
- Remote conditioning applies the stimulus elsewhere, commonly limb cuff cycles; volatile drugs may affect related pathways.
- Mechanistic and small-study effects have not translated into consistent major-outcome benefit in large cardiac trials.
- It is not a universal routine requirement or a reason to guarantee volatile-agent superiority; good protection and safe anaesthetic delivery remain essential.

items.title: What determines oxygenation and CO2 clearance during VV ECMO?
items.q: What determines oxygenation and CO2 clearance during VV ECMO?
items.a:
- Effective circuit blood flow relative to native CO, Hb/oxygen content, membrane function, recirculation and native lung function determine oxygenation.
- Increasing CO/consumption in fever/sepsis can reduce saturation despite unchanged circuit settings.
- Sweep gas flow mainly controls CO2; delivered oxygen fraction is separate. Avoid abrupt large PaCO2 correction.
- VV does not directly replace cardiac output; maintaining adequate oxygen delivery/perfusion matters more than saturation alone.

items.title: How do you assess membrane lung dysfunction?
items.q: How do you assess membrane lung dysfunction?
items.a:
- Confirm oxygen/gas supply, delivered fraction, sweep and actual blood flow before diagnosing membrane failure.
- Trend pre/post-membrane gases/oxygen-content transfer, pressure gradient or resistance and visible clot/haemolysis/consumption.
- At FdO2 1.0, falling post-membrane PO2 or low transfer can warn of failure; interpret against flow/inlet content and device baseline.
- Prepare trained circuit/membrane exchange when needed. Transfer = flow × oxygen-content difference, with consistent units; it is not total systemic delivery.

items.title: What causes drainage chatter or recirculation in VV ECMO?
items.q: What causes drainage chatter or recirculation in VV ECMO?
items.a:
- Chatter suggests intermittent drainage limitation: excessive RPM, low volume, IVC collapse, kink/migration or high thoracic/abdominal pressure.
- Reduce unsafe suction with the ECMO team and correct the cause; fluid is appropriate for underfilling rather than every chatter event.
- Recirculation returns oxygenated blood straight to drainage; assess configuration, cannula tips and return-jet direction with imaging.
- Increasing RPM may worsen both problems; high inlet saturation can support recirculation but is not specific.

items.title: What changed in HeartMate 3 antithrombotic teaching after ARIES-HM3?
items.q: What changed in HeartMate 3 antithrombotic teaching after ARIES-HM3?
items.a:
- In HM3 patients on VKA, aspirin avoidance was non-inferior for the trial’s haemocompatibility endpoint and reduced nonsurgical bleeding.
- Do not teach aspirin as mandatory for every HM3 recipient solely because of the pump.
- Verify other vascular indications and the device-centre regimen; VKA/INR targets remain individualised, commonly 2–3 for HM3.
- This does not establish routine DOAC substitution or automatic avoidance of bridging/reversal; surgery decisions balance device, thrombosis and bleeding risk.

items.title: How do you recognise cardiac arrest in a continuous-flow LVAD patient?
items.q: How do you recognise cardiac arrest in a continuous-flow LVAD patient?
items.a:
- Absence of a palpable pulse alone is not arrest. Assess responsiveness, breathing, colour/capillary refill, MAP, ETCO2 and device function.
- If perfusion is inadequate, start appropriate resuscitation including compressions while another rescuer checks power, controller, driveline and alarms.
- Contact the VAD centre, treat arrhythmia and reversible causes and use echo where available without delaying support.
- Preserved perfusion despite an abnormal rhythm requires urgent management but does not automatically need compressions; AHA 2025 emphasises the perfusion distinction.

items.title: What belongs in a routine cardiac ICU handover and plan?
items.q: What belongs in a routine cardiac ICU handover and plan?
items.a:
- Operation/residual lesions, CPB/clamp times, TOE/graft result, airway/access, blood products/heparin/protamine and major events.
- Rhythm/pacing dependence/settings, vasoactive/inhaled support, perfusion targets, drains/output/patency and bleeding rescue triggers.
- Ventilation/analgesia/sedation/extubation plan, temperature/gases/electrolytes/glucose, neurological and renal monitoring.
- Medication/antithrombotic restart, infection/VTE prevention when safe, delirium screening, mobilisation/nutrition and escalation contacts.

items.title: How can a post-cardiac-surgery pericardial effusion present six weeks later?
items.q: How can a post-cardiac-surgery pericardial effusion present six weeks later?
items.a:
- It may be indolent: dyspnoea, orthopnoea, fatigue, poor exercise tolerance or inflammatory pain/fever, not only acute shock.
- Tachycardia/JVP elevation can progress to low output, narrow pulse pressure, syncope, oliguria and altered consciousness.
- Loculated postoperative clot may lack classic tamponade/echo signs; assess distribution and filling/output, not size alone.
- Deteriorating perfusion or clinical tamponade requires urgent drainage/surgical review, with resuscitation and careful induction planning.

items.title: Give a balanced answer to the 2007 aprotinin debate.
items.q: Give a balanced answer to the 2007 aprotinin debate.
items.a:
- Benefit: randomised/meta-analytic evidence of less bleeding/transfusion in CPB surgery, especially high-risk procedures.
- Concern: renal/cardiovascular signals in observational data, plus allergy/re-exposure and cost/alternatives.
- Explain confounding by indication without dismissing safety signals; small efficacy trials cannot exclude all uncommon harm.
- Conclude by balancing absolute benefit and risk. BART/current restricted authorisation came later and must be separated from what was known in 2007.

items.title: Identify the A–F landmarks on the 2022.1 IABP trace.
items.q: Identify the A–F landmarks on the 2022.1 IABP trace.
items.a:
- A: systolic peak at the beginning; the report accepts assisted/unassisted systole because of the illustrated commencement. B: dicrotic notch/aortic closure.
- C: unassisted end-diastolic pressure; D: diastolic augmentation; E: assisted end-diastolic pressure; F: assisted systolic peak.
- Explain the two mechanisms: increased diastolic coronary driving pressure and reduced pre-systolic afterload.
- Use the original trace in SAQ8 for rehearsal; the letters are figure-specific, not universal device labels.

items.title: Explain VV versus V-V, VV-V, V-AV and dual-lumen nomenclature.
items.q: Explain VV versus V-V, VV-V, V-AV and dual-lumen nomenclature.
items.a:
- Mode describes support: VV gas exchange; VA direct circulatory/respiratory support.
- Configuration uses a hyphen at the membrane lung: drainage left, return right. V-V has one venous drainage and one venous return cannula.
- VV-V has two venous drainage cannulae and one return; V-AV returns to arterial and venous sites, for selected combined/upper-body oxygenation problems.
- (dl)V-V uses a dual-lumen cannula; state actual sites, tip/jet position and purpose as well as letters.

items.title: Outline the surgical steps of aortic valve replacement.
items.q: Outline the surgical steps of aortic valve replacement.
items.a:
- Access, heparinisation, cannulation/CPB, cross-clamp and myocardial protection, then aortotomy.
- Excise/decalcify the diseased valve, size the annulus and implant the selected prosthesis, protecting coronary ostia and conduction tissue.
- Close the aorta, de-air, reperfuse/rewarm and separate using the standard readiness checklist.
- TOE checks seating, leaflet motion, gradients in flow context, paravalvular leak, ventricular/regional function and aortic integrity; assess pacing, haemostasis and postoperative anticoagulation.

items.title: How is VV ECMO weaned and how does this differ from VA ECMO?
items.q: How is VV ECMO weaned and how does this differ from VA ECMO?
items.a:
- Demonstrate recovering lung function with acceptable work of breathing, gases and haemodynamics on safe ventilator support.
- Reduce sweep/delivered gas oxygen and perform a supervised off-sweep assessment according to centre protocol while maintaining adequate circuit blood flow to avoid thrombosis.
- Do not assume reducing VV pump flow is the same as testing native cardiac recovery on VA support. VA weaning uses controlled flow reduction with echo and haemodynamic assessment.
- Decannulate with an anticoagulation, haemostasis, vascular and respiratory rescue plan; failure prompts reassessment rather than forcing a time target.

items.title: What do you do for an IABP patient with poor augmentation and a cold limb?
items.q: What do you do for an IABP patient with poor augmentation and a cold limb?
items.a:
- Treat threatened limb as an emergency: assess Doppler pulses, colour, temperature, refill, motor/sensation and call cardiac/vascular teams urgently.
- Consider access occlusion/dissection/thromboembolism or bleeding; arrange imaging and removal/revascularisation or alternative support without delaying a threatened limb.
- Simultaneously assess worsening shock, rhythm, trigger/timing, balloon position/volume and gas delivery. A high augmentation peak alone is not a perfusion endpoint.
- Blood in helium tubing suggests rupture: stop pumping and obtain urgent specialist removal per protocol. Reassess systemic and limb perfusion repeatedly.

items.title: What are the haemodynamic hazards of off-pump CABG, and when should the team convert to CPB?
items.q: What are the haemodynamic hazards of off-pump CABG, and when should the team convert to CPB?
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: CABG Part 1, 2026 corrected proof; full text read via ClinicalKey](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S205853492600079X) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- The stabiliser immobilises a target while **heart elevation/rotation** can impair RV filling, venous return, LV ejection and provoke MR or regional ischaemia; lateral and inferior targets are often least tolerated.
- **First action in collapse:** tell the surgeon to release/reduce displacement, restore preload and coronary perfusion, check ST changes and TOE; use an intracoronary shunt if appropriate. Avoid indiscriminate large fluid boluses.
- Convert to CPB for **sustained low output, refractory ischaemia or arrhythmia, unsafe target exposure or incomplete revascularisation** despite corrective manoeuvres.
- Off-pump does **not** inherently mean anaortic: side-biting clamps for proximal graft anastomoses can still embolise plaque. A specifically **anaortic/no-touch** strategy avoids aortic instrumentation.

> **Closing point:** In off-pump hypotension, release mechanical displacement before simply increasing drugs.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: What did CORONARY and ROOBY show about on-pump versus off-pump CABG?
