items.q: What did CORONARY and ROOBY show about on-pump versus off-pump CABG?
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [BJA Education: CABG Part 1, 2026 corrected proof; full text read via ClinicalKey](https://www-clinicalkey-com-au.ezproxy.anzca.edu.au/#!/content/journal/1-s2.0-S205853492600079X); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **CORONARY (five-year follow-up):** in 4,752 randomised CABG patients, the composite of death, stroke, MI, renal failure or repeat revascularisation was **23.1% off-pump vs 23.6% on-pump**, without a significant difference.
- **ROOBY (five-year follow-up):** in a predominantly male veteran population, death was **15.2% off-pump vs 11.9% on-pump**, favouring on-pump in that setting.
- **Interpretation:** surgeon/centre experience, target anatomy, complete revascularisation and aortic manipulation matter. Off-pump is **not universally better**; trial findings should not be extrapolated uncritically to every centre.

> **Closing point:** Avoid claiming that eliminating CPB always reduces important long-term outcomes.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: Calculate indexed oxygen delivery on CPB and explain why a normal MAP can mislead.
items.q: Calculate indexed oxygen delivery on CPB and explain why a normal MAP can mislead.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **Indexed DO₂ (mL/min/m²) = pump flow index (L/min/m²) × arterial O₂ content (mL/dL) × 10**.
- **CaO₂ ≈ 1.34 × Hb (g/dL) × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂ (mmHg)**. Hb-bound O₂ dominates.
- At **Hb 8 g/dL, SaO₂ 100%, pump flow index 2.4 L/min/m²**, CaO₂ ≈ 10.7 mL/dL and **indexed DO₂ ≈ 257 ≈ 260 mL/min/m²** (before the small dissolved fraction).
- Normothermic goal-directed perfusion protocols commonly target about **280–300 mL/min/m²**, but not as an absolute safe threshold. Assess Hb, flow, SvO₂, lactate, temperature, cerebral oximetry and organs together.
- **MAP largely reflects flow × SVR**; vasoconstriction can raise MAP without improving an inadequate flow/Hb-derived DO₂.

> **Closing point:** Deliver adequate oxygen, not merely an attractive arterial pressure.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: Compare alpha-stat and pH-stat blood-gas management during hypothermic CPB.
items.q: Compare alpha-stat and pH-stat blood-gas management during hypothermic CPB.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [Consensus on hypothermia in aortic arch surgery (temperature definitions)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3741830/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **Alpha-stat:** interpret and target blood-gas values as measured at **37°C** without temperature correction. During cooling, actual in-vivo PaCO₂ falls and pH rises; cerebral autoregulation and protein charge regulation tend to be preserved. Common in **adult CPB**.
- **pH-stat:** add CO₂ during cooling so **temperature-corrected** pH ≈ 7.40 and PaCO₂ ≈ 40 mmHg. Cerebral vasodilation can improve cooling uniformity but may increase embolic delivery and blunt autoregulation.
- pH-stat has a role in selected **paediatric/deep-cooling** protocols; neither is universally superior for every operation.

> **Closing point:** The difference is which temperature the blood gas is interpreted at—and how CO₂ changes cerebral flow.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: Choose antegrade, retrograde or selective ostial cardioplegia for different cardiac lesions.
items.q: Choose antegrade, retrograde or selective ostial cardioplegia for different cardiac lesions.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **Antegrade aortic-root cardioplegia** distributes down patent coronary arteries after cross-clamping; important **coronary obstruction** may impair distal delivery.
- In **severe aortic regurgitation**, antegrade root cardioplegia may run into the LV, distend it and inadequately protect myocardium; choose **retrograde coronary-sinus** delivery and/or **direct coronary ostial** dosing once the aorta is open.
- **Retrograde** delivery can bypass proximal coronary stenoses but may be less reliable for the **RV**, and requires appropriate coronary-sinus positioning/pressure.
- **Selective ostial** delivery is useful during AVR/aortic root operations. Maintain correct temperature, dose/interval, coronary perfusion and venting; inadequate protection causes stunning, ischaemia and failure to wean.

> **Closing point:** The valve lesion and coronary anatomy determine how cardioplegia reaches the myocardium.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: Interpret common ROTEM/TEG abnormalities after CPB and give targeted treatments.
items.q: Interpret common ROTEM/TEG abnormalities after CPB and give targeted treatments.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [Blue Book 2025: Goal-directed bleeding management, pp59–79](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/d8402efb-afbb-4300-8c72-c86edd93edad/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/2025_Blue_Book_PDF.pdf?language=en) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC patient blood management guideline](https://www.eacts.org/clinical-practice-guideline/2024-eacts-eactaic-guidelines-on-patient-blood-management-in-adult-cardiac-surgery-in-collaboration-with-ebcp/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- First consider **surgical bleeding, temperature, pH, calcium** and residual heparin; viscoelastic tests complement rather than replace the operative assessment.
- **Prolonged EXTEM clotting time** may indicate **coagulation-factor deficit** (consider protocol-guided plasma/PCC), but compare with heparin-sensitive channels and standard tests before treating.
- A **heparin effect** is suggested when **INTEM is abnormal but HEPTEM corrects** (or the equivalent heparinase comparison): reassess heparin/protamine balance.
- **Low FIBTEM clot amplitude/MCF** supports fibrinogen deficiency → fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate under protocol.
- **Low EXTEM clot firmness with relatively preserved FIBTEM** points toward platelet-number/function contribution → consider platelets according to labs/clinical bleeding.
- **Excess lysis** suggests hyperfibrinolysis → TXA when appropriate. Local **A5/A10/MCF thresholds vary by assay and centre**; routine channels can miss P2Y12-related dysfunction.

> **Closing point:** Match the faulty clot component to treatment rather than giving every product indiscriminately.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: What do TRICS III and ATACAS mean for cardiac-surgical blood conservation?
items.q: What do TRICS III and ATACAS mean for cardiac-surgical blood conservation?
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC patient blood management guideline](https://www.eacts.org/clinical-practice-guideline/2024-eacts-eactaic-guidelines-on-patient-blood-management-in-adult-cardiac-surgery-in-collaboration-with-ebcp/) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/); supplied expanded Set 13 notes.

- **TRICS III:** in moderate/high-risk cardiac surgery, a **restrictive RBC threshold around Hb 75 g/L** was **non-inferior** to a liberal strategy for a major composite of death, MI, stroke and new dialysis (11.4% vs 12.5%). It is not a rule for unstable haemorrhage or active ischaemia.
- **ATACAS:** **tranexamic acid** reduced blood-product use and reoperation for bleeding/tamponade, but increased **seizures**; no significant primary composite thrombotic/death benefit. Choose dose using renal function, seizure risk and local protocol.
- Practical application: use a **patient-blood-management programme**, treat surgical bleeding and specific coagulation deficits, and interpret the trial population before changing care.

> **Closing point:** Restrictive transfusion is contextual, and TXA benefits must be weighed against dose-related harm.

> **Source:** Expanded Set 13 chapters

items.title: How does cardiac surgical arrest differ from routine ALS?
items.q: How does cardiac surgical arrest differ from routine ALS?
items.a:
- Use CALS-ANZ with a trained team; rapid rhythm confirmation and reversible-cause assessment.
- Witnessed monitored VF/pulseless VT may receive three stacked shocks; severe bradycardia/asystole may receive immediate epicardial pacing.
- Start CPR promptly if immediate treatment fails/is unavailable; arrange resternotomy within 5 minutes of arrest onset where indicated, including PEA/tamponade.
- This specialised pathway is for arrest after cardiac surgery, not a perfusing postoperative arrhythmia.

> **Closing point:** Prepare reopening and treat the arrest simultaneously.

items.title: Why does atropine fail in a transplanted heart?
items.q: Why does atropine fail in a transplanted heart?
items.a:
- Cardiac denervation makes the atropine/glycopyrrolate chronotropic response unreliable; variable reinnervation prevents an absolute rule.
- Resting rate is often around 90–100; reflex compensation may be blunted.
- For important bradycardia prepare direct chronotropy (e.g. isoprenaline/adrenaline as appropriate) and pacing.
- Ephedrine has mixed direct/indirect action, with variable response.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: Which drugs behave differently in a heart transplant recipient?
items.q: Which drugs behave differently in a heart transplant recipient?
items.a:
- Ephedrine: mixed direct/indirect effects; less predictable after denervation.
- Noradrenaline, adrenaline, dobutamine: exaggerated.
- Phenylephrine and metaraminol: effective, no reflex bradycardia.
- Adenosine: exaggerated bradycardia.
- Neostigmine: bradycardia possible.

> **Closing point:** Titrate catecholamines carefully.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: How is the transplanted heart different physiologically?
items.q: How is the transplanted heart different physiologically?
items.a:
- No reflex tachycardia; preload dependent.
- Silent ischaemia: no angina.
- Arrhythmia and pacing requirements vary with surgical technique, timing and cohort; investigate new arrhythmia for rejection or vasculopathy.
- Re-innervation is partial and unpredictable (sympathetic from 6 to 8 months).
- Ventricular arrhythmias suggest rejection or vasculopathy.

> **Closing point:** No reflex means volume matters most.

Source: Blue Book 2019

items.title: State the anticoagulation targets and plan for an LVAD patient needing surgery.
items.q: State the anticoagulation targets and plan for an LVAD patient needing surgery.
items.a:
- Verify device, INR target and VAD-centre protocol; commonly INR 2–3 for contemporary durable LVAD care.
- HeartMate 3 aspirin omission can be appropriate under ARIES-HM3-informed care; do not add aspirin automatically.
- Individualise interruption/bridging; urgent sustained VKA reversal generally uses an appropriate **four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K**, with an early re-anticoagulation plan.
- Do not treat all PCC brands as identical or omit vitamin K solely to make warfarin restart easier.

Source: Blue Book 2021

items.title: What is rapid ventricular pacing in TAVI?
items.q: What is rapid ventricular pacing in TAVI?
items.a:
- Rapid pacing transiently reduces forward output during selected valvuloplasty/deployment steps; often 180–220/min for balloon-expandable procedures.
- Rate/duration depend on device and tolerance; not every valve step needs the same manoeuvre.
- Confirm capture, communicate start/stop, prepare vasopressors and assess rhythm/perfusion recovery.
- Persistent collapse needs immediate assessment for coronary obstruction, severe AR, tamponade or vascular bleeding.

Source: BJA Educ 2021

items.title: 1. Vasoplegia after bypass in a patient on an ACE inhibitor
items.q: A 68-year-old man on an ACE inhibitor has a good ejection fraction on TOE but a MAP of 48 mmHg, cardiac index 4.2 and SVR 450 after separation from bypass for CABG. Explain the pathophysiology and outline your management.
items.a:
## Recognition and exclusion of other causes

**Vasoplegic shock** is sustained hypotension from pathological vasodilation, a rising vasopressor requirement and capillary leak with tissue hypoperfusion. It follows 5 to 25% of cardiac operations, and mortality is 25 to 50%. The usual phenotype is hypotension with low SVR and preserved/high output, but mixed shock is common and high output is not unique to post-CPB vasoplegia. Use correct units: non-indexed SVR is in dyn·s·cm−5; SVRI uses cardiac index and is in dyn·s·cm−5·m². Do not interchange their normal ranges or cut-offs. In this patient (CI 4.2, SVR 450, good EF) the diagnosis fits, but exclude hypovolaemia or bleeding, LV or RV dysfunction, tamponade, LVOT obstruction and protamine reaction first. After cardiac surgery the femoral pressure often exceeds the radial, so confirm with a central pressure before escalating.

## Pathophysiology

Circuit contact, tissue trauma, ischaemia-reperfusion and gut translocation cause a systemic inflammatory response. This induces **nitric oxide synthase**, so nitric oxide raises cGMP and relaxes smooth muscle; **KATP channels** open and hyperpolarise it; adrenergic receptors down-regulate; **vasopressin stores are depleted**; and acidaemia and glycocalyx shedding add microcirculatory failure. Risk factors are an **ACE inhibitor or ARB** (as here), impaired ventricular function, prolonged bypass and milrinone, which causes vasodilation.

## Management

- **1.** Assess fluid responsiveness and optimise preload with small observed increments of pump blood/appropriate fluid if underfilled, avoiding indiscriminate loading of a congested patient and treat acidosis, hypocalcaemia and hypothermia.
- **2.** **Noradrenaline** first for MAP above 65.
- **3.** Add **vasopressin** early (about 0.02 to 0.04 units/min commonly, titrated within the local protocol), which replaces the depleted hormone, spares catecholamine dose, causes little rise in PVR (so is suitable if the RV is vulnerable) and gives less AF than catecholamines.
- **4.** Rescue: **methylene blue** 1 to 2 mg/kg, which inhibits nitric oxide synthase and guanylate cyclase. Cautions: serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs, G6PD deficiency, pulmonary hypertension, interference with pulse oximetry, green urine.
- **5.** Consider **hydrocortisone** in persistent vasopressor-dependent shock or suspected adrenal insufficiency; much of its outcome evidence comes from sepsis and cannot establish routine benefit after CPB. **Angiotensin II** or hydroxocobalamin are selected rescue options with limited cardiac-surgery outcome evidence.
- **6.** Keep adrenaline for combined low output.

Avoid escalating catecholamines alone, because of arrhythmia and splanchnic or limb ischaemia. Review the cause if the picture persists beyond 24 hours.

## Prevention

Consider omitting ACE inhibitors or ARBs before surgery, and limit bypass time.

## Apply the physiology to this patient

The low resistance with CI 4.2 is compatible with a predominant vasodilatory component, but normal EF does not prove adequate stroke volume or exclude RV failure. Check transducer accuracy, pulse contour reliability, TOE filling/function and perfusion (capillary refill, urine, lactate trend). Treat concurrent bleeding/underfilling; avoid treating a radial–central gradient with excessive vasopressors. The initial MAP target is commonly ≥65 mmHg, individualised to coronary, cerebral and renal perfusion. Reassess CO when escalating afterload.

Methylene blue is a rescue drug, commonly 1–2 mg/kg over 15–30 minutes: check serotonergic drugs/MAOI interaction, G6PD deficiency and pulmonary hypertension, and anticipate optical-monitor interference. Hydroxocobalamin (often 5 g) has limited outcome evidence and may interfere with laboratory assays and dialysis blood-leak sensors. Angiotensin II can raise BP in catecholamine-resistant vasodilatory shock, but this is not proof of a survival benefit after CPB; consider thrombotic risk. Treat infection/adrenal insufficiency when present, and reassess mixed shock repeatedly. Review the perioperative RAAS-drug plan individually rather than implying universal mandatory cessation.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Identifies predominant vasodilation and excludes mixed/monitor causes
- **2 marks** — Explains inflammatory NO/receptor/vasopressin mechanisms
- **2 marks** — Assesses preload and organ perfusion with appropriate targets
- **2 marks** — Selects catecholamine/vasopressin and checks rescue contraindications
- **2 marks** — Reassesses response and qualifies steroid/novel-drug evidence

items.title: 2. Acute RV failure when weaning after mitral valve replacement
items.q: As you wean a patient from cardiopulmonary bypass after mitral valve replacement, the right ventricle dilates, the CVP rises to 24 and the systolic pressure falls. Explain the mechanisms and your management.
items.a:
## Why the RV fails

The RV is a thin free wall (2 to 3 mm) that contracts longitudinally and is perfused in **systole and diastole** by the right coronary artery. It tolerates preload but not sudden afterload; acute pressure overload can overwhelm an unadapted RV, but no single mean PA pressure defines failure in all patients. After bypass the causes are:

- **Pre-existing RV dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension**, which is common after long-standing mitral disease as here;
- **prolonged bypass and inadequate RV protection**;
- **air in the right coronary artery** (the ostium is anterior) or graft failure;
- **protamine**, which can cause pulmonary vasoconstriction;
- atelectasis, hypoxia, hypercarbia and acidosis, which raise PVR; and LVAD insertion or transplantation.

RV dilatation then causes septal shift and leftward ventricular interdependence, reducing LV filling, so systemic pressure falls and RV perfusion pressure drops, closing a spiral.

## Diagnosis

Integrate rising CVP, systemic hypotension, low output and organ perfusion with TOE. PA pressure can be high or may fall as the RV loses the ability to generate flow. A prominent c–v wave suggests TR. Assess RV size, global/regional function, septal shift, TR, pulmonary pressures and LV filling. Conventional TAPSE/S′/FAC values are load- and view-dependent; longitudinal indices change after pericardiotomy and must not be used alone as diagnostic cut-offs. A substantial RV-to-PA gradient suggests RV outflow obstruction, potentially dynamic with inotropes. Also exclude tamponade, prosthetic obstruction, pulmonary venous/left-sided disease and coronary injury.

## Management guided by physiology

- **1.** **Stabilise and diagnose:** tell the surgeon and perfusionist; resume adequate CPB support if unstable while checking de-airing, myocardial protection, RCA flow, valve result and mechanical obstruction.
- **2.** **Preload:** use TOE and pressure trends, not CVP <15 as an automatic fluid trigger. Small boluses help an underfilled RV; a distended congested RV may require controlled unloading. Venodilators/head-up positioning can worsen perfusion and are not default treatment for CVP 24.
- **3.** **Rhythm:** restore sinus rhythm/AV synchrony where feasible; pace block and cardiovert an unstable tachyarrhythmia. Select rate against filling and perfusion.
- **4.** **Perfusion pressure:** noradrenaline and/or low-dose vasopressin support coronary driving pressure. Vasopressin generally causes less increase in PVR than pure alpha stimulation; it does not have literally zero pulmonary or ischaemic effect, and no universal noradrenaline ceiling of 0.2 applies.
- **5.** **Contractility:** select dobutamine, adrenaline or IV milrinone according to pressure and severity, with vasopressor support if needed. Adjust milrinone for renal dysfunction and watch hypotension and arrhythmia; no fixed sequence is compulsory.
- **6.** **Afterload:** oxygenate, correct hypercarbia/acidaemia, optimise lung volume and airway pressures. Use predicted-body-weight ventilation with individualised PEEP, not an absolute maximum. Consider inhaled nitric oxide or prostacyclin, with monitoring and a weaning plan to avoid rebound. Intratracheal milrinone is not a routine first-line bolus.
- **7.** **Refractory failure:** rest/reperfuse on CPB, correct structural lesions, then consider RVAD for isolated RV failure or VA ECMO for biventricular/cardiopulmonary failure. IABP may help associated LV ischaemia/coronary perfusion but is not full RV support. Reassess after sternal closure.

Prevention is FiO2 1.0, avoiding hypercarbia, and starting inhaled vasodilator before bypass ends in high-risk cases.

## Mitral-specific diagnostic priorities

Review the pre-bypass RV and pulmonary pressures. A newly obstructed or poorly functioning mitral prosthesis, residual severe regurgitation, LV dysfunction or pulmonary venous obstruction can raise pulmonary venous pressure and RV afterload. Examine the prosthesis and both ventricles before labelling this isolated pulmonary vasoconstriction. Coronary air, circumflex injury in mitral surgery, RCA compromise and inadequate myocardial protection need prompt surgical assessment. Use any PAC data as trends in context: a single low PA pressure may mean a severely failing RV, rather than reassuringly low PVR. Recheck mechanical support needs and transport readiness, including inhaled vasodilator continuity, pacing and monitored ICU care.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Explains RV afterload/ischaemia and ventricular interdependence
- **2 marks** — Uses integrated TOE/pressure trends and checks mitral result
- **2 marks** — Optimises preload/rhythm and systemic coronary pressure
- **2 marks** — Selects inotropy and ventilatory/inhaled pulmonary therapy
- **2 marks** — Escalates to CPB/RVAD/ECMO and corrects structural causes

items.title: 3. HeartMate 3 LVAD for laparoscopic cholecystectomy
items.q: A 58-year-old man with a HeartMate 3 left ventricular assist device presents for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. Outline the physiology of the device and your perioperative management.
items.a:
## The device and physiology

A continuous-flow **LVAD** draws from the LV apex and returns to the ascending aorta, with a driveline and controller. Current practice is the **HeartMate 3** (magnetically levitated centrifugal; speed, power, estimated flow and pulsatility index must be compared with this patient’s prescribed settings and baseline, not universal “normal” ranges); the HeartMate II is axial. The patient may have **no palpable pulse**, so Doppler opening pressure may approximate MAP when pulsatility is minimal; with meaningful native pulsatility it may reflect systolic pressure. The pump is **preload dependent and afterload sensitive**, and the RV must supply the preload (RV failure after LVAD occurs in 15 to 25%).

## Preoperative

- Elective surgery in a VAD centre; for emergencies contact the VAD team early. Published mortality varies greatly by procedure, urgency and cohort; historical aggregate figures should not be applied as a prediction for this elective HM3 patient.
- Interrogate the controller, review echo for RV function, aortic regurgitation and thrombus, and plan device settings.
- **Anticoagulation:** verify the actual device-centre regimen. HeartMate 3 commonly uses VKA with INR 2–3, individualised to bleeding/thrombotic history. **ARIES-HM3 (2023)** supports aspirin avoidance alongside VKA in HM3 recipients; aspirin is no longer an automatic requirement solely for this device. Do not substitute a DOAC without specialist direction. Whether to continue/interrupt warfarin and bridge depends on the procedure, INR, device and thrombotic/bleeding risk. For urgent major bleeding or surgery requiring immediate reversal, a specialist plan may use 4-factor PCC **with IV vitamin K** for sustained reversal; product and dose follow local guidance. Neither PCC for every emergency nor avoidance of vitamin K is appropriate. Acquired von Willebrand syndrome/AVMs add bleeding risk; desmopressin is selective rather than routine prophylaxis.
- Pacemaker or ICD: manage as usual, according to pacing dependence and anticipated EMI: asynchronous pacing only if indicated, separate suspension of ICD tachytherapy, external rescue pads and restoration afterwards; defibrillator pads on, and CPR is still given with a pump.

## Intraoperative

- **Arterial line** (Doppler cuff unreliable); NIRS if oximetry fails; TOE if needed.
- **MAP 60 to 80 mmHg**: above 80 reduces pump flow; above 90 raises regurgitation, thrombosis and stroke.
- Avoid hypovolaemia, vasodilatation and high PEEP; avoid hypoxia and hypercarbia, which raise PVR and endanger the RV. Use a slowly titrated induction matched to ventricular reserve, with vasopressors ready; no agent is universally superior. Avoid hypoventilation, large abrupt sympathetic changes and loss of preload.
- Differentiate low flow: **hypovolaemia** (small LV, suction), **RV failure** (dilated RV, high CVP), **tamponade**, or pump thrombosis. For **suction**, immediately involve the VAD specialist, remove triggers (including pneumoperitoneum), and confirm filling/RV status with echo. Speed reduction may be required by the trained team; treat the cause with fluid only for underfilling, inotropy/pulmonary vasodilation for RV failure. Do not reflexively increase speed or volume for every low-flow alarm.
- Neuraxial blocks are possible once anticoagulation is cleared; use procedure-appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis, meticulous asepsis and protect the driveline exit site; do not prescribe broad antifungal cover solely because a VAD is present.

## Postoperative

Monitored care with early return of anticoagulation, watch for bleeding and thrombosis (rising power and falling flow), and keep the VAD team informed.

## Laparoscopy, alarms and rescue

Map the pump/outflow graft/driveline before ports; secure the controller and both power sources, with spare charged batteries and trained device support. Position gradually. Establish pneumoperitoneum slowly at the lowest effective pressure (often ≤10–12 mmHg if feasible), watching MAP, flow, ventilation and RV function. Reverse Trendelenburg, IVC compression, hypercarbia and increased afterload may combine to reduce LVAD flow; ask for deflation if unstable.

Low flow requires simultaneous patient and device assessment: haemorrhage/underfilling, RV failure, tamponade, hypertension, arrhythmia, inflow/outflow obstruction or pump fault. Estimated flow is derived from controller variables, not a direct cardiac output measurement, and rising power does not occur in every thrombosis/obstruction. Assess haemolysis (LDH, plasma-free Hb, urine), echo and device trends with the centre. Do not disconnect both power sources. In an unresponsive patient assess perfusion rather than pulse alone; if perfusion is inadequate, provide resuscitation including compressions and device/power checks in parallel, following AHA 2025 and local VAD guidance. An absent pulse alone does not diagnose arrest.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Explains HM3 preload/afterload/RV and monitor limitations
- **2 marks** — Plans specialist device/power/driveline/CIED care
- **2 marks** — Individualises VKA/aspirin/bridging/reversal using current evidence
- **2 marks** — Plans laparoscopy, anaesthesia and low-flow diagnosis
- **2 marks** — Provides postoperative anticoagulation and perfusion-based resuscitation

items.title: 4. IABP, Impella and VA-ECMO in post-infarct cardiogenic shock
items.q: Compare the intra-aortic balloon pump, a percutaneous microaxial pump (Impella) and venoarterial ECMO in the management of cardiogenic shock after myocardial infarction.
items.a:
## Approach

Cardiogenic shock (hypoperfusion from cardiac pump failure, often hypotension/vasopressor need, low CI and elevated filling pressures; not every case has each numeric feature) is treated by **revascularisation or the underlying cause first**, optimising volume, rate, rhythm and oxygenation, vasopressors and inotropes, and **early shock-team assessment for selected mechanical circulatory support (MCS)** when perfusion remains inadequate. Define the goal: bridge to recovery, to a durable VAD or transplant, or to decision.

## Devices

| Device | Mechanism | Support | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **IABP** | Diastolic augmentation and afterload reduction (coronary flow) | 0.5 to 1 L/min | Needs some native contractility and regular rhythm; contraindicated in significant AR and aortic dissection; IABP-SHOCK II showed no mortality benefit in infarct shock  |
| **Impella** (percutaneous LVAD) | Axial pump LV to aorta | 2.5 to 5.5 L/min | Unloads LV; haemolysis, bleeding, limb ischaemia, needs anticoagulation; RV support by Impella RP |
| **VA-ECMO** | Venous drainage to oxygenated arterial return | Full support | The 2017 chapter: refractory cardiogenic shock, extracorporeal CPR, failure to wean from CPB, bridge; ELSO 2015 survival 41% |
| **Surgical VAD** | LV apex to aorta | Full | Bridge to transplant or candidacy |

## Anaesthesia for MCS

- **VA-ECMO** increases afterload and may distend the LV, so unloading (IABP, Impella, venting) is often needed; differential hypoxia (Harlequin) shows as low right-arm saturation; flow may have little pulsatility; MAP depends on ECMO flow, native output and SVR, with vasopressors only as indicated.
- Complications: bleeding and circuit thrombosis, with platelet/haemostasis targets individualised to active bleeding, procedure and centre protocol, infection, limb ischaemia, stroke, haemolysis and circuit failure.
- **Drug effects:** the circuit sequesters lipophilic drugs such as propofol, and doses need re-titration.
- Weaning: gradual flow reduction with echo to confirm LV recovery, and low-dose inotropes.

## Anaesthetic considerations for cannulation

Resuscitation-level monitoring with arterial line, TOE and defibrillation ready; titrated induction (etomidate or ketamine) with vasopressors; heparinise as per protocol; manage right-sided failure and coagulopathy; transport on support with a perfusionist.

## Evidence that changes selection

- **IABP-SHOCK II:** no routine survival benefit for infarct-related shock treated with revascularisation. This does not eliminate selected use for mechanical complications or difficult postoperative weaning.
- **DanGer-Shock (2024):** selected STEMI-related, predominantly LV shock patients treated with Impella CP had lower 180-day mortality (45.8% versus 58.5%), but substantially more serious adverse events, including bleeding, limb injury and renal replacement. Do not extrapolate to all shock, comatose post-arrest patients or isolated RV/biventricular failure.
- **ECLS-SHOCK (2023):** routine early VA ECMO in AMI shock did not reduce 30-day mortality and increased bleeding/vascular complications. Rescue support after individual assessment differs from indiscriminate routine deployment.

Select support by the failing ventricle(s), oxygenation, vascular anatomy, valve disease and exit strategy. Impella requires adequate RV delivery and suitable aortic-valve/LV anatomy; LV thrombus, mechanical aortic valve and significant AR are important constraints. VA ECMO can worsen LV distension: monitor aortic-valve opening and pulmonary oedema and consider venting/unloading when indicated, balancing extra-device harm. Monitor right radial gases for differential upper-body hypoxaemia with peripheral femoral return and provide distal-limb perfusion as appropriate. Reassess escalation/weaning and goals with the shock team.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Defines shock phenotype and treats revascularisable cause
- **2 marks** — Compares mechanisms/support and suitability of three devices
- **2 marks** — Explains current IABP/DanGer/ECLS evidence and populations
- **2 marks** — Anticipates unloading/differential hypoxia/vascular/bleeding harm
- **2 marks** — Sets shock-team destination, monitoring and weaning plan

items.title: 5. Complications in the first 24 hours after cardiac surgery
items.q: Outline the common complications in the first 24 hours after cardiac surgery and their management.
items.a:
## Approach

Deterioration after cardiac surgery is approached systematically: **A, B, C** then **C** for the circulation, using the causes of low cardiac output.

## Circulation (commonest)

- **Bleeding and tamponade:** drain output above about 200 mL/h or suddenly stopping drains, rising CVP and falling pressure ; classic equalised pressures may be absent with localised postoperative clot. Tamponade can be localised and missed on TTE (use TOE). Treat coagulopathy and return to theatre; in arrest, resternotomy within five minutes.
- **Pump failure:** LV from graft failure or perioperative infarct; **RV failure** (see R02); valve or prosthesis problem. Use ECG, troponin, echo.
- **Vasoplegia** (R01), hypovolaemia.
- **Arrhythmia:** AF occurs in 10 to 40% after CABG, 37 to 50% after valve and up to 70% after combined surgery, peaking at about 48 hours. Rate control first when stable; synchronised DC cardioversion if unstable; K, Mg, beta-blocker continuation and amiodarone for prevention. Heart block is more frequent after valve surgery (selected cited series reported mitral 23.5% and aortic 10.3%; these are not universal rates); assess/establish epicardial pacing when needed.

## Other systems

- **Respiratory:** atelectasis, pneumothorax, phrenic injury, pleural effusion, ARDS.
- **Neurological:** stroke, delirium, cognitive change (R15).
- **Renal:** AKI (R06).
- **Gastrointestinal and metabolic:** gut ischaemia, hyperglycaemia, lactate.
- **Infection:** sternal wound infection and mediastinitis.

## Immediate management

Reassess, monitor with arterial line and CVP, **12-lead ECG, chest X-ray, ABG and lactate**, and TOE for tamponade, ventricular function and valves. Correct electrolytes, ventilate, treat the cause, and communicate with the surgeon early.

## Cardiac arrest

In a witnessed monitored arrest with a trained cardiac surgical team, follow the local specialised pathway: three rapid shocks for VF/pVT or immediate pacing for brady/asystole, with at most a brief initial delay before CPR (within 1 minute if unsuccessful). Prepare emergency resternotomy, generally within 5 minutes when indicated. Do not omit compressions while waiting. Full-dose adrenaline is not routine in the specialised pathway because of rebound hypertension; dosing follows the team protocol. If the pathway/team is unavailable, provide standard ALS without delay.

## Routine ICU management as well as emergencies

Use a structured theatre-to-ICU handover: operation and residual lesions, CPB/cross-clamp times, airway and vascular access, TOE result, blood products/heparin/protamine, rhythm/pacing dependence and settings, vasoactive support, drain locations/output and immediate concerns. Verify the ventilator, gas exchange, analgesia/sedation, temperature, neurology, perfusion, urine output, glucose/electrolytes, ECG and haemostasis. Set explicit targets and escalation triggers with the surgeon/intensivist.

Repeatedly inspect drain patency and output; falling output with deterioration can represent retained clot rather than recovery. Optimise cardiac loading and treat the cause of low output, avoiding reflex fluid for all hypotension. Provide multimodal analgesia, delirium screening, pressure care, infection prevention, mobilisation/nutrition and VTE prophylaxis when bleeding risk permits. Reinstitute aspirin/anticoagulation and other cardiac medication according to procedure and haemostasis. Plan paced-wire/line/drain removal and checks. AF often peaks after the first 24 hours; mediastinitis typically presents later, but prevention begins immediately. Postoperative ECG/troponin changes need clinical context: isolated biomarker rise after surgery is not by itself proof of graft occlusion.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Provides structured routine ICU handover and targets
- **2 marks** — Recognises bleeding/tamponade and LV/RV/structural low output
- **2 marks** — Treats vasoplegia/rhythm and respiratory/metabolic complications
- **2 marks** — Plans renal/neuro/delirium/prevention/analgesia care
- **2 marks** — Provides safe specialised arrest escalation with CPR limits

items.title: 6. Acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery
items.q: Discuss the pathophysiology, risk factors and prevention of acute kidney injury after cardiac surgery.
items.a:
## Importance

AKI affects up to 30% of patients after cardiac surgery, and dialysis-requiring AKI carries a high mortality. It is also a feature of VAD surgery (AKI 18 to 43.5% in non-cardiac surgery) and vasoplegia.

## Pathophysiology

- **Ischaemia-reperfusion injury** and low flow on bypass: non-pulsatile flow and a perfusion pressure below the renal autoregulatory limit, with the kidney's medulla borderline for oxygen.
- **Inflammation** (SIRS), complement activation and **haemolysis**: free haemoglobin and iron, particularly with excessive suction and prolonged pump time; appropriately used washed cell salvage is still a blood-conservation strategy.
- **Microemboli, atheroma and nephrotoxins** (contrast, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, vancomycin).
- **Low cardiac output, vasoplegia, high-dose vasoconstrictors and venous congestion.**
- **Transfusion**, anaemia and hyperthermia on rewarming.

## Risk factors

Preexisting CKD, diabetes, age, heart failure and low EF, emergency or redo surgery, combined procedures, long bypass and cross-clamp times, preoperative ACE inhibitor or diuretic, anaemia, and peripheral vascular disease.

## Prevention (bundle)

- Preoperative: assess recent contrast exposure and kidney function; defer an elective case only where the benefit outweighs the cardiac risk; stop nephrotoxins.
- **Perfusion/oxygen delivery:** individualise MAP to organ and coronary perfusion and use adequate measured flow, Hb and arterial saturation; no fixed MAP or haematocrit is a universal renal-protection threshold. Avoid excessive haemodilution and assess DO2, venous saturation and lactate trends.
- Minimise bypass time, consider off-pump surgery, avoid haemolysis and suction.
- Avoid hypotension, vasoconstrictor overuse, hyperglycaemia and hypovolaemia; use goal-directed haemodynamics and balanced crystalloid.
- Treat cause of low output; avoid nephrotoxins. Dopamine, routine furosemide, mannitol and bicarbonate should not be used as established renal protection. New evidence for IV amino acids is discussed below; it does not establish benefit for every drug or every renal outcome.

## Management of established AKI

Define with KDIGO stage (creatinine rise or urine below 0.5 mL/kg/h). Optimise volume and perfusion, remove nephrotoxins, correct hyperkalaemia and acidosis, adjust drug doses, and start renal replacement for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload or uraemia; timing of early versus delayed RRT remains debated.

## 2026 review and recent evidence

Define **KDIGO AKI**: creatinine rise ≥26.5 micromol/L within 48 hours, or ≥1.5 times baseline within 7 days, or urine <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours. Creatinine may be delayed/diluted; oliguria is not proof of volume depletion. Diagnose congestion, obstruction, low output or intrinsic injury before giving more fluid.

The 2026 BJAEd review emphasises renal medullary oxygen imbalance, haemolysis/NO scavenging, venous congestion and inflammation. Use a KDIGO-style bundle: maintain appropriate volume and perfusion, adequate oxygen delivery on CPB, avoid nephrotoxins and excessive glucose, monitor urine/creatinine and adjust drug doses. Pump flow, Hb, saturation and temperature interact; simply raising MAP or giving fluid is not a complete protection strategy. Avoid hyperthermic/rapid rewarming. TIMP-2×IGFBP7 can identify high-risk patients for targeted bundles where available; NGAL and other markers have limitations and are not automatic dialysis triggers.

**PROTECTION (2024)** randomised 3512 adult CPB patients: IV amino acids reduced AKI (26.9% versus 31.7%; RR 0.85). This is a relevant recent question theme. It does not establish a universal mortality/dialysis benefit, and application should follow centre review of patient selection and protocol. New SGLT2-inhibitor signals remain a developing area; do not initiate or continue these routinely around surgery for presumed renal protection without a perioperative plan, because ketoacidosis risk matters. Diuretics treat congestion, not intrinsic renal recovery; RRT is guided by refractory complications and trajectory rather than a creatinine number alone.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Defines KDIGO and interprets urine/creatinine limits
- **2 marks** — Explains oxygen imbalance, inflammation/haemolysis and congestion
- **2 marks** — Identifies patient/procedural risks
- **2 marks** — Provides KDIGO/oxygen-delivery bundle and avoids harmful recipes
- **2 marks** — Explains PROTECTION/biomarker evidence and RRT indications

items.title: 7. Bleeding 400 mL/hour after CABG
items.q: A patient is bleeding 400 mL/hour from the chest drains two hours after CABG. Outline your assessment and management.
items.a:
## Causes

| Cause | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Surgical bleeding** | Anastomoses, sternal edges, cannulation sites; needs surgical re-exploration |
| **Heparin effect** | Inadequate protamine or **heparin rebound** |
| **Platelet dysfunction** | Bypass activation, hypothermia, antiplatelet drugs (aspirin, clopidogrel, ticagrelor) |
| **Dilutional and consumptive coagulopathy** | fibrinogen can become an early important deficit; assess rather than assume the same deficit in every patient; factor consumption |
| **Hyperfibrinolysis** | Bypass, DHCA, redo surgery |
| **Hypothermia, acidosis, hypocalcaemia** | Slow enzymatic coagulation |
| **Preoperative** | DOACs, warfarin, liver disease, renal failure, von Willebrand disease |

## Protamine

Dose roughly **1 mg per 100 units of heparin**, with onset in about 5 minutes and half-life about 10 minutes; base the dose on residual circulating heparin or a validated titration protocol, accounting for dose/time and clearance; a fixed 15-minute rule is not valid, and excess protamine is itself anticoagulant. Adverse effects: **vasodilation and hypotension, pulmonary vasoconstriction with RV dysfunction, and anaphylaxis**; risk factors are previous exposure, NPH insulin, prior protamine reaction or exposure to protamine-containing insulin; fish allergy or vasectomy alone does not mandate avoidance. Give slowly.

## Assessment

Assess **residual heparin using validated testing**; a normal ACT alone does not exclude residual heparin and a prolonged ACT may have non-heparin causes, platelet count, fibrinogen, and **viscoelastic testing** (ROTEM or TEG) to separate heparin effect, fibrinogen, platelet and fibrinolytic problems; check temperature, pH, ionised calcium and chest drain volume.

## Management

- **1.** **Correct physiology first:** warm above 36 degrees, calcium, pH, MAP control.
- **2.** **Heparin:** additional carefully titrated protamine only if residual heparin is demonstrated or strongly supported; use heparinase comparison/heparin concentration where available.
- **3.** **Targeted products:** fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate to fibrinogen about 2 g/L; platelets if dysfunction (low count or antiplatelet); prothrombin complex or plasma for factor deficiency.
- **4.** **Antifibrinolytic:** tranexamic acid, with dose restraint due to seizure risk at high doses.
- **5.** **Desmopressin** in von Willebrand disease or uraemia; cell salvage.
- **6.** **Surgical re-exploration** urgently for this 400 mL/h scenario if ongoing, particularly instability or suspected surgical bleeding/tamponade. Do not wait several hours for an arbitrary threshold while transfusion or shock continues.

Transfuse to a rational threshold and treat massive bleeding with the massive transfusion protocol.

## Act now, investigate in parallel

For 400 mL/h ongoing drainage, call the surgeon immediately, assess haemodynamics and perfusion, activate a major-haemorrhage pathway if indicated, ensure large-bore access, crossmatched blood/rapid infusion, warming and calcium. Reassess airway/ventilation, anticoagulant exposure and all drain outputs; bedside TOE helps detect retained clot but must not delay re-exploration in an unstable patient. Surgical and coagulopathic causes often coexist.

Use paired heparinase/non-heparinase viscoelastic channels or measured residual heparin where available; ACT alone cannot distinguish residual heparin from factor deficiency or excess protamine. Match treatment to defect: fibrinogen replacement for low functional fibrinogen, platelets for demonstrated quantitative/functional deficit, and plasma or selected PCC for factor deficiency under the local cardiac bleeding algorithm. Do not use PCC as a replacement for platelets/fibrinogen or give repeated empiric protamine. Reassess after each intervention. Blue Book 2025 supports protocolised goal-directed haemostasis; evidence such as FARES-II favours PCC over plasma for selected post-CPB factor-deficiency bleeding, not all bleeding phenotypes. TXA reduces fibrinolytic bleeding but excess dosing/renal accumulation increases seizure risk. Repeated product administration must not delay control of an anastomotic bleed.

**Drain safety:** verify patency and retained blood with the surgical team; routine stripping/milking or breaking the closed sterile system can be harmful. Use the approved clearance protocol. A reassuring external output cannot exclude retained mediastinal blood.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Calls surgeon early and resuscitates active severe bleeding
- **2 marks** — Distinguishes surgical/coagulopathic/residual-heparin causes
- **2 marks** — Uses labs/viscoelastic/heparinase and corrects physiology
- **2 marks** — Matches products/TXA/protamine to demonstrated deficits
- **2 marks** — Prioritises timely source control and reassesses

items.title: 8. On-pump CABG: surgical steps and anaesthetic technique
items.q: Outline the surgical steps and the anaesthetic technique for an on-pump coronary artery bypass graft in a patient with triple vessel disease and an ejection fraction of 40%.
items.a:
## Preoperative

Assess ventricular function, coronary anatomy (left main or triple-vessel disease), valve disease, carotid disease, renal function, diabetes and pulmonary disease. **Continue established beta-blockers** unless contraindicated; individualise **ACE inhibitor/ARB** management with the cardiac team; manage antiplatelets against ACS/stent and bleeding risk (for elective cardiac surgery common P2Y12 interruption intervals are ticagrelor 3, clopidogrel 5, prasugrel 7 days; these are not neuraxial intervals); avoid long fasting and hypotension; premedicate lightly.

## Pre-bypass

- **Monitoring:** five-lead ECG with ST analysis, arterial line before induction, central venous access (PA catheter if poor function), TOE, temperature, urine output and processed EEG or NIRS.
- **Induction:** haemodynamic stability with titrated opioid, hypnotic and rocuronium; avoid tachycardia, hypotension and hypertension. Maintain coronary perfusion pressure (diastolic pressure minus LVEDP) and a low-normal heart rate.
- **Sternotomy and other stimulation** may produce marked haemodynamic responses; anticipate hypertension and bradycardia.
- **Heparin** before cannulation (300 to 400 units/kg; ACT above 480 seconds for bypass, from the heparin chapter), antifibrinolytic.

## On bypass

Maintain anaesthesia (volatile through the oxygenator or TIVA), muscle relaxation, individualised MAP (often within a 50–80 mmHg adult CPB range), measured flow initially around 2.2–2.4 L/min/m² and adjusted for Hb, temperature and oxygen delivery, temperature per surgeon, glucose control, ventilator off or low CPAP, and report ACT periodically.

## Separation

Follow a checklist (rate and rhythm, ventilation, temperature, electrolytes, de-airing, graft flow): see 2016.2-10. Treat RV failure (R02) or vasoplegia (R01) promptly.

## Post-bypass and ICU

Protamine slowly, haemostasis and coagulation testing, ST monitoring, epicardial pacing wires, transfer with monitors, and **fast-track** extubation (R18). Surgical technique matters: on-pump versus **off-pump**, with off-pump needing careful positioning, with hypotension and RV compression during lifting, atrial wires and vasopressor-supported pressure.

Complications to anticipate: perioperative infarction, AF, bleeding, AKI, stroke, delirium and sternal wound infection.

## Surgical sequence and phase-specific risks

Harvest LITA/radial/vein conduits while exposing the heart by sternotomy; protect a planned radial conduit from arterial cannulation. After systemic heparin and demonstrated adequate ACT, place arterial and venous cannulae, confirm safe drainage/return, commence CPB, cross-clamp the aorta and deliver cardioplegia. Perform distal and proximal graft anastomoses according to the surgical strategy; not every graft requires the same clamp sequence. Reperfuse, de-air, rewarm, check graft flow and wall motion, and separate with the full checklist. Reverse heparin only after stable separation, inspect haemostasis (including cannulation sites, mammary bed, anastomoses and drains), place/check wires and drains and reassess during closure.

For EF 40%, evaluate ischaemia, scar, RV/valve function and current perfusion rather than assigning risk from EF alone. Preserve myocardial oxygen balance and avoid abrupt reduction in coronary driving pressure during induction. A PAC is selected for the question it will answer, not mandatory for every reduced EF. On CPB check delivered oxygen, indexed flow, Hb, gases, venous saturation/lactate and NIRS/pressure trends; common flow values are starting points, not universal organ-perfusion guarantees. Minimise haemodilution and excessive suction, maintain anaesthesia despite changes in clearance/protein binding and confirm delivery through every transition. Plan postoperative antiplatelets and renal/neuro/bleeding surveillance. The 2026 CABG Part 1 corrected proof supplies current preoperative/surgical coverage; no unpublished Part 2 is presumed read.

**Systematic haemostasis check:** inspect anastomoses, aortic/venous cannulation and cardioplegia/vent sites, mammary bed, sternal edges/wire sites, pericardial surfaces and chest-drain entry sites; combine surgical control with coagulation assessment rather than relying on laboratory correction alone.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Describes CABG conduit/cannulation/clamp/graft/reperfusion steps
- **2 marks** — Assesses EF40 patient and protects myocardial oxygen balance
- **2 marks** — Provides monitoring/induction/antiplatelet plan
- **2 marks** — Maintains CPB anaesthesia, oxygen delivery and protection
- **2 marks** — Separates safely, checks graft/haemostasis and hands over

items.title: 9. Surgical AVR versus TAVI for aortic stenosis
items.q: Compare surgical aortic valve replacement and transcatheter aortic valve implantation, and outline the anaesthetic considerations for severe aortic stenosis in each.
items.a:
## Pathophysiology of aortic stenosis

Normal valve area is 2.6 to 3.5 cm2; **severe** AS is below 1.0 cm2, peak velocity of at least 4 m/s, mean gradient of at least 40 mmHg, or a velocity ratio below 0.25. Untreated symptomatic severe AS carries a poor prognosis, particularly with heart failure; the individual risk depends on the phenotype and clinical course. The LV hypertrophies and develops diastolic dysfunction, so it depends on **atrial contraction** (AF is poorly tolerated), preload and **diastolic coronary driving pressure** (aortic diastolic pressure minus LV diastolic pressure). There are four categories: high-gradient; low-flow low-gradient with reduced EF (including pseudo-severe, tested by dobutamine); low-flow low-gradient with preserved EF; and normal-flow low-gradient. Calcium scoring on CT (at least 2000 in men, 1200 in women) supports severity.

## Choice of procedure

STS 30-day mortality risk: low below 4%, intermediate 4 to 8%, high above 8%. **PARTNER A** (high risk) showed TAVI non-inferior to surgery at one year; **PARTNER B** (inoperable) showed lower mortality with TAVI but more stroke. CT is now the standard for planning (annulus size, coronary heights, access vessels). Do not treat annulus dimensions or bicuspid anatomy as universal device-independent exclusions. Active infection, unsuitable valve/access anatomy, coronary obstruction risk, associated aortopathy, need for CABG/other valve surgery, expected durability, life expectancy and patient goals all affect suitability. **ESC/EACTS 2025** favours TAVI for anatomically suitable tricuspid AS at age ≥70, and SAVR for younger low-surgical-risk patients; Heart Team assessment and lifetime strategy remain essential. These are named guideline recommendations, not a rigid rule that age alone decides.

## Anaesthetic goals (AS)

- Maintain **sinus rhythm, preload, afterload (SVR) and contractility**; avoid tachycardia and hypotension.
- **Vasopressors** (phenylephrine, noradrenaline) to treat vasodilation; cardiovert unstable AF immediately.
- Slow, titrated induction with arterial line before induction and defibrillator pads on.

## Surgical AVR

Standard cardiac anaesthetic with bypass, protection and postoperative pacing for heart block.

## TAVI

Usually transfemoral under **local anaesthesia with appropriate sedation or general anaesthesia when indicated** with TOE or TTE, arterial line and rapid pacing for selected deployment/valvuloplasty steps (rate and duration are device/protocol-specific, commonly around 180–220/min for balloon deployment); be ready for conversion to open surgery. Complications: annular rupture, coronary obstruction, conduction block needing a pacemaker, paravalvular leak, vascular injury and stroke. Plan for postoperative monitoring, and an arrangement for emergency sternotomy.

## Surgical AVR steps and procedural anaesthesia

Sternotomy/minimal access, heparinisation and CPB are followed by cross-clamping, cardioplegia, aortotomy, excision/decalcification of the diseased valve, annular sizing and prosthesis implantation. Preserve coronary ostia and conduction tissue, close the aortotomy, de-air, reperfuse and rewarm. TOE checks seating, leaflet motion, gradients in flow context, paravalvular leak, ventricular/regional function and aortic integrity before separation; reassess pacing and haemostasis. Discuss mechanical versus biological prosthesis against age, durability, anticoagulation and patient preference.

TAVI usually uses percutaneous transfemoral access with CT-planned annular sizing, coronary heights and access vessels. Minimal sedation or GA is chosen for access, patient cooperation, respiratory needs, imaging and rescue feasibility; GA/TOE is not universal. Heparin, wire passage, valvuloplasty when required and deployment may involve transient rapid pacing according to valve/technique. Anticipate hypotension and recovery of perfusion promptly. Sudden collapse requires immediate operator communication and echo/angiography for tamponade, annular/aortic injury, acute AR, coronary obstruction, embolised valve, bleeding or heart block, with pacing, perfusion and surgical rescue organised. Severe AS is diagnosed integratively: low-flow/low-gradient disease may not meet every gradient/velocity criterion, and untreated prognosis depends on symptoms and ventricular state.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Explains AS physiology and integrative severity
- **2 marks** — Compares current Heart Team/lifetime SAVR–TAVI selection
- **2 marks** — Describes surgical AVR steps and TOE checks
- **2 marks** — Plans TAVI anaesthesia/deployment/pacing and monitoring
- **2 marks** — Recognises collapse causes and provides procedural/surgical rescue

items.title: 10. Anaesthetic issues on bypass and aortic cannulation
items.q: Outline the anaesthetic issues during cardiopulmonary bypass, including the implications of aortic disease for aortic cannulation.
items.a:
## The circuit

Venous blood drains by gravity or vacuum from the right atrium (or bicaval cannulae) to a **reservoir**, through a **pump** (roller or centrifugal), a **membrane oxygenator with heat exchanger**, arterial filter and bubble trap, and returns via an **aortic cannula**. Added: cardiotomy suction, vent, cell saver, cardioplegia delivery and haemofilter.

## Cannulation

- **Aortic:** ascending aorta; risks are dissection, atheroemboli and malposition (high line pressure, asymmetric arm pressures). Alternatives are femoral or axillary in dissection or porcelain aorta.
- **Venous:** two-stage right atrial, or bicaval cannulation for right-sided opening; risks are air lock, arrhythmia and poor drainage with hypotension.
- **Confirm heparinisation before cannulation.**

## Anticoagulation

Give **unfractionated heparin 300 to 400 units/kg** and confirm an **ACT above 480 seconds** before bypass, then recheck regularly (ACT every 30 minutes, adding heparin if falling). Heparin resistance (more than 500 units/kg to reach ACT 400 to 480) occurs in up to 20%, from antithrombin deficiency (congenital or acquired by heparin therapy, falling 5 to 7% per day, or liver disease and DIC); treat by mechanism with additional heparin, antithrombin supplementation (e.g. an initial 1000 units in some protocols, adjusted to activity/response) or selected plasma. **After stable separation**, reverse residual heparin with titrated protamine, slowly (approximately 1 mg per 100 units remaining heparin, often less than a fixed dose based on all administered heparin) (vasodilation, pulmonary hypertension, anaphylaxis).

## Myocardial protection

The aim is a still, bloodless, protected heart after **aortic cross-clamping**. **Cardioplegia** (hyperkalaemic, cold blood or crystalloid, antegrade via the aortic root or retrograde via the coronary sinus, redosed according to formulation, temperature, route and operative protocol rather than a fixed universal interval) causes depolarised diastolic arrest, with hypothermia and a reduced metabolic rate. The heart is vulnerable to poor distribution (severe coronary disease, LV hypertrophy, aortic regurgitation causing LV distension), so check for aortic regurgitation before cross-clamping (LV vent) and check the left ventricle is not distended.

## Anaesthetic role on bypass

Maintain anaesthesia and relaxation, individualised perfusion pressure, measured flow/oxygen delivery (indexed flow often initially 2.2–2.4 L/min/m²), temperature, glucose and electrolytes, review ACT, and watch for hypotension (haemodilution, vasodilation), inadequate venous drainage, high arterial line pressure, awareness and cerebral perfusion.

## Safe CPB initiation and anaesthesia delivery

Use the team checklist before flow: correct patient/operation/circuit, anticoagulation demonstrated with the relevant ACT instrument, oxygen/sweep and heater-cooler working, primed/de-aired circuit, bubble/level/pressure alarms and arterial filter active, cannula sites/positions secure and monitoring baselines recorded. Start with observed venous drainage and arterial return, watch line pressure, bilateral pressure/NIRS where appropriate and the heart for distension or dissection. Confirm pump output can supply the intended oxygen delivery. Do not proceed on a dose of heparin alone without demonstrated anticoagulation.

**Anaesthesia on CPB** is an active task: haemodilution, hypothermia and circuit binding change drug concentration and EEG. Verify volatile-agent delivery via a compatible oxygenator/vaporiser and scavenging if used; otherwise maintain a reliable IV infusion, with its delivery line reaching the patient/circuit as intended. The machine vaporiser being on does not prove anaesthetic delivery to a patient fully on CPB. Continue analgesia and appropriate neuromuscular blockade, use processed EEG in context and ensure delivery when changing pump/ventilator support. Blood-gas sampling and oxygen delivery, anticoagulation and temperature checks continue at the local frequency. For aortic atheroma, epiaortic ultrasound complements TOE (which has a blind region); consider a no-touch or alternative inflow strategy. In dissection, confirm true-lumen perfusion and watch for regional malperfusion. Detailed myocardial protection and CPB emergencies are worked in R28 and R24.

**Oxygenator compatibility:** volatile transfer differs by membrane type; the 2024 CPB guideline cautions against relying on volatile delivery with polymethylpentene oxygenators. Confirm the approved system and use reliable IV anaesthesia when transfer is unsuitable. Most ECMO membranes are not interchangeable with CPB volatile-delivery equipment.

**Goal-directed perfusion example:** indexed oxygen delivery depends on actual arterial flow × arterial oxygen content (Hb, saturation and dissolved O2), not pump RPM alone. The 2024 CPB guideline supports limiting depth/duration of low DO2 and gives a normothermic lower-target range around **280–300 mL O2/min/m²** to consider. Individualise with temperature/risk and venous saturation/extraction/lactate; do not transfuse or increase flow from one number without checking measurement, drainage and oxygenator function.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Describes circuit and cannulation/aortic-disease implications
- **2 marks** — Safely initiates CPB with demonstrated anticoagulation
- **2 marks** — Maintains anaesthesia and verifies route/delivery
- **2 marks** — Monitors flow/oxygen delivery, gas, temperature and metabolites
- **2 marks** — Explains myocardial protection and safe separation/reversal

items.title: 11. Therapeutic hypothermia: cooling and rewarming problems
items.q: Discuss the physiological effects of therapeutic hypothermia in cardiac surgery and the problems of cooling and rewarming.
items.a:
## Why cool on bypass

Hypothermia reduces **metabolic rate** (about 6 to 7% per degree for the brain, roughly halving at 28 degrees and falling to about 20 to 25% of normal at 18 degrees), allowing lower flows and protecting organs, and enables circulatory arrest. State the classification and site: aortic-arch consensus uses mild 28.1–34, moderate 20.1–28, deep 14.1–20 and profound ≤14 °C; other perioperative classifications differ. DHCA often uses approximately 18–20 °C, and contemporary arch strategies may use moderate cooling with cerebral perfusion.

## Physiological effects

| System | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Cardiac** | Bradycardia, prolonged conduction (PR, QRS, QT), **Increasing ventricular irritability/VF risk with deeper cooling (no deterministic temperature threshold)**, reduced contractility; Osborn J waves |
| **Cerebral** | Reduced metabolic rate and flow; autoregulation lost at deep levels |
| **Respiratory/blood gas** | Gases become more soluble, so measured PaCO2 and pH at 37 degrees differ from the patient's; left shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin curve and impaired tissue oxygen release |
| **Coagulation** | Platelet dysfunction, slowed enzyme cascade, fibrinolysis |
| **Renal and metabolic** | Cold diuresis, insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia, reduced drug metabolism |
| **Immune/wound** | Infection risk |

## Acid-base strategy

**Alpha-stat** (gases interpreted at 37 degrees, no CO2 added; preserves enzyme function and cerebral autoregulation) is usual in adults; **pH-stat** (CO2 added to correct for temperature; increases cerebral blood flow, uncoupling it from metabolism) is used in deep cooling and paediatrics.

## Management on bypass

- Cool and rewarm at controlled rates; keep the oxygenator arterial–venous gradient within the perfusion protocol (generally no more than 10 °C, with a smaller gradient during later rewarming), and arterial outlet blood temperature below 37 °C to avoid gas bubble formation and cerebral hyperthermia.
- Maintain anaesthesia and relaxation (shivering after rewarming raises oxygen demand), and monitor brain temperature (nasopharyngeal) with core (bladder or rectal) readings.
- Recheck potassium, glucose and ionised calcium and anticipate rewarming vasodilation.
- After bypass, avoid **afterdrop** by rewarming to over 36 degrees with warming blankets and warmed fluids, and remember that cooling lowers drug requirement but residual hypothermia prolongs recovery.

## Cooling, gas strategy and safe rewarming

Arterial outlet, nasopharyngeal and slower core sites measure different compartments; no single reading proves uniform brain/body temperature. Avoid large temperature gradients and rewarm slowly (commonly ≤0.5 °C/min in the later phase); an oxygenator arterial–venous gradient ≤4 °C when arterial outlet is ≥30 °C is a commonly cited adult strategy. Keep arterial outlet below 37 °C to avoid cerebral hyperthermia. Do not confuse these with an arbitrary body-to-water bath gradient. Monitor tissue perfusion and oxygen delivery throughout cooling/rewarming; metabolic demand rises on warming before all compartments equilibrate.

Alpha-stat is common for adult routine CPB; pH-stat may aid homogeneous deep cooling but increases cerebral flow and embolic delivery. Agree the strategy and when it changes. Cold blood gases measured at 37 °C must be interpreted consistently, rather than “corrected” twice. Watch K shifts from cardioplegia/cooling/rewarming, ionised calcium, glucose, rhythm, coagulation and drug accumulation. Treat afterdrop with ongoing warming and avoid shivering; separate only when the heart, ventilation and systemic state are ready, not on temperature alone.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Explains cooling metabolic benefits and correct convention
- **2 marks** — Explains cardiac/coagulation/gas/metabolic effects
- **2 marks** — Distinguishes alpha-stat and pH-stat
- **2 marks** — Monitors multiple sites and controls rewarming gradients/outlet
- **2 marks** — Anticipates afterdrop/drug accumulation and separation readiness

items.title: 12. Ventricular fibrillation in ICU after cardiac surgery
items.q: A patient fibrillates in the ICU four hours after cardiac surgery. Describe the management, including the role of internal defibrillation.
items.a:
## Context

After cardiac surgery, an arrest is usually VF/pulseless VT, asystole or pacing failure, and **tamponade, bleeding, tension pneumothorax, hypovolaemia and graft occlusion** are common causes. The management follows **cardiac surgical life support** in an appropriate trained setting: rapid correction of VF/pacing failure and tamponade is crucial. Potential injury from compressions does not justify prolonged withholding of CPR.

## Rhythm-specific approach

- Call the arrest/cardiac surgical team, confirm absent output on arterial trace/clinical assessment, give 100% oxygen, and check airway/circuit while allocating roles.
- **Witnessed monitored VF/pVT, trained team and defibrillator immediately available:** deliver up to three rapid sequential shocks within the first minute. If unsuccessful, commence CPR promptly while the team prepares resternotomy. If shocks are not immediately available, start CPR.
- **Asystole/severe bradycardia with wires:** attempt immediate epicardial pacing at adequate output and confirm mechanical capture. If unsuccessful, commence CPR within 1 minute; do not persist with ineffective pacing.
- **PEA:** commence CPR and diagnose reversible causes urgently; briefly assess whether pacing artefact masks VF without a prolonged interruption in support.
- Use the local cardiac surgical drug pathway. Routine full-dose adrenaline can cause severe hypertension when a reversible cause is corrected; this is not a blanket instruction to withhold all vasopressor treatment. Antiarrhythmic treatment follows the refractory VF protocol. Standard ALS applies without delay when the specialised setting/team is absent.

## Defibrillation

External shocks 150 to 200 J biphasic, then increasing. **Internal** sterile paddles applied directly to the exposed heart, commonly starting at **10–20 J** using the device/local protocol during open chest, after sternal opening. If an ICD is in situ, the device should be left or magnet applied only per plan.

## Resternotomy

Do **emergency resternotomy within five minutes** if shocks fail, or if the cause is tamponade. Prepare a pack, ensure the surgeon, perfusionist and scrub nurse call; internal massage is more effective than external; consider rapid return to bypass or ECMO (extracorporeal CPR).

## Anaesthetic role

Airway and ventilation with 100% oxygen, treat reversible causes (volume, K, Mg, calcium, pH, tension pneumothorax), drugs and fluids via central access, TOE for tamponade, and avoid vasopressin or calcium unless indicated. Record the time of arrest.

## Post-arrest

Recovery on ICU with post-arrest temperature control and fever prevention according to the current resuscitation plan, evaluation of cause (echo, ECG, graft assessment), neurological monitoring, and an early plan for mechanical circulatory support if unstable.

## Internal defibrillation and team actions

Ensure everyone is clear, oxygen/fire hazards addressed, sterile paddles correctly contact the heart and low-energy internal shocks follow the defibrillator’s specification. A closed chest cannot receive an “internal” shock; minimally invasive access may require external pads. Assign compressor/airway/defibrillator/pacing, team leader, surgical reopening and perfusion roles. Prepare and perform resternotomy by trained personnel with equipment and PPE; avoid cutting grafts/wires blindly. Once open, relieve clot/tamponade, identify haemorrhage/graft issues and use internal massage while arranging definitive repair or CPB/ECLS. The ≤5-minute resternotomy goal must not become a five-minute pause without circulation. After ROSC treat the cause, recheck devices, perfusion, temperature and neurological status. These principles reflect AHA 2025 special-circumstance recommendations plus the STS cardiac-surgical consensus; apply the unit’s rehearsed pathway.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Recognises arrest and mobilises trained cardiac-surgical team
- **2 marks** — Uses rapid shock/pacing pathway with CPR within one minute if unsuccessful
- **2 marks** — Describes safe internal versus external shock technique
- **2 marks** — Provides timely trained resternotomy/internal massage/source treatment
- **2 marks** — Explains drugs/context/ALS fallback and post-ROSC care

items.title: 13. Complications of interventional cardiology procedures
items.q: Outline the major complications of interventional cardiology procedures (including percutaneous coronary intervention and transcatheter valve procedures), their presentation and their management in the catheter laboratory.
items.a:
## Why the anaesthetist is involved

Interventional procedures are increasingly done under sedation or general anaesthesia in sick patients: AF ablation, TAVI, MitraClip, left atrial appendage closure, coronary intervention for complex disease, and pacemaker or ICD implantation. The anaesthetist manages both the procedure and its complications.

## Complications

**Vascular and bleeding:** access-site haematoma, retroperitoneal bleed, pseudoaneurysm, arteriovenous fistula.

**Cardiac:** **tamponade** (about 1% in AF ablation; the commonest major cause of death), coronary occlusion or dissection, arrhythmia (VF, bradyarrhythmia, heart block), valve injury, device embolisation.

**AF ablation specifics (2021 chapter):** major complications about 2%, left atrial–oesophageal fistula (about 0.1%, high mortality if unrecognised), phrenic nerve injury (risk varies with technique, including cryoballoon), pulmonary vein stenosis, stroke and air embolism.

**Neurological:** stroke from thrombus, air or debris.

**Contrast and radiation:** contrast nephropathy, anaphylaxis, radiation exposure.

## Gas embolism

Detected by TOE, which can detect small amounts of intracardiac gas, presenting with hypotension, arrhythmia, falling end-tidal CO2 and hypoxia. Treatment: stop the source and nitrous oxide, **FiO2 1.0**, volume and vasopressors, avoid further air entry, consider aspiration only through suitably positioned existing access, and use positioning according to venous versus arterial/cerebral embolism; do not delay resuscitation or definitive therapy for a head-down manoeuvre, supportive care and **hyperbaric oxygen** for cerebral or large embolism.

## Anaesthetic management

- **AF ablation:** general anaesthesia preferred (immobility and airway control), often remifentanil with TIVA, jet or high-frequency low-volume ventilation, a thrombus-exclusion strategy according to anticoagulant history and EP protocol, and **heparin** around transseptal access with ACT targets commonly ≥300 seconds, specifically agreed with the operator, uninterrupted anticoagulation.
- Maintain a stable rhythm and haemodynamics, with defibrillation pads and rescue pacing ready.
- Keep reversal of heparin (protamine) and surgical backup for tamponade (pericardiocentesis, thoracotomy).

Recognition of tamponade is a priority: falling pressure, rising CVP, loss of the pulse pressure and a pericardial effusion on echo.

## Presentation-to-action links

| Sudden finding | Suspect | Immediate response with the operator |
|---|---|---|
| Hypotension, rising CVP, effusion | Perforation/tamponade | Resuscitate, urgent echo, pericardial drainage/covered stent or balloon control, surgical rescue; heparin reversal is coordinated against active instrumentation/thrombosis risk |
| ST change, ventricular arrhythmia, new regional dysfunction | Coronary occlusion, dissection, air or no-reflow | Restore oxygenation/perfusion, defibrillate if needed, immediate angiographic diagnosis and PCI/rescue |
| Hypotension with falling Hb, groin/back pain | Access/retroperitoneal haemorrhage | Major-haemorrhage support and endovascular/surgical control; consider concealed blood loss |
| New block after TAVI | Conduction injury | Temporary pacing and monitored conduction pathway; assess permanent pacing need |
| Delayed fever, chest pain, neurological signs after AF ablation | Atrio-oesophageal fistula | Urgent specialist assessment and CT; avoid routine oesophageal instrumentation/endoscopy that can introduce air |
| Focal deficit or reduced consciousness | Cerebral embolism | Activate stroke pathway and imaging, specialist reperfusion decision |

Ensure remote-location anaesthesia standards, radiation protection, accessible airway, reliable infusion extensions, defibrillation/pacing and an explicit emergency surgery/perfusion plan. Procedure-specific complication rates vary with technology (including thermal versus pulsed-field AF ablation) and centre experience; old percentages must not be quoted as universal contemporary rates. Continue anticoagulant management with the operator and protect against both tamponade bleeding and device/stent thrombosis.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Identifies access, coronary, valve, rhythm and neurological complications
- **2 marks** — Links tamponade/bleeding/ischaemia presentations to rescue
- **2 marks** — Explains ablation-specific delayed fistula and other risks
- **2 marks** — Coordinates anticoagulation, imaging and operator/surgical actions
- **2 marks** — Provides remote-site airway/radiation/resuscitation plan

items.title: 14. Bypass and ECMO support for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: Outline the indications for cardiopulmonary bypass and ECMO in non-cardiac surgery and the anaesthetic issues of managing a patient on extracorporeal support.
items.a:
## Indications for bypass or ECMO support in non-cardiac surgery

- **Surgery on or near great vessels and the heart:** large thoracic or abdominal aortic aneurysm, tumours involving the vena cava or right atrium (renal cell carcinoma, thrombus), or pulmonary thromboendarterectomy.
- **Resection of airway or mediastinal masses** with expected airway loss: femoral veno-arterial or veno-venous ECMO before induction.
- **Pulmonary:** lung transplantation, tracheal resection, massive pulmonary embolism.
- **Cardiac or respiratory failure** needing support during an operation, and **hypothermic** or **drowning** rescue cases.
- **Trauma** (hepatic or caval injuries) and rarely **hyperthermia or poisoning** rescue.

## Planning

Multidisciplinary meeting (surgeon, perfusionist, anaesthetist, intensivist), clear **indication and exit plan**, availability of a perfusionist and ECMO team, cannulation under local anaesthetic before induction where airway loss is a risk, and **heparin** with an ACT target matched to configuration, duration and bleeding risk; old heterogeneous bleeding percentages are not patient-specific estimates. Choose anticoagulation and platelet targets for bleeding risk, configuration and duration; a universal platelet count >100 ×10⁹/L is not required for every ECMO situation. Reversal strategy and rescue transfusion are planned.

## Circuit configurations (2017 chapter)

- **VV-ECMO:** oxygenation and CO2 removal; flow 3.5 to 6 L/min; oxygenation depends on ECMO flow relative to cardiac output; sweep gas controls CO2 (BJA 2024).
