- **VA-ECMO:** circulatory and respiratory support; pulsatility varies with native ejection; MAP depends on circuit flow, native output and SVR, and does not automatically require vasopressors; risk of **differential hypoxia** (watch right-arm saturation) and LV distension.

## Anaesthetic issues

- Anticoagulation and bleeding; lung-protective ventilation (driving pressure below 15, plateau below 25); drug sequestration in the circuit (propofol, fentanyl), hypothermia and awareness monitoring.
- Positioning, line placement, and recognition of complications: air embolism, recirculation, access insufficiency, oxygenator failure.

Weaning is stepwise, with echocardiography to confirm recovery, and reversal of heparin avoided in the circuit.

## Choosing support before induction

Separate a plan for respiratory failure from a plan for circulatory collapse: VV ECMO cannot directly replace cardiac output in a patient whose mediastinal lesion obstructs venous return or compresses the heart. VA or another configuration may be needed. In critical airway surgery, agree what loss of airway/haemodynamics is expected, whether cannulation/support must be established awake before induction, and the maximum safe delay to rescue. “ECMO on standby” without access, personnel and a feasible cannulation time is not equivalent to established support. CPB is useful when a reservoir/suction, rapid volume control or planned cardiac entry/arrest is required, at the cost of greater heparinisation/inflammatory exposure; ECMO is a closed longer-duration support circuit with different anticoagulation requirements.

Agree drainage/return sites compatible with the surgical field and positioning, imaging guidance, priming/de-airing, gas/power backup, haemorrhage rescue and an exit/withdrawal strategy. Protect cannulae during transfer and repositioning. Monitor patient gases and perfusion as well as circuit parameters, recognise air entrainment/low flow/oxygenator failure and plan anticoagulation interruption only with the ECMO team. Drug effects vary across the course of support, so titrate anaesthesia and analgesia to clinical/EEG endpoints rather than simply increasing all lipophilic drugs.

## Blue Book 2025: airway tumours and lung transplantation

For near-total distal airway obstruction, conventional intubation/jet ventilation or front-of-neck access may not bypass the lesion. The 2025 tracheal-tumour chapter and 2023 BJAEd airway ECMO review support planned specialist ECMO assessment; severe symptoms, position intolerance and very narrow lumen are warning features, not a universally validated numeric trigger. Establishing support before induction may be necessary. VV is usually suitable for isolated respiratory support; cardiac/great-vessel compression may require VA/hybrid support, with an upper-body oxygenation strategy during prolonged apnoea.

The 2025 lung-transplant chapter illustrates extracorporeal support for hypoxaemia/hypercarbia, RV/pulmonary vascular intolerance to PA clamping, haemodynamic collapse during manipulation, controlled graft reperfusion or primary graft dysfunction. Decide elective versus rescue and VV versus VA by respiratory and circulatory needs. CPB adds reservoir/suction/volume-control options but usually more anticoagulation, dilution and inflammatory exposure. ECMO can continue into ICU when gas exchange or RV/haemodynamic function remains inadequate; assess graft perfusion/venous drainage with TOE and respiratory function with bronchoscopy/gases. The chapter’s specific flow/pressure thresholds are centre strategies, not universal targets. These are Set 13 support principles; full transplant anaesthesia and tracheal resection technique remain in their procedural sets.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Identifies relevant airway/vascular/transplant support indications
- **2 marks** — Chooses VV/VA/CPB for respiratory versus circulatory needs
- **2 marks** — Distinguishes planned support, standby and delayed rescue
- **2 marks** — Plans cannulation, anticoagulation, drugs/monitoring and complications
- **2 marks** — Defines exit/transfer and upper-body oxygenation strategy

items.title: 15. Neurological complications of cardiac surgery
items.q: Discuss the neurological complications of cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass and the strategies to reduce them.
items.a:
## Stroke and delirium after cardiac surgery

Stroke occurs in about 1 to 5% of cardiac operations (higher with valve and aortic surgery), and delirium in up to 30 to 50%. Both increase mortality, stay and long-term cognitive decline.

## Mechanisms

- **Embolic:** atheroma from aortic manipulation (cannulation, cross-clamp), particulate and **gaseous** emboli (see the gas embolism chapter), valve debris, left atrial thrombus, and AF; **postoperative AF** is associated with a higher stroke risk (OR 3.5 in the POISE cohort).
- **Hypoperfusion:** hypotension on or off bypass, carotid or intracranial stenosis, low cardiac output.
- **Inflammation and microvascular injury**, hyperglycaemia, hyperthermia on rewarming, and cerebral oedema.
- **Delirium:** age, preexisting cognitive impairment, alcohol, sleep deprivation, drugs (benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, high-dose opioids), pain, infection and metabolic disturbance.

## Neuroprotection and prevention

- **1.** **Preoperative:** neurological history and selective carotid assessment according to symptoms/risk, identify cognitive impairment and alcohol use, and anticoagulate AF appropriately.
- **2.** **Surgical:** no-touch or epiaortic scanning for atheroma, off-pump or minimal aortic manipulation, de-airing and carbon dioxide field flooding.
- **3.** **Perfusion:** adequate MAP (above 65 to 70, higher in cerebrovascular disease), alpha-stat management, avoid hyperthermia above 37 degrees, arterial filter, and glucose below about 10 mmol/L.
- **4.** **Monitoring:** cerebral oximetry (NIRS) and processed EEG; bypass temperature control.
- **5.** **Anaesthesia:** avoid deep sedation and benzodiazepines; dexmedetomidine may facilitate selected sedation plans but small-study AF figures do not establish universal delirium prevention; weigh bradycardia and hypotension.
- **6.** **Delirium bundle:** reorientation, sleep, early mobilisation, vision and hearing aids, analgesia, avoidance of deliriogenic drugs, and treating infection.

## Management of stroke

Early recognition, CT/CT angiography, discussion with stroke teams (thrombectomy may be considered, while recent major cardiac surgery creates major thrombolysis bleeding risk, requiring specialist assessment rather than delaying stroke activation), blood pressure and temperature control, and rehabilitation.

## Respond to neurological deterioration

Record baseline cognition/deficits and the time last known normal. Check glucose, temperature, oxygenation/CO2, residual sedatives/NMBD, seizures and perfusion promptly; a focal deficit or unexplained coma requires stroke/neurological activation and urgent CT/CTA. Do not attribute every delayed awakening to CPB or sedation. Large-vessel thrombectomy may remain possible despite major surgery, while systemic thrombolysis requires a careful bleeding-risk decision.

NIRS is a trend monitor with extracranial contamination and baseline variability, not a direct guarantee of cerebral flow. A new unilateral fall suggests cannula/arch-vessel malperfusion; a bilateral fall prompts checks of sensor position, MAP/flow, Hb/oxygenation and CO2. Correct the cause with the perfusion/surgical team. Processed EEG helps detect excessive suppression/anaesthetic delivery problems but is temperature-sensitive. Explain that aortic manipulation reduction, de-airing, adequate oxygen delivery and controlled rewarming are mechanistically rational; not every monitor or drug has demonstrated a universal reduction in stroke/cognitive decline. Screen for hypoactive delirium as well as agitation and treat precipitating illness.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Distinguishes stroke/delirium and major mechanisms
- **2 marks** — Targets aortic manipulation/embolism and adequate delivery
- **2 marks** — Controls temperature/glucose/anaesthesia and treats NIRS changes
- **2 marks** — Uses delirium prevention/screening bundle
- **2 marks** — Activates neurological imaging/stroke pathway promptly

items.title: 16. ECMO for severe respiratory failure
items.q: Outline the indications for ECMO in severe respiratory failure and the principles of its delivery.
items.a:
## Principle

VV-ECMO drains venous blood, oxygenates it across a membrane and returns it to the right atrium. It supports gas exchange (and reduces ventilator injury) while the lung recovers, in **reversible severe respiratory failure refractory to conventional care**. Flow is 3.5 to 6 L/min. **Oxygenation** depends on the ratio of ECMO flow to cardiac output (so high flow is needed in sepsis), while **CO2 removal** is controlled by sweep gas flow (above 1 L/min sweep does not improve oxygenation). It may also help RV function by reducing hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction and hypercarbia.

## Indications

ELSO-style criteria: P/F below 10.7 kPa (80 mmHg) after optimal care including prone positioning, or pH below 7.25 with respiratory rate 35 and plateau pressure of 30 or less; also bridge to lung transplantation. The 2017 chapter notes mortality of at least 50% for a P/F below 150 on FiO2 0.9 and about 80% below 100.

**Evidence:** CESAR (180 patients; survival without disability at 6 months 63% versus 47%, confounded by transfer to a specialist centre and protective ventilation); EOLIA (249 patients; no significant 60-day mortality difference, but 28% of controls crossed over); meta-analyses showed RR for death 0.73 at 60 days. Survival in the 2015 ELSO registry for VV was 57%.

## Contraindications

Only absolute: an irreversible diagnosis without a plan for decannulation. Relative: ventilation above 7 days, immunosuppression, age, obesity affecting cannulation, multiorgan failure, severe neurological injury and cardiac arrest of over 15 minutes.

## Management on ECMO

- **Ultraprotective ventilation:** driving pressure below 15, plateau below 25, rate 4 to 15, tidal volume below 4 mL/kg, to rest the lung.
- **Anticoagulation** with heparin; bleeding and thrombosis require repeated reassessment, with anticoagulation/platelet targets individualised. Temporary reduced/no systemic anticoagulation may be required for severe bleeding under ECMO-centre supervision; examine the circuit.
- Complications: **recirculation** (depends on cannula configuration, separation, return-jet direction and flow, not one universal tip distance), access insufficiency, air embolism, oxygenator failure, infection up to 45%, and haemolysis.
- Drug sequestration in the circuit (lipophilic drugs).

## Weaning

When lung recovery permits, reduce sweep/oxygen fraction and perform a supervised off-sweep trial on safe ventilator settings, while maintaining adequate circuit blood flow to avoid thrombosis. Assess oxygenation, CO2, work of breathing and haemodynamics; decannulate with a bleeding/anticoagulation plan. VV weaning is not simply progressively reducing pump flow as in VA weaning.

## Use referral criteria correctly

A referral threshold is not automatic acceptance or cannulation. Discuss trajectory early with a specialist centre after protective ventilation, appropriate PEEP and prone positioning where feasible; do not wait until unsafe transfer or irreversible multiorgan injury. Reversibility or a bridge-to-transplant destination is essential. Age, ventilation duration, frailty, neurological injury and extrapulmonary organ failure inform a case-specific decision rather than one absolute age/BMI/arrest-duration cut-off. RESP/PRESET-type scores support prognostic discussion but are not stand-alone exclusion rules. Historic registry survival and the very broad bleeding range are not current patient-specific predictions.

The 2026 physiology review differentiates **mode** VV from **configuration** V-V, (dl)V-V or VV-V: drainage is left of the hyphen and return right. State sites and return-jet direction as well as letters. Oxygen transfer depends on effective circuit blood flow, Hb, inlet content and membrane function; systemic oxygenation also depends on native CO, recirculation and lung function. Sweep predominantly controls CO2, and its oxygen fraction is a separate variable. Avoid rapid large PaCO2 corrections, assess neurological/perfusion consequences and maintain ultraprotective ventilation while treating the lung disease. R29 provides a worked hypoxaemia/membrane-failure calculation rather than treating all desaturation by turning up sweep.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — States refractory respiratory/bridge indications and referral nuance
- **2 marks** — Interprets selection/risk and CESAR/EOLIA limits
- **2 marks** — Explains circuit/configuration, flow versus sweep and Hb
- **2 marks** — Plans protective ventilation, anticoagulation and complications
- **2 marks** — Describes safe off-sweep trial and decannulation

items.title: 17. IABP with falling augmentation and a cold leg
items.q: A patient with an intra-aortic balloon pump develops a falling augmentation pressure and a cold left leg. Describe how you would troubleshoot the device and its complications.
items.a:
## Principle

The balloon inflates at the **dicrotic notch** and deflates just before systole. Diastolic inflation raises aortic root diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion; systolic deflation reduces afterload. The 2022.1 trace (labels A–F) tests recognition of unassisted and assisted systole, the dicrotic notch, unassisted and assisted end-diastolic pressure, and diastolic augmentation.

## Timing errors

| Fault | Trace | Effect | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Early inflation** | Inflation before the notch | Valve closes early, lower stroke volume | Delay inflation |
| **Late inflation** | Notch visible, loss of augmentation | Less coronary flow | Advance inflation |
| **Early deflation** | Assisted end-diastolic pressure not lowered | Coronary steal, loss of afterload benefit | Delay deflation |
| **Late deflation** | Prolonged slope into systole | Raised afterload | Advance deflation |

## Other problems

- **Poor augmentation:** low volume in the balloon, balloon not inflated fully, kinked or low position, hypovolaemia, tachycardia or AF.
- **Trigger failure** with arrhythmia or pacing artefact: optimise ECG/pacer triggering or use arterial-pressure triggering where appropriate; an ungated internal trigger is reserved for specific circumstances and is unsafe as a reflex in a beating heart.
- **Gas leak** (blood in the tubing, alarms): stop and remove urgently, as the balloon can clot.
- **Position:** tip below the left subclavian (about 2 cm below the aortic knob).

## Complications

Limb ischaemia (the commonest), aortic injury or dissection, thrombocytopenia and haemolysis, infection, stroke or embolism, renal artery occlusion and gut ischaemia from migration, and bleeding.

## Weaning

Reduce the assist ratio from 1:1 to 1:2 to 1:3, or reduce augmentation, over hours, while monitoring pressures, urine output and lactate; remove when stable and anticoagulation allows, with firm pressure at the site and distal pulse checks. Avoid prolonged 1:3 ratio because of thrombosis.

## The cold leg is an emergency

Confirm both limbs’ colour, temperature, capillary refill, Doppler pulses, pain (if awake), motor/sensory state and insertion-site bleeding; call the cardiac/interventional and vascular teams immediately. Consider access-vessel occlusion, dissection, thromboembolism or a tight sheath, and do not postpone assessment while adjusting augmentation. Use bedside Doppler/vascular imaging as clinically feasible; threatened limb may need urgent catheter/sheath removal, revascularisation or alternative access while maintaining circulatory support by another means. Document the time and reassess perfusion repeatedly.

Poor augmentation also requires patient assessment: worsening shock, low stroke volume, AR, hypovolaemia, tachyarrhythmia and high afterload can all alter the trace. Inspect the complete trigger–timing–position–gas-delivery chain and compare assisted with unassisted beats using a brief safe 1:2 assessment. Positioning is judged with imaging/manufacturer landmarks, not a single distance below the aortic knob. An internal asynchronous trigger should not be selected indiscriminately in a heart with native beats. If balloon rupture is suspected, stop pumping and arrange urgent removal under the protocol; do not repeatedly inflate a balloon containing blood.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Treats threatened limb as urgent vascular complication
- **2 marks** — Assesses patient shock and compares assisted/unassisted traces
- **2 marks** — Corrects timing/trigger/position/gas faults safely
- **2 marks** — Recognises rupture/bleeding/thromboembolism/haemolysis
- **2 marks** — Plans specialist removal or alternative support and reassessment

items.title: 18. Duration of ventilation and fast-track after cardiac surgery
items.q: Discuss the factors that influence the duration of postoperative ventilation after cardiac surgery and the role of fast-track management.
items.a:
## Concept

**Fast-track** cardiac anaesthesia aims for **early extubation (within about 6 hours, often 1 to 4)** after cardiac surgery, with early mobilisation and discharge from ICU, without increasing mortality or complications. Benefits are less ventilator-related lung injury and sedation, earlier mobilisation, less delirium, shorter stay and lower cost. Risks: bleeding, agitation, haemodynamic instability and reintubation.

## Patient selection

Favourable: elective, preserved ventricular function, no major comorbidity (pulmonary, renal, obesity), simple surgery (CABG, valve), short bypass time, stable haemodynamics. Unfavourable: emergency, poor ventricular function, redo or complex surgery, long bypass, bleeding, or neurological complications.

## Anaesthetic techniques

- **Premedication** light; avoid long-acting benzodiazepines.
- **Opioid-sparing or titrated short-acting opioids** (remifentanil, low-dose fentanyl or sufentanil), propofol or volatile agents for maintenance, rocuronium with sugammadex reversal, and selected **dexmedetomidine**, considering bradycardia/hypotension; it does not guarantee prevention of AF or delirium.
- **Multimodal analgesia:** paracetamol, regional blocks (parasternal, erector spinae, serratus), ketamine; avoid NSAIDs in renal risk.
- Temperature control, early haemostasis and antifibrinolytic reduce bleeding.

## Extubation criteria

Normothermia, warm and haemodynamically stable with minimal vasopressors, no important ongoing bleeding/tamponade risk, with drain trend and patency assessed rather than a universal 100 mL/h gate, adequate gas exchange on low support, alert, cooperative and pain controlled, no arrhythmia, and normal acid-base and electrolytes.

## Postoperative care

Protocolised ICU or recovery care, extubation after a spontaneous breathing trial, mobilisation, early oral intake, analgesia and removal of drains and lines.

## Outcomes

Fast-track pathways can reduce ventilation time and resource use in selected patients; studies do not establish a universal mortality benefit; keep a low threshold for slowing the plan if bleeding, instability or unmet extubation criteria arise.

## Fast-track versus an enhanced-recovery pathway

Fast-track traditionally focuses on early extubation/short ICU stay. ERAS extends from education, nutrition, exercise and anaemia optimisation through safe anaesthesia, blood conservation, analgesia, delirium prevention, mobilisation and discharge support. Higher-risk patients may still benefit from ERAS elements even when early extubation is inappropriate. Do not require “no comorbidity” or make a time target override physiology.

Confirm adequate consciousness/airway protection, respiratory effort and gas exchange on suitable support, quantitative reversal of block, normothermia, stable rhythm/perfusion and an acceptable bleeding trajectory. Treat pain and PONV without excessive sedation; consider parasternal/fascial-plane techniques within anticoagulation and local-expertise limits. Neuraxial/deep techniques carry particular full-heparinisation risk, and gabapentinoids/dexmedetomidine are not automatically appropriate for every patient. Plan who will extubate, staffing and reintubation rescue, especially overnight. Follow mobilisation, oral nutrition, delirium screening, chest physiotherapy, glucose control, infection/VTE prevention and line/drain removal once safe. Report ventilation time and reintubation/complications together when evaluating the pathway.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Categorises patient/surgery/anaesthetic/postoperative ventilation factors
- **2 marks** — Distinguishes extubation target from whole ERAS pathway
- **2 marks** — Plans short-acting/titrated anaesthesia and safe multimodal analgesia
- **2 marks** — Uses physiological extubation readiness and rescue criteria
- **2 marks** — Plans staffed ICU mobilisation/nutrition/prevention and measures harm

items.title: 19. Failure to reach target ACT and HIT for bypass
items.q: A patient fails to reach an ACT of 480 seconds after 400 units/kg of heparin before cardiopulmonary bypass. Outline your approach, and describe the management of a patient with heparin-induced thrombocytopenia requiring bypass.
items.a:
## Heparin resistance

**Definition:** inability to reach the target ACT despite adequate dose: non-bypass more than 35,000 units over 24 hours; bypass more than **500 units/kg** to reach an ACT of 400 to 480 seconds (occurs in up to 20%).

**Causes:** **antithrombin deficiency**, congenital (about 1 in 5000) or acquired (heparin therapy lowers antithrombin 5 to 7% per day; liver disease; DIC; nephrotic syndrome; oestrogen), increased heparin binding proteins, thrombocytosis, high factor VIII or fibrinogen, and a wrong ACT test (haemodilution or hypothermia changes ACT).

**Management:** check dose, drug and ACT cartridge; give more heparin, then **antithrombin concentrate** (1000 units) or FFP if resistance persists. use validated heparin-concentration/anti-Xa testing with AT activity where available to clarify the mechanism; assay range and turnaround may limit its immediate CPB use.

## Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT)

**Type 2 HIT** is immune mediated: IgG antibodies to platelet factor 4–heparin complex cause platelet activation, thrombocytopenia and **thrombosis** (frequency varies by population and exposure; cardiac surgery has important risk and many non-HIT causes of thrombocytopenia), typically day 5 to 11 (earlier with recent exposure). Thrombotic mortality is up to 30%. Use the **4T score** (thrombocytopenia, timing, thrombosis, other causes) and confirm with immunoassay and functional assay.

**Management:** stop all heparin including flushes and heparin-coated lines, **no LMWH**; start a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, which is hepatically cleared, or bivalirudin, which has mainly proteolytic clearance but accumulates in renal dysfunction and requires infusion adjustment), avoid platelet transfusion unless bleeding, and avoid warfarin until platelets recover.

## Cardiac surgery with HIT

- **Acute HIT/subacute A (functional assay positive):** postpone if feasible until functional activity resolves. If urgent, **bivalirudin** is a usual CPB alternative in an experienced service; plasma exchange plus intraoperative heparin or heparin plus potent antiplatelet are specialist alternatives. An immunoassay-positive result alone is not equivalent to active HIT.
- **Subacute B (functional assay negative, immunoassay positive) or remote HIT (both negative):** ASH supports heparin limited to the intraoperative exposure, avoiding it before/after where indicated; this need not be a single bolus, since adequate CPB anticoagulation may require redosing. Monitor platelets after re-exposure.
- Monitor with ACT (ecarin clotting time where available) and ensure the pump prime is free of heparin.

## Anaesthetic points

Anticipate bleeding (no simple reversal for bivalirudin or argatroban), use cell salvage and viscoelastic testing, and involve haematology.

## Assay interpretation and a workable HIT CPB plan

Do not start CPB until anticoagulation is demonstrated by the team’s validated method. Recheck actual delivery/dose, sample timing and cartridge/instrument, review baseline ACT and supplements/drugs. Hypothermia, dilution and factor deficiency can prolong ACT without adequate heparin; high factor VIII/fibrinogen can create apparent resistance. Where available use heparin concentration/anti-Xa and AT activity to distinguish mechanisms, recognising that standard anti-Xa assays need dilution/validation at CPB concentrations and are not an immediate universal bedside substitute. Give further UFH or AT based on the findings; plasma supplies AT but adds volume and transfusion risk. Andexanet exposure can produce profound heparin resistance, so anticipate it and obtain specialist advice.

Use a correct 4Ts interpretation (0–3 low, 4–5 intermediate, 6–8 high) with clinical context; a biphasic platelet fall after CPB is more suspicious than the expected immediate fall. Do not equate PF4 immunoassay positivity with platelet-activating HIT. For urgent bivalirudin CPB, an experienced team uses a validated loading/prime/infusion regimen and ACT/ECT strategy, adjusts for renal function and avoids stagnant blood in reservoirs, shunts and operative pools because local drug breakdown permits clotting. There is no protamine reversal. Plan timing of cessation, bleeding management and postoperative non-heparin anticoagulation. Argatroban is hepatically cleared and may be considered in severe renal failure but has difficult CPB monitoring/bleeding management; it is not an interchangeable casual substitution.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Checks heparin delivery, test validity and actual resistance mechanisms
- **2 marks** — Treats with appropriate UFH/AT/plasma and verifies anticoagulation
- **2 marks** — Diagnoses HIT with correct 4Ts/functional versus immunoassay distinction
- **2 marks** — Uses phase-specific timing/heparin versus alternative strategy
- **2 marks** — Plans bivalirudin monitoring/renal/stasis/reversal limitations

items.title: 20. Redo cardiac surgery
items.q: Outline the specific anaesthetic and surgical issues associated with redo cardiac surgery.
items.a:
## Why redo surgery is high risk

Adhesions between the sternum and heart/grafts cause a risk of **catastrophic haemorrhage on resternotomy** (RV, aorta, vein grafts, and a patent LIMA graft); longer operating and bypass times; more coagulopathy; and patients are older and sicker. Operative mortality is higher than first-time surgery.

## Preoperative

- **CT of the chest** to show the relationship between the sternum, RV, aorta and grafts; plan peripheral cannulation (femoral or axillary) and **bypass before sternotomy** if the heart or grafts lie directly beneath the sternum.
- Assess ventricular function, graft status and comorbidity; antiplatelet and anticoagulant management.
- **Two large-bore IV lines, arterial line and defibrillator pads on** before sternotomy; cross-matched blood available; perfusionist ready with the circuit primed.
- Cell salvage.

## Intraoperative

- Oscillating saw resternotomy with pauses, and surgeon-led dissection; ventilation held at apnoea during sternal division.
- If injury occurs: **immediate pressure**, urgent institution of bypass via femoral vessels, and volume resuscitation from the pump.
- Plan for **longer procedures and bypass times**, adequate protocolised heparinisation (redo surgery alone does not require a higher anticoagulation target), cardioprotection for patent grafts (a patent graft can wash out cardioplegia; planned isolation/occlusion or alternative cardioplegia delivery may be needed), and managing the RV.

## Haemostasis

Higher bleeding risk from dissection surfaces and prolonged bypass: antifibrinolytic, protamine reversal, fibrinogen, platelets and viscoelastic-guided therapy (R07).

## Postoperative

Expect more bleeding and tamponade, vasoplegia, AKI and arrhythmia, a need for pacing wires, and a higher chance of prolonged ventilation; mechanical support may be needed (R04, R17).

## Anaesthetic summary

Anticipate bleeding, prepare for emergency bypass, maintain haemodynamic stability, and communicate closely with the surgeon.

## Nuance from the 2024 redo-sternotomy review

Review the previous operative record and graft angiography as well as CT: identify patent IMA/vein graft routes, valves/conduits and structures close to the sternum. Agree protected peripheral access, elective pre-entry CPB versus a ready rescue strategy, cannulation/perfusion sites and a plan for graft injury with surgeon/perfusionist. Pre-entry peripheral CPB may reduce the consequences of re-entry injury but adds anticoagulation, bypass time, embolic/limb risks and bleeding during dissection; reserve it for the risk profile rather than every redo. Confirm adequate drainage and return before removing volume into a reservoir; assess distal-limb perfusion for femoral inflow.

Patent grafts can wash out cardioplegia or expose territories unevenly. Avoid unnecessary graft manipulation and plan myocardial protection with retrograde/selective delivery or temporary control as appropriate; monitor regional ischaemia. Prepare external pads, rapid infuser, blood/cell salvage and a rehearsed response to catastrophic entry bleeding: communicate, pressure/control bleeding, resuscitate and rapidly establish safe CPB with adequate anticoagulation. Do not assume emergency femoral cannulation is immediately possible without imaging/access preparation. After repair reassess residual lesions, haemostasis, chest closure effects and support needs; hand over increased risk of bleeding/tamponade, renal/neurological injury and infection.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Reviews CT/operative notes/grafts and stratifies re-entry risk
- **2 marks** — Weighs peripheral access/pre-entry CPB and its harms
- **2 marks** — Prepares blood/rapid infusion/cell salvage/pads/team roles
- **2 marks** — Explains graft protection/cardioplegia and catastrophic-bleed rescue
- **2 marks** — Provides haemostasis/closure reassessment and ICU plan

items.title: 21. Outline the surgical steps and anaesthetic management of off-pump CABG, includin
items.q: Outline the surgical steps and anaesthetic management of off-pump CABG, including haemodynamic collapse during cardiac displacement.
items.a:
## Surgical strategy and preparation

Off-pump CABG constructs anastomoses on the beating heart using displacement and local stabilisation rather than planned CPB/cardioplegic arrest. Sternotomy and conduit harvest are followed by systemic heparinisation to the off-pump protocol, exposure of each target, local stabiliser/intracoronary shunt where required, distal/proximal anastomoses and graft-flow assessment. A proximal aortic clamp may still be used: off-pump does **not** automatically mean no aortic manipulation. An anaortic/no-touch strategy is a separate surgical choice. Limited-access/robotic CABG may additionally require lung isolation and restrict emergency access.

Assess coronary anatomy, LV/RV function, valve disease, aortic atheroma and anticipated target access. Establish arterial pressure, ECG/ST, central access and TOE as appropriate, with defibrillation/pacing and a perfusionist/primed CPB rescue plan. Maintain anaesthesia, temperature, oxygenation, normal relevant electrolytes and myocardial supply–demand balance; off-pump does not remove blood-loss, awareness or anticoagulation risk. Have volume/vasoactive support ready before displacement, particularly for lateral/posterior targets.

## Why displacement causes instability

Lifting/rotating the heart can compress the RV, obstruct venous return, distort valves, impair filling and cause ischaemia/arrhythmia. Coronary occlusion during anastomosis can add regional dysfunction. A small underfilled LV and reduced output may reflect mechanical restriction rather than a need for a large fluid load. Observe TOE, pressure, ECG and the surgeon’s manoeuvres together.

For sudden hypotension, announce the change immediately, reduce/stop displacement or stabiliser pressure and restore the heart towards its normal position. Check rhythm, oxygenation, filling, regional ischaemia and the adequacy of the surgical shunt; treat arrhythmia, maintain coronary pressure with appropriate vasopressor and give small assessed volume increments only if helpful. Positioning may improve filling but must be coordinated. Avoid persisting with a technically convenient position while perfusion collapses.

## Rescue and postoperative implications

Agree a low threshold for **controlled conversion to CPB** if instability, ischaemia or inadequate exposure persists; emergency conversion after profound shock is riskier. Confirm adequate anticoagulation and a safe cannulation strategy, especially with a diseased aorta. Complete graft-flow/wall-motion checks, haemostasis, protamine when appropriate and postoperative monitoring. Discuss the balance: less extracorporeal exposure/haemodilution may help selected patients, but completeness and durability of revascularisation depend on anatomy and expertise; off-pump is not universally superior in survival, stroke or graft patency. The 2026 CABG review provides the surgical context; the physiological rescue sequence is an educator synthesis.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Explains beating-heart/stabilisation steps and aortic-manipulation distinction
- **2 marks** — Plans monitoring, anticoagulation and CPB rescue
- **3 marks** — Links displacement to RV/filling/ischaemia and immediately reverses the manoeuvre
- **2 marks** — Provides targeted support and controlled conversion triggers
- **1 mark** — Checks graft result and explains evidence limitations

items.title: 22. Describe the surgical steps and an appropriate anaesthetic technique for mitral
items.q: Describe the surgical steps and an appropriate anaesthetic technique for mitral valve replacement, distinguishing mitral stenosis from regurgitation and problems after separation.
items.a:
## Assess lesion and reserve

Review mechanism/severity, symptoms, LV and RV function, pulmonary hypertension, rhythm, prior embolism/endocarditis, anticoagulation and coronary disease. Severe **mitral stenosis** obstructs diastolic filling: avoid tachycardia, preserve sinus rhythm/AV contribution if possible, maintain appropriate preload without pulmonary oedema, preserve systemic perfusion and avoid increases in PVR. In **chronic MR**, forward flow benefits from avoiding bradycardia and excessive systemic afterload; maintain contractility and a suitable normal-to-moderate rate, with adequate rather than excessive preload. Acute MR or ventricular failure may need more urgent afterload/contractility support. These are lesion-specific goals, not a single fixed HR for every patient.

## Surgical steps

Sternotomy (or selected right thoracic access), systemic heparinisation, arterial/venous cannulation and CPB are followed by cross-clamp/cardioplegia and left atrial exposure. The diseased valve is excised as appropriate, preserving chordal/subvalvular continuity where feasible to maintain LV geometry. Size and seat the mechanical or tissue prosthesis, confirm unhindered leaflet/disc movement, close the atrium, de-air the left heart, reperfuse/rewarm and separate. Choice of prosthesis balances durability, anticoagulation, pregnancy considerations where applicable and patient preferences.

## Anaesthetic conduct

Use titrated cardiac GA with arterial pressure, central access, TOE, temperature, anticoagulation and gas/metabolic monitoring. Select a PAC for significant pulmonary hypertension/RV disease where its data will change treatment. Prepare pacing, vasopressors, inotropes and inhaled pulmonary vasodilator support. Maintain anaesthesia on CPB, adequate myocardial protection, anticoagulation and oxygen delivery. A minimally invasive approach may require OLV, peripheral CPB, specialised venous drainage and careful TOE guidance; an endoaortic balloon may migrate and compromise arch-vessel or coronary flow, requiring bilateral pressure/cerebral monitoring according to the technique. Plan external defibrillation and conversion access.

## Separation and postoperative checks

TOE assesses prosthesis movement/seating, residual/paravalvular regurgitation, gradients interpreted against flow/HR, LV/RV function, new regional changes, air and outflow obstruction. Exclude circumflex coronary injury, which may cause new lateral wall dysfunction. After correcting MR, removing the low-impedance regurgitant outlet can expose **afterload mismatch** and previously hidden LV dysfunction. Treat with appropriate inotropy/afterload/perfusion support and exclude ischaemia or a mechanical lesion. RV failure can follow longstanding pulmonary hypertension or perioperative injury (R2).

If a repair rather than replacement has been performed, assess residual MR/stenosis and **SAM/LVOT obstruction**. For SAM, optimise filling and afterload, reduce excessive inotropy/tachycardia and seek surgical reassessment if persistent. Do not treat all post-mitral hypotension with an inotrope. Plan prosthesis-specific anticoagulation, bleeding surveillance, pacing/conduction review and ICU handover. Mechanical mitral valves require VKA-based long-term anticoagulation rather than a DOAC.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Contrasts MS and MR physiological goals
- **2 marks** — Describes surgical sequence and chordal/prosthesis considerations
- **2 marks** — Plans cardiac anaesthesia/TOE and minimally invasive modifications
- **3 marks** — Checks prosthesis, circumflex injury, afterload mismatch, RV and SAM
- **1 mark** — Provides ICU and prosthesis-specific anticoagulation plan

items.title: 23. Outline the basic surgical steps of acute type A aortic dissection repair and th
items.q: Outline the basic surgical steps of acute type A aortic dissection repair and the anaesthetic implications of cannulation, cerebral protection and malperfusion.
items.a:
## Define the immediate problem

Type A dissection involves the ascending aorta and may cause rupture/tamponade, acute AR, coronary compromise and cerebral, renal, visceral or limb malperfusion. Review CT/echo and identify entry tear, true/false lumen, root/arch extent and branch involvement without delaying emergency repair. Record baseline neurological and limb/renal findings. Involve an experienced aortic surgical/perfusion/anaesthetic team, blood bank and ICU.

Analgesia and controlled heart rate/BP reduce shear when perfusion allows, but rigid anti-impulse targets are unsafe in shock, tamponade or critical malperfusion. Establish large-bore access, blood/rapid infusion/cell salvage, external pads and arterial monitoring appropriate to the anatomy (often more than one site); use TOE after careful induction. Avoid an abrupt fall in preload/SVR in tamponade or severe AR and be ready for immediate cannulation/rescue.

## Basic operation and perfusion strategy

After exposure, systemic heparinisation and cannulation establish CPB with confirmed **true-lumen perfusion**. The team may use axillary/innominate, imaging-guided central or selected femoral inflow according to anatomy and urgency. Axillary inflow can facilitate antegrade cerebral perfusion and avoid retrograde malperfusion, but no site is universally best or immediately feasible. Venous drainage, cooling, LV venting and myocardial protection are established. Severe AR may make root cardioplegia ineffective and distend the LV, requiring selective ostial/retrograde delivery and venting.

Resect the proximal tear/diseased ascending segment, replace it with a graft, and perform the distal anastomosis, often with systemic circulatory arrest and cerebral perfusion. Extent may include hemiarch/total arch and selected distal techniques. Preserve/resuspend the native valve when suitable; root replacement with valve-sparing reconstruction or a composite valved conduit/coronary reimplantation is selected for root destruction, aneurysm or other pathology. Re-establish systemic flow, complete anastomoses, de-air, reperfuse, rewarm and separate after checking repair and organ perfusion.

## Anaesthetic risks through the phases

Monitor bilateral cerebral oxygenation/pressure trends, temperature at appropriate sites, gases, Hb/oxygen delivery, ACT and urine/perfusion. Sudden unilateral desaturation or pressure change can signal arch-vessel malperfusion; a high pump-line pressure may indicate cannula obstruction or false-lumen perfusion. Inform the team, assess the circuit/cannula/true lumen and correct the source rather than simply increasing pump pressure.

Cerebral protection uses controlled hypothermia and selective cerebral perfusion according to planned arrest duration/anatomy; do not promise a universally safe arrest time. Avoid cerebral hyperthermia on rewarming. Anticipate long CPB, fibrinogen/platelet dysfunction and major surgical bleeding; use goal-directed haemostasis and recheck for tamponade/AR/coronary or distal malperfusion after repair. ICU priorities include neurological examination, BP/organ-perfusion management, kidney/lactate/limb assessment and bleeding. This case covers the operative component allocated to Set 13; detailed chronic aortopathy and non-cardiac dissection management remain elsewhere.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Identifies rupture/AR/coronary and branch malperfusion
- **2 marks** — Describes resection/graft/root/arch steps
- **2 marks** — Explains true-lumen cannulation and cardioplegia in AR
- **2 marks** — Plans cerebral perfusion, temperature and monitoring
- **2 marks** — Responds to malperfusion/bleeding and hands over organ risks

items.title: 24. During CPB there is sudden loss of perfusion, a high arterial-line pressure or v
items.q: During CPB there is sudden loss of perfusion, a high arterial-line pressure or visible air. Describe a structured response to major bypass emergencies.
items.a:
## Common immediate response

Announce the emergency, call surgeon/perfusionist and additional help, and identify whether the problem is patient, circuit or monitoring. Protect systemic/cerebral perfusion and prevent delivery of air/clot. The perfusionist controls clamps/pump/circuit using the unit’s rehearsed protocol; do not give a generic instruction to keep a pump running into an obstructed line or empty reservoir. Maintain anaesthesia by a route that remains effective, and ask the surgeon to prepare restoration of native output or alternative support if possible. Confirm the arterial trace/transducer before treating a false alarm.

## Low flow/poor drainage/empty reservoir

Look for kink/clamp, displaced venous cannula, SVC/IVC obstruction, air lock, low circulating volume, heart position or excessive vacuum-assisted drainage. Inspect the operative field/heart and circuit with the team. Reduce unsafe pump speed/flow as appropriate to avoid reservoir emptying and air delivery; correct drainage or volume loss and maintain adequate circulation by the safest available means. Treat a sudden bleed and ensure the reservoir-level and bubble safeguards work. Persistent suction/chatter is not always hypovolaemia; increasing vacuum or giving litres blindly may cause haemolysis/air entry or overload.

## High arterial-line pressure or asymmetric perfusion

Check line/clamps/cannula position, kinking, arterial cannula against the aortic wall, dissection/false-lumen perfusion and regional outflow obstruction. Compare patient pressures and cerebral oximetry and use surgical/echo assessment. Distinguish high circuit pressure from adequate patient perfusion. Avoid forcing flow through an obstruction: urgently correct/reposition or recannulate with surgical control. New aortic dissection requires a definitive true-lumen repair/perfusion plan.

## Inadequate gas exchange/oxygenator failure

Check oxygen supply, tubing/blender/sweep, gas fractions, circuit flow and blood-gas sampling accuracy first; a gas-supply problem is not automatically a failed membrane. Assess oxygenator performance, pressure gradient, visible clot/haemolysis and anticoagulation. Deliver available safe oxygen/ventilation/native support and prepare a trained oxygenator/circuit exchange when indicated. Communicate anticipated interruption and protective measures; do not improvise an unfamiliar exchange sequence from memory.

## Air entrainment/arterial air

Stop the source and isolate unsafe circuit segments according to the emergency protocol, preventing air reaching the patient. Identify open suction/venous connections, cannula exposure, low reservoir or oxygenator/circuit defects. Coordinate cessation/adjustment of unsafe flow, de-airing, surgical aspiration/venting and safe restoration of perfusion. Give 100% oxygen by the appropriate patient/circuit route, assess cerebral/systemic injury and involve specialists after stabilisation. Arbitrary Trendelenburg or prolonged unperfused waiting is not definitive treatment. Document duration of impaired flow/oxygen delivery, assess organ injury and debrief the event. Device-specific operational steps require training; the examination answer should prioritise recognition, source control and maintained safe perfusion.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Communicates, verifies and protects patient perfusion/anaesthesia
- **2 marks** — Explains low-drainage/reservoir causes and safe correction
- **2 marks** — Explains high pressure, obstruction and true-lumen malperfusion
- **2 marks** — Checks gas delivery versus oxygenator failure and plans exchange
- **2 marks** — Prevents arterial air delivery and coordinates de-airing/restoration

items.title: 25. Describe pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies to relieve anxiety b
items.q: Describe pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies to relieve anxiety before cardiac surgery, and explain how you would individualise them.
items.a:
## Assess before prescribing

Ask what the patient fears: death/stroke, pain, awareness, ventilation/ICU, loss of independence, previous traumatic treatment, communication or family issues. Check understanding, language/hearing needs, capacity and preferences. Anxiety may coexist with angina, dyspnoea, delirium, substance withdrawal or depression; physiological symptoms should not simply be sedated. Review frailty, OSA, respiratory disease, ventricular function/severe valve obstruction, haemodynamics and regular sedative/opioid use.

## Non-pharmacological care

Explain the operation and anaesthetic in plain language with an interpreter/accessible written or visual material where needed. Discuss monitoring, waking with tubes, expected ICU sensations, analgesia, communication while intubated, mobilisation and recovery milestones, without guaranteeing a complication-free course. Invite questions, use teach-back, involve a chosen support person and establish realistic shared goals. A cardiac surgery school, prehabilitation, relaxation/breathing techniques, music and psychological support may help. Provide privacy, a quiet environment, clear waiting times and continuity of staff; minimise unnecessary fasting, thirst, pain and sleep disruption. Resolve practical concerns and document what works for this patient.

## Pharmacological strategy

Continue important regular treatment when appropriate and plan for withdrawal risk. Treat pain or other symptoms directly. Routine heavy sedative premedication conflicts with early recovery and increases respiratory depression, delirium and haemodynamic risk, particularly in frail/OSA patients. If severe distress persists after discussion, a small titrated short-acting anxiolytic may be appropriate in a monitored environment with staff able to manage airway/haemodynamics. Choose dose and timing to age, reserve and concurrent opioids; do not give a fixed benzodiazepine dose to everyone. Dexmedetomidine may provide cooperative sedation in selected settings but can cause bradycardia/hypotension; it is not a routine substitute without monitoring. Avoid deep sedation in an unstable patient or one with critical obstruction/tamponade before rescue plans are ready.

## Review and integrate with enhanced recovery

Check relief, oversedation, ventilation and BP after any medication; continue reassurance rather than assuming the drug has solved the problem. Communicate preferences and previous adverse experiences to theatre/ICU staff. Optimise sleep, pain, hearing/vision aids and orientation after surgery. For disabling anxiety, depression or trauma symptoms, arrange appropriate psychological/medical support alongside the cardiac team. Document patient consent and individual priorities. The 2021 cardiac perioperative-care and 2024 redo reviews support patient education, psychological preparation and selective medication; evidence does not justify claiming information is always more effective than all drugs for every person.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Identifies specific fears and reversible symptoms
- **3 marks** — Provides accessible education/support/teach-back and practical measures
- **3 marks** — Individualises medication with respiratory/delirium/haemodynamic safeguards
- **2 marks** — Reassesses effect and integrates theatre/ICU recovery plan

items.title: 26. A patient develops severe hypotension and pulmonary hypertension during protamin
items.q: A patient develops severe hypotension and pulmonary hypertension during protamine administration after CPB. Explain the differential diagnosis and management.
items.a:
## Recognise the syndrome and act

Stop protamine, announce the reaction, call surgeon/perfusionist for immediate support, give 100% oxygen and assess ECG, arterial/CVP/PA pressures, TOE and the operative field. Check timing, dose/rate and other concurrent drugs. Hypotension may reflect rapid-infusion systemic vasodilation, immune/non-immune anaphylaxis, or catastrophic pulmonary vasoconstriction with acute RV failure. Also exclude haemorrhage, coronary air/ischaemia, tamponade, mechanical obstruction and inadequate ventricular function; more than one process can coexist.

## Phenotype-specific treatment

**Vasodilatory hypotension:** support perfusion with titrated vasopressor and assessed volume if underfilled. Rapid protamine administration can worsen systemic vasodilation; do not keep giving it while trying to counteract the fall in pressure.

**Anaphylaxis:** follow the perioperative anaphylaxis protocol, using titrated IV adrenaline in an appropriately monitored cardiac operating room, airway/ventilation support and volume to the phenotype. Treat bronchospasm and obtain timed tryptase when feasible after resuscitation. Steroids/antihistamines are not first-line substitutes for adrenaline or perfusion support. Severe anaphylaxis can present without obvious skin signs.

**Pulmonary hypertensive reaction/RV failure:** sudden high RV afterload causes RV dilation, impaired LV filling and systemic collapse; PA pressure may later fall with profound RV failure. Maintain systemic/RV coronary perfusion, correct hypoxaemia/hypercarbia/acidaemia and excessive airway pressures, give an appropriate inotrope and inhaled nitric oxide/prostacyclin where available. Avoid uncontrolled fluid loading of a distended RV. If refractory, urgently re-establish CPB with adequate **re-heparinisation** and perfusion-team coordination; the prior heparin has been reversed. Consider ongoing RV/cardiopulmonary support if required.

## Prevention and follow-through

Base reversal on residual heparin or a validated titration protocol, give slowly with close haemodynamic observation, and anticipate risk with prior protamine reaction or protamine-containing insulin. Fish allergy/vasectomy alone is not proof of a contraindication. A small test dose cannot rule out severe reaction. Excess protamine can impair platelet/coagulation function and prolong ACT; repeated dosing for any prolonged ACT can worsen bleeding. Use measured heparin/heparinase comparison and the whole haemostatic picture.

Do not restart protamine automatically. Balance residual-heparin bleeding against recurrent reaction with surgeon, perfusionist and haematology; document the exact exposure/phenotype, allergy referral where appropriate and future planning. Monitor RV function, oxygenation, haemostasis and organ perfusion in ICU. The distinction between dose-rate hypotension, anaphylaxis and pulmonary vasoconstriction explains why no single rescue drug treats every protamine reaction.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Stops protamine and rapidly assesses competing causes
- **2 marks** — Distinguishes vasodilation, anaphylaxis and pulmonary/RV failure
- **3 marks** — Provides phenotype-directed perfusion/adrenaline/pulmonary therapy
- **1 mark** — Plans re-heparinised return to CPB when refractory
- **2 marks** — Explains titrated reversal, testing limits and future documentation

items.title: 27. Explain the haematological and inflammatory effects of CPB, the role of antifibr
items.q: Explain the haematological and inflammatory effects of CPB, the role of antifibrinolytics, and the clinical implications of reperfusion injury and ischaemic preconditioning.
items.a:
## Blood–circuit interaction and haemostasis

Contact with artificial surfaces, tissue injury, blood–air interface and cardiotomy suction activate coagulation/contact pathways, complement, platelets and leukocytes. Haemodilution lowers Hb, platelet and factor concentrations. Platelet activation/consumption, dysfunction from CPB and antiplatelet drugs, fibrinogen depletion, fibrinolysis, residual heparin, excess protamine, hypothermia, acidosis and low ionised calcium can combine to cause bleeding. Shear/excessive suction can cause haemolysis, with free Hb/iron contributing to renal injury and NO scavenging. Microthrombi/embolism and postoperative thrombosis may coexist with bleeding: a long clotting time does not mean all thrombotic risk is absent.

Clinical management combines careful surgery, limited unnecessary dilution/suction, adequate anticoagulation on CPB, temperature/pH/calcium correction, titrated reversal and algorithm-guided haemostatic treatment. Use platelet count/function, fibrinogen, conventional tests and appropriate viscoelastic/heparinase channels to identify the problem; avoid treating every abnormality with plasma or protamine.

## Antifibrinolytics in cardiac surgery

TXA is a lysine analogue that interferes with plasminogen binding/activation on fibrin, reducing fibrinolysis, blood loss and transfusion/re-exploration. Give a validated local cardiac regimen matched to renal function rather than borrowing an obstetric or hip-arthroplasty dose. Higher exposure can increase seizures, particularly with renal accumulation. Discuss thrombosis risk in context, avoid wrong-route administration and do not claim TXA repairs a surgical anastomotic leak. Aminocaproic acid is another lysine analogue. Aprotinin inhibits serine proteases and has efficacy but important renal/allergy/regulatory restrictions; the actual 2007 debate is worked in SAQ10. ACT assay selection matters with aprotinin. Antifibrinolysis is one part of patient blood management, not a substitute for diagnosis.

## Inflammation and organ consequences

DAMPs, cytokines, complement and endothelial/glycocalyx injury increase permeability, oedema, vasodilation and microcirculatory heterogeneity. NO signalling and vascular hyporesponsiveness contribute to vasoplegia. Myocardial, pulmonary, renal, gut and cerebral injury can follow, particularly after prolonged CPB, poor oxygen delivery or marked haemolysis. The inflammatory phenotype does not automatically prove infection or justify routine steroids for everyone; continue to look for treatable low output, bleeding, obstruction and sepsis.

## Reperfusion and preconditioning

After ischaemia, reoxygenation can generate reactive oxygen species, calcium overload, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory activation and endothelial injury. Clinically this contributes to myocardial stunning, arrhythmia, oedema, microvascular no-reflow and remote organ injury. Minimise ischaemic time, provide effective cardioplegia, avoid distension and restore perfusion/oxygen delivery/metabolic conditions carefully; allow time for recovery before concluding permanent failure, while excluding graft/valve lesions.

Ischaemic preconditioning describes brief sublethal ischaemic episodes activating endogenous protective signalling; remote conditioning applies a stimulus elsewhere, commonly limb cuff cycles. Mechanistic plausibility and small-study effects have not produced a consistent major-outcome benefit in large cardiac trials, so it is not a universal routine requirement. Similarly, volatile-agent conditioning mechanisms do not establish guaranteed outcome superiority over well-conducted TIVA. Explain mechanism, evidence and applicability separately.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Explains circuit/dilution/platelet/factor/fibrinolytic changes
- **2 marks** — Links inflammation/haemolysis to organ injury and vasoplegia
- **2 marks** — Explains TXA mechanism, benefit and renal/seizure/route precautions
- **2 marks** — Explains reperfusion injury and practical prevention
- **2 marks** — Explains preconditioning and limitations of outcome evidence

items.title: 28. Describe intraoperative myocardial protection during CPB, including cardioplegia
items.q: Describe intraoperative myocardial protection during CPB, including cardioplegia delivery problems and assessment after reperfusion.
items.a:
## Objective and pre-bypass information

Maintain myocardial viability during interruption of normal coronary flow, reduce oxygen demand and prevent distension/ischaemia–reperfusion injury while permitting repair. Review coronary distribution/stenoses/grafts, ventricular hypertrophy/function, AR and planned cross-clamp time. Agree the solution, route, pressure, temperature, redose interval and rescue strategy with surgeon/perfusionist; no single formulation or fixed 20-minute interval suits every operation.

## Arrest, cooling and delivery

Hyperkalaemic cardioplegia causes depolarised arrest, reducing electrical/mechanical work. Blood or crystalloid solutions, cold/warm strategies and intermittent/continuous delivery are selected according to the operation and team protocol. Arrest does not abolish metabolism; adequate distribution, temperature and repeat delivery remain essential. Systemic cooling can add metabolic protection but is distinct from cardioplegia and from global circulatory arrest.

**Antegrade aortic-root delivery** uses normal coronary flow direction after cross-clamping. Severe proximal coronary stenosis can produce maldistribution; significant AR allows solution into the LV, causing distension and inadequate coronary protection. Use direct ostial delivery or another agreed route where necessary, with an LV vent. Monitor root pressure and the heart’s arrest/temperature/distension; an expected dose delivered does not prove tissue protection.

**Retrograde coronary-sinus delivery** can bypass proximal arterial obstruction and assist with AR or patent graft washout. Correct catheter position and pressure are essential: excessive pressure can injure the sinus, and RV protection may be incomplete because some venous drainage bypasses the sinus. Combining routes may improve distribution; do not assume retrograde alone protects every territory equally. Patent IMA/other graft flow in redo surgery can wash out cardioplegia and rewarm a region, requiring a tailored surgical strategy.

## Ongoing anaesthetic/perfusion role

Maintain adequate systemic oxygen delivery and anticoagulation, record clamp/cardioplegia times, watch electrical activity and myocardial distension, and communicate unexpected return of activity or delivery-pressure changes. Avoid unnecessary LV distension, which increases wall stress and impairs subendocardial perfusion. Account for cardioplegia-related K and volume load, glucose/calcium/acid-base changes and temperature. Verify anaesthesia continues while heart/ventilation signs are absent.

## Reperfusion and separation

De-air carefully before restoring ejection; maintain coronary driving pressure, correct major electrolyte/acidaemic abnormalities, restore a suitable rhythm/pacing and allow reperfusion. Assess TOE for new regional wall-motion changes versus global stunning, RV failure, residual valve/outflow lesions and air; the surgeon checks graft flow and repair. Treat ischaemia, spasm or a mechanical problem directly. If function remains poor, support/rest on CPB and select inotropic/mechanical support by phenotype rather than rushing separation. Reperfusion arrhythmias, calcium/oxidant injury and stunning can occur despite technically adequate cardioplegia; preconditioning/volatile mechanisms are not proof of universal clinical benefit (R27).

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Defines objective and relevant coronary/valve/anatomical assessment
- **2 marks** — Explains arrest, temperature and repeat delivery
- **3 marks** — Contrasts antegrade/retrograde failure modes and distension
- **1 mark** — Monitors delivery, systemic perfusion and metabolic load
- **2 marks** — Assesses reperfusion/regional dysfunction and provides a failed-wean plan

items.title: 29. A patient on VV ECMO becomes hypoxaemic
items.q: A patient on VV ECMO becomes hypoxaemic. Explain your assessment, how to distinguish membrane failure from other causes, and how to calculate membrane oxygen transfer.
items.a:
## Assess patient and support together

Call the ECMO team, confirm a reliable saturation/arterial sample, assess perfusion, Hb, lactate, temperature and respiratory/circulatory state. Give appropriate native-lung oxygen/ventilatory rescue while protecting the lung. Inspect gas supply, blender delivered O2 fraction, sweep tubing, pump power/settings, measured blood flow, circuit/cannula integrity and alarms. A normal RPM does not prove normal flow.

**Oxygenation** depends strongly on effective ECMO flow relative to cardiac output, Hb/oxygen content, recirculation, membrane function and residual lung gas exchange. Sepsis/fever or agitation can raise CO and oxygen consumption so a previously adequate flow becomes inadequate. Treat the precipitant and optimise safe flow; indiscriminate beta-blockade to raise saturation can reduce oxygen delivery. **Sweep flow** primarily changes CO2 clearance, whereas delivered gas oxygen fraction is a separate oxygenation setting. Turning up sweep alone does not correct every desaturation.

## Drainage and recirculation

Check for kink/migration, IVC collapse, high intrathoracic/intra-abdominal pressure, tamponade or true hypovolaemia. Chatter/negative drainage pressure may worsen when RPM is increased. Reduce excessive suction under specialist control and correct the cause; fluid is appropriate only when underfilling is demonstrated. Recirculation returns oxygenated blood directly to drainage instead of systemic delivery. Check cannula positions and dual-lumen return-jet direction with imaging; adjust configuration/position with the ECMO team. High drainage saturation may reflect recirculation but can also reflect altered systemic extraction; integrate findings.

## Membrane assessment

Compare pre/post-membrane gases at known blood flow and delivered oxygen fraction, pressure-gradient/resistance trends, visible thrombus, haemolysis, falling platelets/fibrinogen and rising D-dimer. Falling post-membrane oxygen tension/content, poor CO2 removal or increasing resistance suggests dysfunction; exclude gas-supply/condensation problems first. The 2026 review cites post-membrane PaO2 <25 kPa or a >50% decline at FdO2 1.0 and low oxygen transfer as warning features, not stand-alone universal exchange rules. Pressure gradient is flow- and device-dependent: compare resistance/trends rather than a fixed pressure alone. Prepare a planned trained membrane/circuit exchange when indicated before sudden failure.

## Worked calculation (new educator example)

With Hb **9 g/dL**, pre-membrane saturation **65%**, PO2 **5 kPa**, post-membrane saturation **100%**, PO2 **40 kPa**, and flow **4 L/min**:

- Oxygen content (mL/dL) = **1.34 × Hb × saturation fraction + 0.023 × PO2(kPa)**.
- Pre-membrane content = 1.34×9×0.65 + 0.023×5 = **7.95 mL/dL**.
- Post-membrane content = 1.34×9×1.00 + 0.023×40 = **12.98 mL/dL**.
- Transfer = 4 L/min × (12.98−7.95) mL/dL × 10 dL/L = **approximately 201 mL O2/min**.

This measures oxygen added by the membrane, not total systemic oxygen delivery or proof the patient has adequate oxygenation. A low value may reflect low flow or high inlet saturation as well as membrane failure. Evaluate it in context and avoid rapid large CO2 changes during support adjustments.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Assesses patient/perfusion and verifies actual circuit/gas function
- **2 marks** — Explains flow/CO/Hb/consumption versus sweep physiology
- **2 marks** — Distinguishes drainage failure and recirculation
- **2 marks** — Uses gases/resistance/haemolysis trends to assess membrane function
- **2 marks** — Calculates content difference × flow with correct units and limitations

items.title: 30. Systolic anterior motion and hypotension after mitral repair
items.q: After mitral valve repair, hypotension worsens as adrenaline is increased. TOE reveals a very small hyperdynamic LV, systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet and posteriorly directed MR. Explain the diagnosis and management.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** [2025 ESC/EACTS valvular heart disease guideline](https://www.escardio.org/guidelines/clinical-practice-guidelines/all-esc-practice-guidelines/valvular-heart-disease/) · [2024 EACTS/EACTAIC/EBCP CPB guideline (published 2025)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11826095/) · Expanded Set 13 notes (chapters listed in model answer).

## Diagnosis and mechanism

- This is **dynamic left-ventricular outflow tract obstruction (LVOTO) due to SAM after mitral repair**, not simply low contractility. Repair geometry can bring the anterior leaflet/coaptation point towards the septum.
- A small underfilled **hyperdynamic LV** generates high systolic flow velocity/drag, drawing the anterior leaflet into the LVOT, generating **dynamic obstruction** and often **posteriorly directed MR**.
- Beta-agonists increase contractility and LVOT velocity; vasodilation reduces afterload; tachycardia and low preload decrease LV cavity size. **More adrenaline can make pressure and forward flow worse.**

## Differentiate from alternatives

- TOE: look for anterior leaflet motion against the septum, a dynamic LVOT Doppler gradient (often late-peaking), MR direction, LV cavity size, regional wall-motion abnormalities and ventricular function.
- **Afterload mismatch** after eliminating severe MR can cause low output, but typically shows **depressed LV systolic function**, not a tiny vigorous ventricle with SAM. Exclude residual primary MR, prosthesis/repair dysfunction, coronary air/ischaemia, RV failure, bleeding and tamponade.

## Immediate management

- **1.** **Call surgeon and perfusionist**, reassess TOE and the valve repair while maintaining coronary/systemic perfusion.
- **2.** **Reduce or stop positive inotropy** driving obstruction, if haemodynamics permit. Avoid inappropriate vasodilators.
- **3.** **Restore SVR/afterload** with titrated **phenylephrine or vasopressin** (other vasopressors depending on physiology); this opposes dynamic obstruction. Assess coronary perfusion.
- **4.** **Correct genuine LV underfilling cautiously** with a targeted volume challenge; avoid reflexive fluid loading if other signs suggest congestion.
- **5.** Control tachycardia; consider cautious **short-acting beta-blockade once perfusion pressure is supported** and under TOE/arterial monitoring.
- **6.** If severe obstruction persists or repair geometry is responsible, **surgical revision** may be necessary; reinstitute CPB if unable to stabilise.

## Postoperative plan

Document mechanism and the final TOE gradient/MR, avoid triggers and hand over a clear haemodynamic and rhythm strategy to ICU.

**Evidence:** Expanded Set 13 notes, chapters 3, 7 and worked Case B; cardiac valve/CPB guidance.

## Self-marking checklist

- Identifies SAM-related dynamic LVOTO rather than assuming contractile failure
- Explains why low preload/SVR, tachycardia and beta-agonists worsen obstruction
- Distinguishes SAM from afterload mismatch and other post-repair causes using TOE
- Stops/reduces inappropriate inotropy and restores SVR
- Uses a cautious assessed fluid challenge and rate control when appropriate
- Escalates to surgical review/revision or CPB if refractory
- Gives an ICU handover and reassessment plan

items.title: 31. Complete heart block after aortic valve replacement
items.q: A patient develops symptomatic complete heart block after aortic valve replacement and has temporary epicardial pacing wires. Describe how you would set up and programme an external pacemaker, and how you would troubleshoot failure to capture.
items.a:
[BJA Education: Temporary epicardial pacing after cardiac surgery, 2023][TEMP]

### Types of temporary pacing

Transcutaneous, transvenous and epicardial pacing are the principal rescue options; transoesophageal pacing mainly stimulates the atrium and is not reliable ventricular rescue for complete AV block.

### Set-up for this patient

- **1.** **Assess ABCs and perfusion**, call the cardiac surgical/ICU team, attach ECG and a pulse-based monitor, and have external pacing/defibrillation ready. Symptomatic complete block needs effective **ventricular** pacing; AAI cannot bridge AV block.
- **2.** Check the generator battery, correct leads/cables, labelled atrial/ventricular wire pairs, connector security, insulation and manufacturer instructions. **Bipolar epicardial wires have both poles in the myocardium**. A unipolar system needs a dedicated return electrode—often subcutaneous—not an assumed ordinary surface ECG electrode. Do not improvise the connection or touch exposed conductors (microshock risk).
- **3.** Select **VVI** for ventricular rescue if only ventricular wires, AF or unreliable atrial sensing. **DDD** can preserve AV synchrony with reliable atrial/ventricular wires in sinus rhythm. AAI is only suitable when AV conduction is intact. Avoid unmonitored asynchronous pacing because of competitive R-on-T risk; reserve DOO/VOO for a specific indication with continuous observation.
- **4.** Set a rate suitable for perfusion (often 70–90/min initially after adult cardiac surgery, then titrate). In urgent failure, increase output sufficiently to achieve capture; once stable establish the capture threshold safely. Set **output generally at least twice the measured threshold**, within generator limits. Rate/output/sensing values are patient-specific, not guaranteed by a default setting.
- **5.** For dual-chamber pacing, set AV delay (often around 150–200 ms initially, then optimise clinically) and both atrial/ventricular output and sensitivity. Confirm **electrical and mechanical capture**, not simply pacing spikes.

### Threshold and sensing checks

- Perform checks only with trained staff, continuous monitoring and an immediately available rescue plan. **Do not deliberately lose capture in an unprotected pacing-dependent patient**. Test according to the local protocol, with backup pacing where required.
- Capture threshold is the lowest output producing consistent depolarisation; a rising threshold prompts review of wires, temperature, electrolytes and myocardium. A threshold >10 mA is concerning and requires an urgent reliable alternative rather than accepting a small safety margin.
- Sensing threshold is the smallest intrinsic signal reliably detected. If no intrinsic rhythm exists, it cannot be safely measured in the usual way. Sensitivity is expressed in **mV: lower number = more sensitive**. A common programmed margin is about half the measured sensing threshold, while avoiding oversensing; follow the generator-specific protocol.

### Failure to capture

Pacing spike without atrial depolarisation or QRS, with absent expected pulse: **support perfusion and increase output immediately**. Check power, connections, correct port/polarity and wires; consider displacement/fracture, high threshold from oedema/ischaemia, hypothermia, acidosis/electrolytes or drugs. Check echo for tamponade/major postoperative causes of deterioration. Use functioning alternative wires or external pacing while arranging urgent transvenous/other rescue. Atropine may fail in infranodal block; a titrated adrenaline/isoprenaline infusion can bridge to pacing where appropriate, without delaying it.

### Failure to sense

**Undersensing:** intrinsic beats are missed and inappropriate spikes may land on T waves; check leads and lower the mV setting to increase sensitivity. **Oversensing:** EMI/myopotentials are mistaken for beats, inhibiting pacing and causing pauses; remove interference, check wires and increase the mV setting if appropriate. Any R-on-T VT/VF requires immediate resuscitation/defibrillation and expert correction of the pacing system.

### Ongoing care

Document settings, capture/sensing thresholds, dependence and backup plan; inspect/check regularly (usually at least daily early after surgery). Persistent AV block requires cardiology assessment; timing of a permanent device depends on operation, escape rhythm, recovery and stability rather than a compulsory day-7 rule.

**Key evidence:** [TEMP][TEMP] · [BRADY][BRADY]

## Self-marking checklist
- Recognises complete block requires reliable ventricular pacing and cannot be treated by AAI
- Checks labelled wires, battery, insulated connections and bipolar/unipolar return arrangements
- Selects VVI or DDD appropriately and confirms mechanical capture
- Sets rate, output, sensitivity and AV delay with a safe capture margin
- Avoids unprotected threshold testing in a pacing-dependent patient
- Troubleshoots failure to capture while providing immediate backup pacing
- Explains lower mV = greater sensitivity, oversensing pauses and undersensing R-on-T
- Documents daily checks, escalation and individualised permanent-pacing review

items.title: 32. Failing RV at separation from bypass (primary Set 13 overlap)
items.q: You cannot wean a patient from cardiopulmonary bypass after valve surgery because the right ventricle is failing. Describe your diagnosis and management.
items.a:
> **Evidence:** Source-specific clinical checks and review depth are recorded in the audit register; examiner priorities are stated separately below.

### Look for the cause while you stabilise

Right ventricular (RV) failure after bypass can spiral: hypotension reduces right coronary perfusion, which worsens RV function and then LV filling. Causes are pre-existing RV dysfunction or pulmonary hypertension, long bypass or poor myocardial protection, protamine-associated pulmonary hypertension, LVAD insertion (RV failure in 20 to 40%) or heart transplantation (long ischaemic time, size mismatch), and **right coronary obstruction**: inadequate de-airing is among the commonest causes because the right coronary ostium is anterior and air collects there; also graft problems, ostial injury and thrombus.

### Diagnosis

On **TOE** check the RV free wall, septum (flattened or displaced towards the LV), RV:LV size ratio interpreted by view, loading and the full examination (not a universal diagnostic cutoff of 0.6), TAPSE below 1.7 cm (interpret cautiously after bypass and sternotomy), fractional area change below 35%, TR velocity interpreted with image quality and the absence/presence of RVOT obstruction; a value alone does not diagnose acute RV failure, and look for air and RCA flow. Haemodynamics: CVP above 20 mmHg or above wedge pressure, cardiac index below 2.1, and direct pressure/flow assessment for suspected RVOT obstruction; neither CVP nor a single pressure gradient establishes the whole diagnosis. The pulmonary artery pulsatility index has no agreed threshold.

### Management in order

- **1.** **Preload:** if low, a small challenge preferably with pump blood; if high, remove blood into the circuit, controlled volume removal/ultrafiltration; venodilation only when perfusion pressure and the cause permit it.
- **2.** **Ventilation:** FiO2 1.0, avoid hypercarbia, acidaemia, large tidal volume and high PEEP, with gentle recruitment.
