- **3.** **Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators first line:** nitric oxide 10 to 20 ppm (up to 40), or inhaled milrinone, epoprostenol or iloprost; intravenous vasodilators only if these fail, because of systemic hypotension. Intratracheal milrinone has only limited observational support; it is not a standard rescue dose/route and must not substitute for a validated inhaled delivery protocol.
- **4.** **Perfusion pressure:** selected low-dose vasopressin may support SVR with relatively favourable PVR effects, but effects are dose-dependent and it is not universally ideal; cautious noradrenaline; phenylephrine raises PVR more.
- **5.** **Inotropy:** dobutamine first, then adrenaline or milrinone (milrinone causes more hypotension); adrenaline bolus and infusion for severe compromise.
- **6.** **Rhythm:** restore sinus rhythm, atrial epicardial pacing, pace heart block.
- **7.** **Escalate:** return promptly to adequate CPB support while correcting a mechanical/coronary cause if separation is unsafe, then selected VA-ECMO or RVAD. IABP may help selected associated LV/ischaemic problems; it does not directly support isolated RV output. Treat the cause: de-air, re-graft or revise a right coronary problem.

### Evidence

The chapter recommends routine haemodynamic monitoring, TOE and direct inspection for every case; most recommendations come from case series and expert opinion.

### Source safety check: vasopressin and perfusion support

The 2021 Blue Book RV chapter (p111) prints **1–4 units/min**. Do **not** use that value: it is incompatible with usual low-dose vasopressin practice. A current regional reference gives **0.6–2.4 units/hour**, equivalent to **0.01–0.04 units/min**, with titration under the local ICU protocol; monitor for ischaemic effects. A 2026 BJA Education corrigendum also identifies the same erroneous units/min range in the older RV review. This audit does not claim a formal Blue Book erratum. Noradrenaline is titrated to perfusion and haemodynamics; an old review's 0.2 microgram/kg/min suggestion is not a universal maximum. Vasopressin's PVR effects are dose-dependent, not guaranteed zero.

### Practical integration

Distinguish primary RV contractile failure from excessive PVR, inadequate preload, a new valve lesion, dynamic RVOT obstruction, tamponade and LV distension. Notify the surgeon and perfusionist early and reassess after each intervention; repeated attempts to separate from bypass with severe hypotension compound myocardial injury. Maintain appropriate coronary and systemic perfusion and verify de-airing and the surgical repair. Use serial TOE, arterial pressure, mixed venous oxygenation and lactate trends to assess whether the circulation actually improves rather than treating a single pressure number. Postoperative handover must specify RV loading conditions, inotrope/vasopressor targets, pacing mode and reliable capture, pulmonary vasodilator delivery/weaning, fluid strategy and the threshold for mechanical support.

## Self-marking checklist
- Causes (air in right coronary, protamine, pre-existing PH, LVAD, poor protection)
- Diagnosis on TOE and haemodynamics
- Preload and ventilation strategy
- Inhaled pulmonary vasodilators
- Vasopressor and inotrope choices
- Rhythm and pacing
- Mechanical support and return to bypass
- Evidence summary

items.title: 33. Polymorphic VT with epicardial wires in DDD
items.q: A patient with temporary epicardial wires develops recurrent polymorphic VT despite a normal QT. The pacing box is in DDD mode and pacing spikes appear near T waves. Explain the mechanism and your management.
items.a:
### Recognise a pacing-induced arrhythmia

Assess pulse and circulation immediately. Sustained unstable polymorphic VT or VF requires **unsynchronised defibrillation** and the applicable resuscitation pathway; do not wait for synchronisation or a full device analysis. Ask for cardiac surgery/ICU and EP assistance and review saved telemetry without delaying rescue. Stop the pacing system from continuing to trigger unsafe impulses while providing resuscitation and a reliable alternative if the patient is dependent. Simply turning off all pacing and leaving a dependent patient unsupported is unsafe.

### Why a demand mode can still produce R-on-T

Demand pacing is safe only when intrinsic signals are sensed reliably. **Undersensing** may result from poor wire signal, migration, cable/connection problems or a sensitivity value set too high. Inappropriate impulses can then fall during ventricular repolarisation and trigger polymorphic VT/VF. Normal QT does not exclude this mechanism and does not make the rhythm torsades de pointes.

In DDD pacing, poor **atrial** sensing can also provoke ventricular R-on-T. An unsensed intrinsic P wave may be followed by an inappropriate atrial impulse overlapping a conducted ventricular beat. Ventricular blanking after that atrial impulse can conceal the true R wave; the box subsequently emits a ventricular impulse after its programmed AV interval, potentially onto the T wave. Thus the atrial circuit and timing need review, not only the ventricular output. Higher output does not repair an inability to sense intrinsic activity.

### Restore a safe system

Review dependence, underlying atrial/ventricular rhythm and perfusion. Check the patient, wires, connections and generator systematically; correct hypothermia, hypoxia, K/Mg/Ca abnormalities, acidosis and ischaemia. Confirm settings and inspect for oversensing, crosstalk, tracking of AF/flutter or pacemaker-mediated re-entry. These mechanisms need different solutions.

With expert staff and immediate rescue available, establish sensing and capture thresholds when safe. **Lower mV setting means greater sensitivity**; set an appropriate margin below the measured intrinsic signal without producing noise oversensing. If no intrinsic rhythm exists, routine sensing measurement is not possible. If the patient does not need pacing, leaving an unreliable backup system switched on can add danger: an expert may turn it off and continue observation. If dependent, use a reliably functioning simpler mode/wire system or urgent transvenous/new epicardial support, maintaining intensive monitoring. Asynchronous mode is a supervised emergency option when necessary, not routine ward backup.

### Prevent recurrence and identify complications

Verify electrical and mechanical capture and monitor continuously after any change. A low rate setting is not inherently safe in an inadequately sensing DDD system. Document thresholds, settings, dependence, rationale and backup plan, checking at least daily and after major clinical changes. Do not transfer a patient with unreliable sensing to an unmonitored ward.

The same safety review includes wire removal: coordinate pacing need, coagulation/antithrombotics and local removal policy. Resistance requires stopping and surgical advice. New shock after removal needs urgent echo for tamponade; the observation plan must continue after the wire is out. Evidence is largely practical/observational, but the mechanisms and preventable hazards are directly relevant to external pacemaker programming outcomes. [TEMP][TEMP]

## Self-marking checklist
- Treats sustained polymorphic VT/VF immediately
- Identifies R-on-T from undersensing rather than assuming long-QT torsades
- Explains the atrial-sensing/ventricular-blanking DDD mechanism
- Protects pacing-dependent patients during system interruption
- Distinguishes output from sensing and lower mV from greater numerical sensitivity
- Uses a systematic patient–wire–generator check and a reliable alternative
- Avoids unsafe ward backup and documents daily checks
- Recognises wire-removal tamponade and plans surveillance

items.title: 34. Heart transplant recipient for non-cardiac surgery
items.q: A patient who received a heart transplant 3 years ago presents for non-cardiac surgery. Describe the physiology of the transplanted heart and the implications for anaesthetic drugs and management.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2019, "Perioperative management of heart transplantation" (Edwards, Allen).

### Physiology of the denervated heart

- Vagal and sympathetic supply is cut. The SA node runs at its intrinsic rate of **90 to 100 beats/min**.
- The heart cannot mount a reflex tachycardia to hypovolaemia, vasodilation or afterload change; cardiac output depends on **preload** and slow rise of circulating catecholamines. It is "preload dependent".
- Angina may be absent, so **ischaemia can be silent**, although reinnervation may restore symptoms. Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is suspected from new wall motion or diastolic abnormalities or ventricular arrhythmias; coronary angiography with IVUS/OCT and other modalities is selected by the transplant service; IVUS can detect early intimal disease but is not the sole diagnostic test.
- Reinnervation is partial and unpredictable (sympathetic from 6 to 8 months, parasympathetic 1 to 3 years).
- Arrhythmias: conduction delay and heart block, arrhythmia and pacing rates vary by timing, surgical technique and cohort; ventricular arrhythmias suggest rejection or CAV. Double P waves can occur. Carotid sinus massage and Valsalva have no effect.

### Drug responses

| Drug | Effect |
|---|---|
| Atropine, glycopyrrolate | Usually absent/unreliable response; variable reinnervation; use direct chronotropy/pacing |
| Ephedrine | Mixed direct/indirect; effect can be reduced or unpredictable |
| Noradrenaline, adrenaline, dobutamine | Exaggerated (more adrenoreceptors): titrate |
| Phenylephrine, metaraminol | Effective, no reflex bradycardia |
| Isoprenaline | Effective; use for bradycardia |
| Adenosine | Exaggerated bradycardia |
| Neostigmine | Bradycardia possible, especially beyond 6 months |

### Other issues

BJA Education 2021 (heart transplantation) adds that **primary graft dysfunction** is the main cause of early death, and that mechanical support (ideally ECMO) should be started early when graft dysfunction does not respond to moderate-dose inotropes.


Immunosuppression (calcineurin inhibitors: nephrotoxicity; continue on time), infection risk (asepsis, antibiotics), malignancy (more than 10% develop de novo cancer; skin cancers 100 times), tricuspid regurgitation, and drug interactions with tacrolimus or ciclosporin. Monitor ECG, arterial line for major surgery, and warm, preload-aware induction.

## Self-marking checklist
- Explains denervation, resting rate of 90 to 100 and absent reflex tachycardia
- Notes preload dependence and silent ischaemia
- Describes atropine/glycopyrrolate responses as unreliable and names direct chronotropy/pacing alternatives
- Describes exaggerated responses to catecholamines
- Mentions CAV, arrhythmias and pacemaker risk
- Covers immunosuppression and infection precautions

**Audit evidence map:** BB19; ISHLT23. Source depth and any limitations are recorded in the audit register.

items.title: 35. LVAD patient needing urgent laparotomy
items.q: A patient with a durable left ventricular assist device (LVAD) needs an urgent laparotomy. Outline the key perioperative issues and your management.
items.a:
> **Blue Book:** Australasian Anaesthesia 2021, "The perioperative management of patients with ventricular assist devices undergoing non-cardiac surgery" (Falland, Sidebotham, Allen).

### Context

Between 4 and 33% of VAD patients have non-cardiac surgery while supported, most often GI endoscopy (bleeding on anticoagulation). Outcomes are good when a **multidisciplinary team** is involved. Commonest problems: **hypotension**, acute kidney injury, bleeding and arrhythmia.

### Preop

- Team: anaesthetist, proceduralist, heart failure cardiologist, VAD nurse or perfusionist.
- Assess function, organ function, medications and device performance; echo with attention to **RV function**.
- Examination is hard: pulses are often impalpable (non-pulsatile flow), NIBP may need Doppler, and device hum masks heart sounds.
- Device plan depends on pacing dependence, device/magnet response and expected EMI; reprogram/magnet only when indicated and restore therapies before leaving monitoring.
- Plan ICU or HDU. Expect greater blood loss; crossmatch.

### Anticoagulation

Warfarin targets are device- and patient-specific, commonly INR 2.0–3.0 for contemporary durable LVAD care; confirm the VAD centre’s plan. HeartMate 3 patients may omit aspirin under an appropriate protocol (ARIES-HM3), rather than receiving an antiplatelet automatically. If interruption is needed, individualise bridging. Urgent sustained reversal generally uses four-factor PCC plus IV vitamin K; coordinate dose, haemostasis and prompt re-anticoagulation with the VAD team.

### Intraop

Invasive arterial monitoring and strict asepsis (driveline infection risk). VAD output is preload and afterload dependent: reduced VAD preload (hypovolaemia, RV failure, tamponade, high intrathoracic pressure, arrhythmia) causes low flow and hypotension. Protect the RV (see the right ventricular failure item), avoid raised PVR, replace volume promptly and use vasopressors for vasodilation.

### Key themes (the chapter's five)

Haemodynamics, determinants of VAD performance, monitoring challenges, anticoagulation and asepsis.

### Postop

Plan monitored recovery appropriate to severity and surgical stress; assess perfusion, rhythm, oxygenation, bleeding and congestion. Resume indicated medicines/antithrombotics when haemostasis, renal function and intake permit, observing neuraxial timing. Escalate persistent instability to HDU/ICU.


## Self-marking checklist
- Identifies the multidisciplinary team and the usual complications
- Notes assessment difficulties (non-pulsatile flow, Doppler BP)
- Gives device-specific anticoagulation targets, individualised interruption/bridging and the HeartMate 3 aspirin exception
- Coordinates four-factor PCC plus vitamin K when urgent sustained reversal is indicated, with VAD-team advice and a restart plan
- Uses an individual device/EMI plan and restores therapies
- Explains determinants of VAD preload and the role of the RV
- Stresses asepsis and postoperative ICU or HDU care

**Audit evidence map:** BB21 VAD; ARIES-HM3. Source depth and any limitations are recorded in the audit register.

items.title: 2026.2 Q9: Failure to wean from bypass after CABG
items.source: Past SAQ 2026.2 Q9 · no examiner's report yet
items.q: Describe your approach to the management of a patient who has failed to wean from cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) following coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG).
items.model:
## Principle

A failed wean is a **diagnostic problem under time pressure**. Return to or stay on bypass, keep the heart decompressed and perfused, and work through a structured list rather than escalating inotropes blindly, communicating with the surgeon and perfusionist.

## 1. Check the basics (on bypass)

- **Rate and rhythm:** sinus rhythm at a good rate or pacing (rate 70 to 90 per minute; confirm reliable electrical and mechanical capture and a suitable output safety margin; discuss high or rising thresholds); synchronise cardioversion for haemodynamically significant AF; defibrillate VF without synchronisation; atrial wires matter if the RV is hypertrophied or failing.
- **Metabolic:** temperature above 36 degrees, potassium within the appropriate normal range, ionised calcium, magnesium, pH, haemoglobin and glucose.
- **Ventilation:** lungs re-expanded, FiO2 1.0, no pneumothorax or secretions, no hypercarbia.
- **Anaesthesia and drugs:** adequate depth, review all infusions: stop unintended vasodilators; an indicated inodilator may still be needed for ventricular failure with pressure support.

## 2. Find the cause: TOE, pressures and direct vision

| Cause | Clue | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **LV ischaemia** (graft kink or thrombosis, air in a coronary, poor protection) | Regional wall motion abnormality, ST change | Surgeon checks grafts and flows; revise or add a graft; GTN for spasm |
| **RV failure** (air down the anterior right coronary ostium, failed right grafting, protamine pulmonary hypertension, high PVR) | Dilated, poorly contracting RV, septal shift, increasing CVP, reduced forward flow and new TR; PA pressure may be high or fall as the RV fails. Assess multiple TOE views: TAPSE alone is unreliable after pericardiotomy | See the sequence below |
| **Vasoplegia** | Good function, high output, low SVR, MAP below 65 | Noradrenaline and/or vasopressin with preload assessment; rescue agents after contraindication checks, not an automatic fixed sequence |
| **Hypovolaemia or bleeding** | Empty LV | Transfuse from the pump |
| **Tamponade, valve dysfunction, dissection, LVOT obstruction, tension pneumothorax** | TOE | Surgeon intervenes |
| **Heart block** | ECG | Epicardial pacing |

## 3. Treat the demonstrated phenotype (RV failure as the model)

- **1.** **Preload and rhythm:** judge ventricular filling using TOE, surgical inspection and pressure trends. Give small assessed volume increments if underfilled. A dilated congested RV may require unloading, not more fluid; no single CVP threshold predicts responsiveness. Maintain sinus rhythm or appropriate AV sequential pacing.
- **2.** **Coronary perfusion:** restore systemic pressure promptly with noradrenaline and/or low-dose vasopressin. The aim is adequate aortic-to-RV perfusion pressure, not a universal drug ceiling. Vasopressin generally has less pulmonary vasoconstrictor effect, but is not free of pulmonary or ischaemic effects.
- **3.** **Contractility:** select dobutamine, adrenaline or IV milrinone according to pressure, rhythm, renal function and severity. Milrinone and dobutamine may require accompanying vasopressor support; there is no mandatory order. Do not use intratracheal milrinone as a routine rescue bolus.
- **4.** **Afterload:** treat hypoxaemia, hypercarbia, acidaemia and excessive airway pressures; recruit atelectasis gently and choose PEEP for oxygenation and RV loading. Add an inhaled pulmonary vasodilator, such as nitric oxide (commonly 10–20 ppm initially, titrated with monitoring) or prostacyclin. Check pulmonary venous/left-sided obstruction before pulmonary vasodilation. Correct graft or valve lesions rather than masking them with drugs.

## 4. If still failing

- **Rest the heart:** return to full flow for reperfusion and retry.
- **IABP** to promote coronary (including right coronary) flow.
- **Mechanical support:** VA-ECMO (the 2017 chapter lists failure to wean from CPB as an indication), or an RVAD or LVAD; leave the chest open if swelling or bleeding prevents closure. VA-ECMO brings bleeding, limb ischaemia, stroke and differential hypoxia, and MAP depends on extracorporeal flow and vascular resistance; vasopressors are used for vasodilation, not simply because pulsatility is absent.

## Applying the diagnosis and escalating safely

- Reconfirm that “failed wean” is physiological rather than a monitor artefact: inspect the arterial trace and transducer level, compare central and radial pressures where appropriate, and assess organ perfusion, lactate trend and mixed venous saturation.
- Distinguish global stunning from a new regional abnormality. New inferior/RV dysfunction suggests RCA graft compromise or air; persistent regional ischaemia needs surgical graft assessment and correction. Check coronary perfusion pressure, pacing-induced dyssynchrony and coronary spasm. Reassess after reperfusion on full CPB before another planned attempt.
- A small hyperdynamic LV with systolic anterior motion/LVOT obstruction requires reduced inotropy, adequate filling and supported afterload, rather than more inotrope. Residual structural lesions, aortic dissection, pulmonary venous obstruction or compression require definitive intervention.
- Agree a time-limited trial, objective perfusion goals and a mechanical-support destination with the team. IABP provides modest LV support and coronary augmentation; isolated RV failure may need RVAD, and biventricular failure may need VA ECMO. VA ECMO can increase LV afterload: monitor aortic-valve opening, LV distension and pulmonary oedema, and consider unloading if indicated.
- Keep adequate heparin anticoagulation while CPB may be needed. Give protamine only after stable separation and agreement that immediate return is unlikely; if severe protamine reaction necessitates CPB, re-heparinise under perfusion guidance. Document the cause, support plan and ICU handover.

**Examiner linkage:** 2026.2 Q9 is verified from the question paper. No 2026.2 examiner report was available at audit; the framework is a clinical synthesis, not invented examiner feedback.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.
rubric: **2 marks** — Maintains/returns to CPB, communicates and reassesses safe perfusion
**2 marks** — Checks rhythm, ventilation, temperature, metabolites and drug delivery
**3 marks** — Uses TOE/pressures and graft assessment to distinguish LV/RV/structural/vasodilatory causes
**2 marks** — Treats demonstrated loading/perfusion/contractility/afterload problem safely
**1 mark** — Sets reassessment and mechanical-support plan with correct heparin/protamine timing

items.title: 2019.2 Q1: Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest: rationale and consequences
items.q: Describe the rationale for the use of deep hypothermic circulatory arrest and outline the pathophysiological consequences of this technique.
items.model:
## Rationale

**Deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA)** stops the circulation completely at a core temperature of about 18 to 20 degrees Celsius, giving a **bloodless, cannula-free field** for aortic arch surgery, type A dissection, some thoracoabdominal and congenital operations and pulmonary thromboendarterectomy. The cost is ischaemia of every organ, and the aim is **cerebral protection**.

Cooling reduces the **cerebral metabolic rate** by about 6 to 7% per degree, to roughly 20 to 25% of normal at 18 degrees, and reduces excitatory neurotransmitter release and free-radical injury. Tolerance is finite and highly variable: longer arrest increases neurological risk, and no duration such as 30 minutes is guaranteed safe.

## Technique

- Cool on bypass over 20 to 30 minutes, keeping the gradient between blood and body at 10 degrees or less; confirm brain cooling (nasopharyngeal and bladder or rectal temperature, EEG silence or cerebral oximetry).
- Adjuncts include controlled temperature and glucose, an agreed alpha-stat/pH-stat approach, neuromonitoring and **selective antegrade cerebral perfusion** (or selected retrograde strategies). Cerebral perfusion reduces ischaemic exposure during systemic arrest; it does not make duration unlimited. Steroids, barbiturates, propofol or head ice should not be presented as proven independent neurological protection.
- Rewarm slowly, keeping the outflow temperature below 37 degrees, to avoid gas emboli and cerebral hyperthermia.

## Pathophysiological consequences

| System | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Neurological** | Stroke, delirium, seizures, cognitive deficit, choreoathetosis in children; risk rises with arrest time |
| **Coagulation** | Platelet dysfunction, slowed enzyme activity, fibrinolysis, haemodilution and heparin: major bleeding |
| **Cardiac** | Bradycardia, increased ventricular irritability/VF with deep cooling, arrhythmias on rewarming, myocardial stunning |
| **Respiratory** | Left shift of the oxygen–haemoglobin curve, altered gas solubility and pH, lung injury |
| **Renal and visceral** | Ischaemia–reperfusion injury, acute kidney injury, gut ischaemia, cold diuresis |
| **Metabolic and inflammatory** | Hyperglycaemia (insulin resistance), acidosis, electrolyte shifts and a systemic inflammatory response that can lead to **vasoplegia** after rewarming |

Postoperatively expect prolonged ventilation, delayed awakening, bleeding and tamponade. DHCA is a distinct technique from cardioplegic arrest (local myocardial arrest/protection while CPB maintains systemic perfusion) and from ECMO (circulatory support).

## Physiological interpretation and examiner focus

Cooling suppresses cerebral oxygen consumption, buying time when global flow is interrupted; CPB permits controlled cooling and rewarming but is not itself the definition of DHCA. Temperature categories vary: the aortic-arch convention calls 14.1–20 °C deep, 20.1–28 °C moderate and 28.1–34 °C mild hypothermia. Quote the convention and measured site. Contemporary arch surgery often combines moderate hypothermia with antegrade cerebral perfusion; this differs from DHCA alone.

During cooling, gas solubility increases and the haemoglobin dissociation curve shifts left; temperature-corrected gases differ from values measured at 37 °C. Alpha-stat preserves the uncorrected 37 °C interpretation; pH-stat adds CO2 for a temperature-corrected target and increases cerebral flow, with potential embolic implications. Select the strategy with the perfusion team. Hypothermia impairs platelet and enzyme function and slows drug clearance; global arrest adds organ ischaemia. Reperfusion adds oxidant injury, oedema and inflammatory vasodilation. Rewarming adds demand, electrolyte redistribution and gaseous microembolic risk. Avoid arterial outlet temperature above 37 °C and steep thermal gradients; use more than one temperature site and anticipate afterdrop.

**Examiner linkage:** the 2019.2 report was located and read. It specifically distinguishes DHCA/cerebral protection from CPB, cardioplegia, ECMO and cooling after cardiac arrest; explanations of coagulopathy, arrhythmia and neurological consequences are essential.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.
rubric: **2 marks** — Defines systemic arrest under deep hypothermia and the operative rationale
**2 marks** — Explains reduced cerebral metabolism and duration-dependent ischaemic tolerance
**1 mark** — Explains cerebral-perfusion and temperature strategy without guaranteed safety
**3 marks** — Explains neurological, coagulation, rhythm and organ pathophysiological consequences
**2 marks** — Explains reperfusion/rewarming risks and distinguishes CPB/cardioplegia/ECMO

items.title: 2016.2 Q10: Considerations for successful weaning from bypass after CABG
items.q: Outline the considerations for successful weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass after coronary artery graft surgery.
items.model:
## Principle

Weaning is the **return of the native circulation and ventilation** once the heart and patient are ready. Prepare before the surgeon removes the clamp and complete a checklist.

## 1. Native circulation

- **Rate and rhythm:** sinus rhythm or pacing at 70 to 90 per minute; defibrillate or cardiovert if needed. The pacing wires should be tested (capture threshold under 5 mA); if conduction is intact, atrial pacing is preferred, and atrial wires help a hypertrophied or failing RV. Correct K (avoid hypo- and hyperkalaemia) and Mg, which also reduce postoperative AF.
- **Volume and MAP:** adequate preload by TOE and CVP; MAP above 65 with a vasopressor. Vasopressin gives less PVR rise and less AF than catecholamines. Vasoplegia is likelier with ACE inhibitors or ARB use, long bypass and poor ventricular function; milrinone worsens vasodilation.
- **Contractility and ischaemia:** good function on TOE, no new regional wall motion abnormality, graft flows checked.
- **De-airing** of the heart, vents off, cross-clamp off. Air in the anterior right coronary ostium is a classic cause of RV failure.
- **RV protection:** FiO2 1.0, no hypercarbia or acidosis, avoiding excessive tidal volume or PEEP; for patients with pulmonary hypertension or poor RV function start an inhaled pulmonary vasodilator (nitric oxide 10 to 20 ppm, up to 40) before bypass ends. Protamine can cause pulmonary hypertension, so give it slowly.

## 2. Native ventilation

Lungs **re-expanded** under vision (recruitment; check for pneumothorax or secretions), FiO2 1.0 and a working circuit before ventilation restarts.

## 3. Metabolic and haematological

- **Temperature** above 36 degrees (nasopharyngeal) with a small core-to-periphery gradient.
- **Acid-base, gases and electrolytes** normal; ionised calcium above 1.0.
- **Haemoglobin** adequate (about 70 to 80 g/L or above) and glucose controlled.
- **Coagulation:** maintain adequate heparin anticoagulation during CPB and the separation attempt. After stable separation/team agreement, reverse residual heparin with titrated protamine and assess haemostasis, platelets, fibrinogen and viscoelastic testing as indicated.

## 4. Anaesthesia and equipment

Adequate depth and analgesia, transducers zeroed, TOE ready, defibrillator pads, and inotropes, vasopressors and vasodilators (GTN, nitric oxide) prepared.

## 5. The process

Communicate with the surgeon and perfusionist; wean gradually (partial then full clamping of the venous line) watching the heart, pressures and TOE; have a failure plan: reinstitute bypass, optimise preload, rate, contractility and afterload, then IABP or mechanical support.

## Practical completion and examiner linkage

Agree readiness verbally with surgeon and perfusionist: repair/grafts complete, cross-clamp removed, reperfusion time adequate, de-airing satisfactory, cannulae and vents accounted for, lungs ventilated and monitoring reliable. Restore filling gradually while reducing pump flow and judge biventricular function, arterial pressure and systemic perfusion. Persistent abnormalities require a pause or return to full CPB, not repeated unsupported attempts. Continue anaesthesia through the oxygenator/TIVA transitions and verify drug delivery. Individualise MAP, heart rate and Hb to myocardial oxygen balance, comorbidity, bleeding and measured delivery; a fixed Hb threshold is not a substitute for assessment during active low-output ischaemia.

After separation, reassess graft territory wall motion, ventricular function and valves; correct residual lesions, then titrate protamine to residual heparin when the team agrees. Reassess after protamine and after sternal closure for RV compression, tamponade physiology or new low output. Handover pacing dependence/settings, vasoactive support, bleeding, gases/electrolytes and a rescue plan.

**Examiner linkage:** the 2016.2 report was located and read. The expected structure is restoration of native circulation, ventilation and correction of CPB disturbances, with ongoing anaesthesia. Rate, rhythm, volume, perfusion pressure, ventricular performance, gases, temperature and coagulation must all be addressed.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.
rubric: **3 marks** — Restores native rate/rhythm, filling, pressure and ventricular performance
**2 marks** — Restores ventilation/gas exchange and completes de-airing/graft assessment
**2 marks** — Corrects temperature, metabolic/electrolyte and oxygen-delivery disturbances
**1 mark** — Ensures anaesthetic delivery, equipment and communication
**2 marks** — Describes gradual separation, failure plan and post-separation reversal/haemostasis

items.title: 2012.2 Q3: Prerequisites for separation and causes of post-bypass hypotension
items.q: 1. What are the prerequisites for separation from standard cardiopulmonary bypass after uneventful coronary artery bypass surgery? (50%) 2. What are the likely causes of hypotension in the immediate post-separation period? (50%)
items.model:
## 1. Prerequisites for separation (50%)

**Native circulation and ventilation restored**
- **Rhythm and rate:** sinus or paced at 70 to 90 per minute (pacing capture threshold under 5 mA, wires tested), no block or ectopy.
- **Contractility and ischaemia:** good function and no new regional abnormality on TOE; grafts flowing; heart de-aired.
- **Volume and pressure:** adequate preload (CVP and TOE) and MAP above 65.
- **Lungs** re-expanded and ventilating with FiO2 1.0, no pneumothorax.

**Correction of the disturbances of surgery and bypass**
- **Temperature** above 36 degrees nasopharyngeal.
- **Acid-base and electrolytes:** pH, gases, K in the appropriate normal range, ionised calcium and magnesium.
- **Anaemia and coagulation:** haemoglobin 70 to 80 g/L or higher; adequate heparin maintained while on CPB; plan post-separation protamine and assess platelets/fibrinogen. Reversal is not a prerequisite to separation.

**Anaesthesia and equipment:** adequate depth, zeroed monitors, TOE, pacing, defibrillator, and drugs drawn up.

## 2. Causes of hypotension after separation (50%)

| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Pump failure** | LV stunning or ischaemia from graft problems or air; **RV failure** (air in the right coronary artery, pulmonary hypertension, prolonged bypass, inadequate protection); valve dysfunction |
| **Rate and rhythm** | Bradycardia, heart block, AF, ventricular arrhythmia |
| **Preload** | Hypovolaemia and bleeding, venous pooling from vasodilators, **tamponade**, tension pneumothorax, high PEEP |
| **Afterload** | **Vasoplegia** (bypass inflammation, ACE inhibitor or ARB use, prolonged bypass, milrinone), **protamine reaction**, anaphylaxis, sepsis |
| **Other** | Residual anaesthetic, acidosis, hypocalcaemia, hypothermia, LVOT obstruction (inotropes, hypovolaemia) |

**Protamine** can cause vasodilation and hypotension, pulmonary vasoconstriction with RV dysfunction, and anaphylaxis. Prior protamine reaction and protamine-containing insulin exposure matter. Fish allergy or vasectomy alone does not establish a contraindication. Slow infusion reduces dose-rate hypotension but does not prevent every severe immune or pulmonary reaction.

**Approach:** assess the complete shock phenotype: vasoplegia may coexist with low output, and other distributive states can also have high output. CI and SVR/SVRI must use correct units; non-indexed SVR = 80 × (MAP − CVP)/CO, whereas SVRI uses cardiac index. Use TOE and the PA catheter to separate causes. After cardiac surgery the femoral pressure often exceeds the radial in vasoplegia, so check a central pressure before treating a low radial reading. Treat the cause and communicate with the surgeon.

## Practical completion and examiner linkage

Agree readiness verbally with surgeon and perfusionist: repair/grafts complete, cross-clamp removed, reperfusion time adequate, de-airing satisfactory, cannulae and vents accounted for, lungs ventilated and monitoring reliable. Restore filling gradually while reducing pump flow and judge biventricular function, arterial pressure and systemic perfusion. Persistent abnormalities require a pause or return to full CPB, not repeated unsupported attempts. Continue anaesthesia through the oxygenator/TIVA transitions and verify drug delivery. Individualise MAP, heart rate and Hb to myocardial oxygen balance, comorbidity, bleeding and measured delivery; a fixed Hb threshold is not a substitute for assessment during active low-output ischaemia.

After separation, reassess graft territory wall motion, ventricular function and valves; correct residual lesions, then titrate protamine to residual heparin when the team agrees. Reassess after protamine and after sternal closure for RV compression, tamponade physiology or new low output. Handover pacing dependence/settings, vasoactive support, bleeding, gases/electrolytes and a rescue plan.

**Examiner linkage:** the 2012.2 report was located and read. The expected structure is restoration of native circulation, ventilation and correction of CPB disturbances, with ongoing anaesthesia. For part 2, categorise hypotension as pump, rhythm/rate, preload and afterload, including mixed causes; allocate answer time 50:50.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.
rubric: **2 marks** — Prerequisites: native circulation, filling, rhythm and graft/TOE assessment
**1 mark** — Prerequisites: functioning native ventilation
**2 marks** — Prerequisites: metabolic/temperature/Hb, ongoing anaesthesia and anticoagulation plan
**2 marks** — Hypotension: LV/RV pump and rate/rhythm causes
**2 marks** — Hypotension: preload/obstructive and low-SVR causes
**1 mark** — Includes protamine reaction/structural lesions and mixed-shock assessment

items.title: 2008.2 Q12: Intra-aortic balloon pump: indications, contraindications and optimisation
items.q: List the indications and contra-indications for the use of an intra-aortic balloon pump. Describe how its performance is optimised.
items.model:
## Principle

A 30 to 50 mL helium-filled balloon sits in the **descending thoracic aorta**, **inflating in diastole and deflating just before systole**. The 2022.1 examiners' two core points are: diastolic inflation raises aortic root diastolic pressure and so **coronary perfusion**, and systolic deflation lowers **afterload**, improving myocardial oxygen supply against demand. Augmentation of output is modest (about 0.5 to 1 L/min), and it requires useful native ejection; rhythm irregularity makes timing harder but does not always preclude modern arrhythmia-triggered support. The examiners noted poor knowledge of the cardiac cycle, so describe timing against the dicrotic notch.

## Indications

- Cardiogenic shock or severe failure awaiting recovery or definitive treatment.
- **Failure to wean from bypass**, or low output after cardiac surgery; the Blue Book also supports it in RV failure to promote right coronary flow.
- Post-infarction: refractory angina, ventricular arrhythmia, **mechanical complications** (acute mitral regurgitation, VSD) awaiting surgery.
- High-risk revascularisation (left main disease, poor LV function), bridge to transplant or VAD, and LV unloading with VA-ECMO.

## Contraindications

- **Moderate/severe aortic regurgitation:** augmentation increases regurgitant flow; even mild AR requires assessment rather than treating every degree as an automatic absolute contraindication.
- **Aortic dissection or aneurysm**, and severe aorto-iliac or peripheral vascular disease.
- Relative: coagulopathy, sepsis, uncontrolled tachyarrhythmia, bleeding.

## Optimising performance

- **Position:** tip just distal to the left subclavian artery (about 2 cm below the aortic knob on chest X-ray).
- **Balloon volume:** full inflation for the patient's size.
- **Timing (1:2 mode):** inflation at the **dicrotic notch** (aortic valve closure); too early closes the valve prematurely and reduces stroke volume, too late loses augmentation. Deflation **just before systole**, at end-diastole; late deflation raises afterload. A good trace shows a diastolic peak above the unassisted systolic peak and an assisted end-diastolic pressure below the unassisted one.
- **Trigger:** ECG or arterial waveform; regular rhythm and rate (AF, tachycardia and pacing artefact degrade timing).
- Maintain MAP and preload, treat arrhythmias, keep the leg straight, anticoagulate as appropriate, and check limb perfusion, platelets and haemolysis. Trials in infarct shock (IABP-SHOCK II) showed no mortality benefit .

## Physiological and practical optimisation

Coronary driving pressure is approximately aortic diastolic pressure minus LV diastolic pressure. Inflation after aortic closure increases the first term; rapid pre-systolic deflation reduces aortic impedance, LV wall stress and myocardial oxygen demand, potentially reducing LVEDP. Benefit varies with balloon volume, position, aortic compliance, rhythm and native stroke volume; it is not a fixed pump-delivered L/min. Assess assisted systolic and end-diastolic pressures against unassisted beats, ECG and systemic perfusion, not diastolic peak height alone.

Check catheter position using imaging and manufacturer landmarks, preserving left subclavian and renal/visceral perfusion; use the balloon length/volume appropriate to patient anatomy. Review helium supply, tubing, trigger quality and alarms. Adjust ECG/pressure or pacer-specific triggering with the device specialist; do not select an ungated internal trigger in a beating patient indiscriminately. Check insertion site bleeding, distal limb perfusion, platelet count, haemolysis and renal function. Blood in helium tubing suggests rupture: stop the device and obtain urgent specialist removal, following the device protocol. Anticoagulation is individualised to thrombosis, bleeding, duration and local practice.

**Examiner linkage:** the actual 2008.2 report was located and read: indications 3 marks, contraindications 2, optimisation 3 and global assessment 2. Its AR warning should be explained physiologically. Contemporary AMI-shock trial evidence does not support routine IABP for every infarct-related shock patient, but selected mechanical complications/postcardiotomy rescue remain distinct indications.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.
rubric: **3 marks** — Lists relevant selected ischaemic, shock, mechanical and postoperative indications
**2 marks** — Explains AR/aortic/access contraindications and relative bleeding risk
**3 marks** — Optimises timing, trigger, position, volume and patient physiology
**2 marks** — Explains augmentation/unloading, monitors benefit/complications and qualifies routine AMI evidence

items.title: 2026.1 Q7: Epicardial pacing in complete heart block before separation from bypass
items.q: A patient is in complete heart block prior to separation from cardiopulmonary bypass. a. Outline the programming considerations for epicardial pacing in this patient. (30%) b. Describe your approach to troubleshooting intermittent capture of the pacemaker in this patient who is pacing-dependent in the ICU. (70%)
items.model:
## a) Programming considerations

**Mode.** The patient is in complete heart block, so the ventricle must be paced. With atrial and ventricular wires and a sinus atrium, **DDD** (AV sequential) is best, because atrial systole contributes up to 25% of ventricular filling and AV sequential pacing generally improves ejection; AAI is relatively contraindicated in high-grade block. With ventricular wires only, or AF, use **VVI**. On weaning from bypass, an asynchronous mode (**DOO or VOO**) is acceptable while diathermy is in use and the chest is open, then change to a demand mode (DDD) afterwards, because asynchronous pacing risks R-on-T.

**Rate.** About **70 to 90 per minute**, chosen because the intrinsic rate is absent and a stunned, oedematous ventricle has a relatively fixed stroke volume so output is rate dependent; individualise to the output and ischaemia. **AV interval** 160 to 200 ms.

**Output.** Measure the **capture threshold** with experienced assistance, continuous ECG/arterial monitoring and effective backup pacing. In a dependent patient, do not deliberately provoke prolonged loss of capture to test the system. Under 5 mA is acceptable, 5 to 10 mA warrants discussion with the surgeon about new wires, over 10 mA is unacceptable. During supervised wire assessment/closure the surgeon may use a specific threshold-check protocol; the dependent ICU patient needs a reliable safety margin, commonly at least twice the measured capture threshold, with reassessment as thresholds change. **Sensitivity:** the sensing threshold can only be measured if there is an intrinsic rhythm, which a block may not allow; a dependent patient may need an asynchronous mode or close monitoring. Confirm mechanical capture on the arterial waveform.

## b) Intermittent capture in a pacing-dependent ICU patient

**Safety first.** Is the patient stable? If bradycardic or hypotensive, restore pacing immediately and use adrenaline or isoprenaline as a monitored bridge if required; atropine may be ineffective in complete/infranodal block and must not delay pacing, apply **transcutaneous pacing** pads, call for help, and start CPR if asystolic. Keep a defibrillator at the bedside.

**Systematic approach: patient, leads, generator.**

| Domain | Causes | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Patient** | Rising threshold (oedema, ischaemia, fibrosis; thresholds vary most in the first 48 hours), hypothermia (aim above 36 degrees), hypo or hyperkalaemia, acidosis, pericardial effusion or tamponade, drugs | Correct K, Mg, pH and temperature; echocardiogram; review drugs |
| **Leads** | Wire migration or fracture, loose connection at the wire, cable or box | Check from patient to box: wires at the skin, wire-to-cable, cable-to-box; replace the cable; try another wire or pole |
| **Generator** | Box off, flat battery, wrong mode, **output too close to threshold** so respiratory variation causes intermittent capture; oversensing (shivering, T waves, diathermy) inhibiting output; undersensing | Perform a full pacing check; raise output; reduce sensitivity setting for undersensing or raise it for oversensing; correct shivering; use an asynchronous mode if inhibited; change box and battery |

Intermittent pacing may also reflect a native escape rhythm competing with the paced rate: assess with experienced staff and a backup method; do not lower the rate or stop pacing unsafely in a dependent patient. Adjust the pacing rate only while preserving perfusion.

**Alternative modalities** if capture cannot be restored: transcutaneous pacing, a **transvenous wire**, or new epicardial wires; electrophysiology review, and a permanent pacemaker if block persists. If an R-on-T arrest occurs, pause the pacemaker, defibrillate, and follow cardiac surgical life support; do not leave a poorly sensing system running on a ward.

## Distinguish capture, sensing and output failure

**No pacing spikes** suggests inhibition/oversensing, cable/generator failure or an inappropriate rate/mode; **spikes without QRS** indicate failure to capture; **QRS without an arterial pulse** means absent effective mechanical output and requires resuscitation/diagnosis. Increase output promptly for capture failure while correcting causes. For oversensing, a higher numerical mV setting makes the box less sensitive; for undersensing, a lower mV setting makes it more sensitive. Do not assume every intermittent beat is a lead problem. Replace faulty equipment without interrupting effective pacing. Only measure a sensing threshold when intrinsic activity is present and doing so is safe.

DDD requires reliable atrial and ventricular sensing and is not automatically the safest mode with poor atrial sensing. Reassess rate and AV interval against arterial pressure, filling and ischaemia, rather than treating 70–90/min or 160–200 ms as universal prescriptions. Continue continuous monitored care, record mode/rate/output/sensitivity/thresholds and arrange specialist review before ICU discharge.

**Examiner linkage:** the 2026.1 report requires a justified mode/rate, a structured patient–leads–generator assessment, and alternative pacing to ensure safety; rate justification and rescue alternatives were common omissions.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.
rubric: **3 marks** — Justifies mode/rate/output/sensitivity/AV interval and confirms mechanical capture safely (part a)
**2 marks** — Stabilises the dependent patient and provides backup pacing
**3 marks** — Systematically assesses patient, leads and generator with capture versus sensing distinctions
**2 marks** — Corrects the fault and provides transcutaneous/transvenous/new epicardial alternatives and specialist follow-up

items.title: 2022.1 Q8: IABP pressure trace at 1:2 augmentation
items.q: Name A–F on the supplied aortic pressure trace as 1:2 IABP support begins (30%). Explain the objectives of counterpulsation and the physiology producing its effects (70%).
items.model:
## Part 1: identify the trace (30%)

| Label | Identification | Explain its position in the cycle |
|---|---|---|
| A | Unassisted systolic peak at commencement of the illustrated sequence | The report accepts **assisted/unassisted systole**, reflecting ambiguity at the start of augmentation |
| B | Dicrotic notch | Aortic valve closure, timing reference for balloon inflation |
| C | Unassisted aortic end-diastolic pressure | Pressure just before the next unassisted systolic rise |
| D | Diastolic augmentation | Raised aortic diastolic pressure after balloon inflation |
| E | Assisted aortic end-diastolic pressure | Reduced pressure after rapid deflation before the next LV ejection |
| F | Assisted systolic peak | Systole following deflation, against reduced aortic impedance |

The notch is not the onset of the QRS or the balloon peak. Explain aortic events against the pressure cycle rather than guessing ECG labels. A 1:2 assist ratio allows comparison of adjacent assisted and unassisted beats when safe.

## Part 2: aims and physiology (70%)

An IABP is a balloon in the descending thoracic aorta, positioned distal to the left subclavian artery and above major visceral branches. Helium permits rapid inflation/deflation. It is **counterpulsation**, not a forward-flow replacement for native cardiac output.

**Improve myocardial oxygen supply:** inflation immediately after aortic valve closure displaces blood proximally and increases aortic-root diastolic pressure. Coronary perfusion driving pressure is approximately aortic diastolic pressure minus LV end-diastolic pressure; increasing the former can improve coronary flow, particularly in the LV whose systolic intramyocardial compression limits perfusion. Distal displacement also affects systemic diastolic flow. The height of augmentation depends on anatomy, balloon size, vascular compliance and haemodynamics.

**Reduce myocardial oxygen demand and improve ejection:** rapid deflation immediately before systole reduces aortic pressure/impedance seen by the LV. Reduced afterload and LV wall stress facilitate ejection, may lower LV filling pressure and oxygen demand, and can improve the supply–demand balance. Assisted end-diastolic pressure should be lower than the unassisted value; assisted systolic pressure may be lower because unloading has occurred. A high augmented peak alone does not prove correct deflation timing or improved systemic perfusion.

**Practical aims:** stabilisation as a bridge while treating the underlying lesion, selected difficult separation/low output after CPB, refractory ischaemia or mechanical post-MI complications pending definitive treatment. Support is modest and depends on native ejection, not a guaranteed extra litre of pump flow. IABP does not oxygenate blood or provide full RV/biventricular support.

Inflating before aortic closure opposes ejection; late inflation loses diastolic benefit. Early deflation loses the useful diastolic pressure and may reduce unloading benefit; late deflation impedes systole. Optimise trigger, position and balloon volume and assess limb perfusion, lactate, urine output and cardiac function, not the trace alone. Significant AR can be worsened by increased diastolic pressure, and dissection/severe access disease may preclude placement. Routine AMI-shock survival benefit has not been demonstrated; selection and an exit plan matter.

**Examiner linkage:** the report’s two central requirements are increased diastolic aortic-root pressure/coronary perfusion and reduced afterload with improved oxygen supply–demand. Poor cardiac-cycle terminology was a common failure.

> **Marking note:** educator-created 10-mark schedule, not an official ANZCA rubric. Award partial credit within each domain; a numerical total does not establish an ANZCA pass.
rubric: **3 marks** — Correctly identifies A–F, including the report’s accepted ambiguity at A
**3 marks** — Explains diastolic inflation, aortic-root pressure and coronary driving pressure
**2 marks** — Explains pre-systolic deflation, wall stress/afterload and oxygen demand
**1 mark** — Relates physiology to bridge aims and limited native-ejection-dependent support
**1 mark** — Explains timing errors, suitability and assessment of benefit
